sources.news_title: US, China, Russia issue peace declaration after first ever summit
sources.text:
SHENZHEN - The much-anticipated trilateral meeting of US President Donald Trump, China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin concluded with a “peace declaration” focusing on UN reforms, fuel supplies and reducing nuclear risks, but without mentioning the wars in Ukraine and Iran.
Against the backdrop of powerful, historic imagery of the three global powers, the summit appears not to have produced immediate diplomatic breakthroughs, ending without joint statements, despite strong declarations by the leaders at the beginning, and with US President Trump immediately departing the venue for the airport.
A video released by the Kremlin showed Putin telling Xi, “Thank you for organising this, I don’t think anyone even expected everything to go so well,” as Xi accompanied him to the car after the summit.
Chinese state media and Russian officials released a joint statement called the “trilateral peace declaration,” in which Xi, Putin and Trump said that they are committed to upholding strategic stability and international security.
According to the statement, China, Russia and the US agreed on UN reforms, boosting production and supply of petroleum products, engaging in dialogue to reduce nuclear risks, and “respect for the immunity of state officials and opposition to the ICC and similar institutions abusing their jurisdiction.”
The declaration makes no explicit reference to Ukraine, Iran, North Korea or other issues.
Going into the meeting and in his pre-summit bilateral talks with Putin and Xi, Trump said he wanted to talk about reducing nuclear stockpiles, Russia’s war in Ukraine and “all of the problems that are really being discussed in the world.”
With the Russian state apparatus projecting Putin’s participation in the summit as a major legitimisation win, the Russian president was the first of the three leaders to hold a news conference for Russian media after the meeting.
The Russian president said that the summit was an “important chapter in the history of diplomacy” and that “the discussion took place in a completely open atmosphere, which allowed us to understand one another better,” adding that “overall, it was very useful.”
Putin said that he and Trump have a “certain closeness” in their views and “on civilisational values.”
Addressing the topic of Russia’s ongoing all-out war in Ukraine, Putin said that Kyiv and Europe are not yet ready to make compromises to end it.
At the start of the summit, Putin said that Russia’s war in Ukraine would be part of the talks, stating that “we have shared interests in Ukraine.” However, after the meeting, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told the Russian media that Ukraine was not “the central topic” at the summit.
“Russia, the US and China are united not only by their status as victorious nations in World War II, but also by their responsibility for maintaining international peace,” Putin said before the talks.
China’s president Xi Jinping described the summit as “positive, constructive and fruitful,” according to a Chinese state media report.
According to the report, Xi said they agreed that major powers should take the legitimate security concerns of all countries seriously, stating that “as long as dialogue does not stop, doors remain open, there is hope for peace.”
“The seeds planted at today’s trilateral meeting will surely take root, sprout, blossom and bear fruit,” Xi was quoted as saying.
The three leaders posed for a family photo without shaking hands as they started their summit and made no joint statements when it concluded after an hour and 20 minutes.
During joint statements before the summit, Trump said the three global powers “are making history” as they have “great responsibilities to solve problems that affect the entire planet.”
Xi joined Trump in saying their summit “has groundbreaking significance”, adding that “the world is at peace when great powers live in harmony,” calling on the three countries to “abandon Cold War mentality, not pursue decoupling and breaking chains”.
Xi said some 80 years ago, the three countries fought shoulder to shoulder and achieved great victories, bringing peace and tranquility to the world.
He said China, Russia and the US should shoulder the responsibility of upholding and improving the post-World War II international order with the UN at its core.
“The three countries should work together to address global challenges,” and that “major countries should respect each other, coexist peacefully,” Xi said before the talks began, concluding that they “can strengthen coordination to safeguard global energy supply chain stability. “Adversity reveals true responsibility.”
Just as the summit was starting, China’s state news agency published a statement from Xi saying that “nuclear weapons should be comprehensively banned and thoroughly destroyed, building a nuclear-free world.”
In the statement, Xi described nuclear weapons as “the sword of Damocles hanging over humanity”, and that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.”
In his opening statements, Trump said that the “three countries are uniquely positioned to discuss nuclear weapons” and “to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world.”
“Too often past leaders avoided talking to leaders they had disagreements with,” Trump added.
The US and Chinese presidents met bilaterally earlier on Thursday in their third substantial meeting this year.
During the meeting, Trump said that the US and China want to help end the war in Ukraine, stating that “we’re looking to both help with respect to the war with Russia and Ukraine.”
The US president praised their friendship and their shared interest in having oil shipped through the Strait of Hormuz, which has become a key site of attacks in the Iran war.
Xi said that relations between the US and China have been “generally stable and improved” during Trump’s presidency.
“The efforts you have made are there for all to see and will go down in history,” Xi said.
Trump also met Putin ahead of the trilateral, stating that “we’ve had a great relationship for many years.”
Their meeting marks the first time the leaders have held talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal to ease Russia’s war in Ukraine.
“Wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start,” Trump said as he greeted Putin, saying “Who is he? He’s my friend.”
The summit has stoked fears that the three powerful men may seek to divide the globe into spheres of influence, for example by making decisions that affect Ukraine’s fate over the heads of Kyiv or Europe.
France’s Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot reacted to the French media after the Shenzhen summit by saying that “these three leaders fundamentally disagree on everything, so they cannot agree on anything.”
“As for this photograph that has generated so much discussion, it isn’t quite a photograph of the world’s three greatest powers, because the world’s three greatest powers are the United States, of course, China and the European Union,” the French foreign minister told RTL radio

sources.news_title: The Trump-Xi-Putin Summit: A New World Order Rebranded?
sources.text:
The Trump-Xi-Putin Summit: A New World Order Rebranded?
American, Chinese, and Russian heads of state met up in China to talk about world peace. U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin discussed nuclear disarmament, global oil supplies, Ukraine, and reforming the United Nations.
The historic summit came about after Putin reportedly suggested it as a way to hash out plans for ending the Ukraine war. There’s no indication of any progress on that front, and some European leaders have criticized that part of the agenda because it didn’t include the leader of the country Russia is warring against.
Replacing the U.S.-led Order?
A common mainstream talking point is that the summit is more evidence that the unipolar international order, the U.S.-led one, is being replaced by a multipolar one. The Wall Street Journal reported:
The first-ever gathering of the American, Chinese and Russian leaders was a further sign of the end of a unipolar world order dominated by the U.S. — and suggested that what might replace it is a more uncertain, and unsettled, reality.
An analysis in The New York Times framed the meeting as the autocrats taking advantage of a flailing United States. Edward Wong of the Times wrote:
[Xi and Putin] and their nations are transforming the world order by usurping the role of America as the sole superpower, the undisputed victor of the Cold War. Both Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin share a sense of historical grievance shaped by the expansion and dominance of U.S. power in the more than three decades since the fall of the Soviet Union. But from Mr. Xi’s perspective, that situation is evolving, and, rightly or wrongly, he has embraced a vision of America in terminal decline.
For the Eastern leaders, this might be an ideal opportunity to dislodge the U.S. from their neighborhood. Putin and Xi want the United States out of their sphere of influence, and Trump wants Russia and China out of the Western hemisphere. As the Journal noted:
Putin wants Washington to stay out of his way in Ukraine. Xi wants the U.S. to accept his claim that self-ruled Taiwan belongs to China. And Trump has made pushing Chinese and Russian influence out of the Western Hemisphere a central element of his so-called “Donroe Doctrine” to reassert U.S. dominance in the region.
Xi confirmed in a post-summit statement that the Chinese want complete control over their part of the world:
It is important to respect one another, seek common ground while reserving differences, and pursue shared development, including respecting one another’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, the social systems and development paths of their own choice, and their respective core interests and major concerns. It is always important not to interfere in other countries’ domestic affairs or each other’s internal affairs.
While Trump dealt a big blow to China and Russia when he conquered Venezuela, America’s top intelligence agency has only intensified the war it’s waging on Russia through Ukraine, and there is no indication whatsoever that the U.S. would ever consider abandoning Taiwan, especially given its valuable status as a leading semiconductor producer.
The Nuclear Issue
The most pressing issue the three leaders discussed was nuclear weapons. The summit didn’t yield any binding agreements; the point was to get the world’s largest nuclear arsenals talking.
The longer the Ukraine war rages on, the more people grow concerned about a nuclear exchange. The Russians have repeatedly threatened to use nukes if they deem it necessary, and the Western European powers have shown they have no intention of dialing back military support for Ukraine.
The White House said in a statement following the summit that “the three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.”
Trump also held a chummy bilateral meeting with Putin. “We’ve had a great relationship for many years,” Trump told reporters before sitting down with Putin. “We’ve known each other for a long time, and I think a lot of wonderful things can come of this.”
Putin’s comments suggest the talks weren’t designed to generate any major decisions on Ukraine:
The mere existence of agreements is always better than having no agreements at all, even if these agreements are ultimately not fully implemented. … The [meeting] does not set any overarching goals, it does not aim to subordinate anyone to our decisions, it is a format for finding mutually acceptable solutions for the three of us, primarily in the field of security.
“Safeguarding World Peace”
World peace was the official theme of the summit, entitled “Safeguarding World Peace and Promoting Strategic Stability in Major-Country Relations.” The Chinese framed the meeting as one between nations that are not so different. “More than 80 years ago, China, Russia and the United States, the key anti-fascist forces in the world, fought shoulder to shoulder and achieved great victories, winning peace and tranquility for the world,” says a statement by China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs. “China, Russia and the United States should be partners and friends. We should not go for conflict or confrontation among us, and should hold the line on peaceful coexistence.”
The Russian leader seconded that. “Our three nations are united not only by the status of victors in the Second World War but mainly by our responsibility for maintaining international peace,” Putin said at the meeting.
The pitch sounds reasonable. Xi is proposing mutual respect and cooperation between the power nations for the sake of global peace and stability. And the leaders say multipolarity is the way to achieve that.
A Stronger International Order
But there is also some concern that the real aim, or the trajectory that would play out, is a shift not necessarily to multipolarity, but to global order with a façade makeover. In comments on the meeting, Xi appears to imply a desire for a global order with China at the top. Per the Ministry of Foreign Affairs:
President Xi underlined the point that humanity, living in the same global village, is a community with a shared future. In this global village, major countries shoulder special responsibilities. … China, Russia and the United States, all major countries and permanent members of the U.N. Security Council, should set good examples, work together to meet global challenges, jointly uphold world peace and stability, and make greater contribution to the progress of humanity.
The United Nations, created to serve as the nervous system of an emerging world government, has suffered significant blows in trust and viability. Between the Trump administration’s persistent interruption in fee payments and decades of reports of abuse by the organization, it should’ve been disbanded years ago. But the White House reiterated that it would rather “reform the UN so that the UN can respond more effectively to global challenges and conform to its fundamental mission of international peace and security.” Putin agrees. He said, “Given that all our countries are permanent members of the UN Security Council, we naturally discussed the possibility of reforming the UN and making it work better.”
Before the summit took place, Council on Foreign Relations senior fellow Charles Kupchan suggested that cooperation between these three countries comes with the potential to create a stronger international order. He argues for a new global body, a “global concert — an informal steering group of great powers modeled on the nineteenth-century Concert of Europe.” Kupchan’s vision is essentially a different, more powerful version of the UN:
In addition to the United States, China, and Russia, a new concert would include India, Japan, the European Union, and representatives from Africa, Latin America, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Concerts sacrifice representation for efficacy and give only the geopolitically influential states that must be there a seat at the table. They set aside ideological differences and bring democracies and autocracies together to focus on international cooperation. Because concerts eschew binding, enforceable procedures in favor of informal consensus building, they can succeed when formal institutions such as the UN Security Council are paralyzed and when the United States wavers in its commitment to rules-based multilateralism.
Foreign Entanglements Endanger Sovereignty
Friendly relations for the sake of peace and prosperity are good, even when they involve autocrats. George Washington made this pitch in his Farewell Address, essentially saying we should strive to be at peace and do business with every nation willing to reciprocate that good will. And there was no shortage of dictators, kings, and other kinds of tyrants when he left the presidency. But Washington also warned about foreign entanglements. He understood those kinds of arrangements would dampen American sovereignty and individual liberty. The UN, the League of Nations, and the European Union have profoundly reduced the sovereignty of their member nations. The same thing will happen in any other international body with members and rules.
Xi is right: National leaders should strive to foster peace and trade. He’s also correct in saying that nations should stay out of each other’s affairs. And they should certainly talk to one another and agree on mutually beneficial policies. But this should be done through bilateral agreements, not coercive international bodies that usurp national sovereignty.

sources.news_title: Trump, Xi, Putin Pledge Nuclear Talks; Open the Door for Future Dialogue
sources.text:
by Sarah Roderick-Fitch
President Donald Trump wrapped up an historic trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, flexing their power to address a handful of issues, including nuclear arms.
The meeting between the three leaders overshadowed the Asian Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, and the leaders released a joint statement.
The three leaders agreed on four points, which they contend are a commitment towards “maintaining strategic stability and international security.”
The first point calls on the three countries to help “reform” the United Nations “so that the UN can respond more effectively to global challenges and conform to its fundamental mission of international peace and security.”
The second point calls on the three nations to increase production and supply of “refined petroleum products for the benefits of all nations.”
The third point addresses the International Criminial Court, with a commitment to reeling in the court’s power by ensuring of “state consent and respect for immunities of State officials,” and “similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction.”
The final point addresses nuclear proliferation, reaffirming that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.” The three nations have agreed to future talks on “reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.”
During the trilateral meeting, Trump expressed a duty of the three nations to communicate.
“We have a special responsibility to maintain open, respectful and productive dialogue on issues impacting not just our people, but the entire planet,” said the president. No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech.”
Trump also touched on Iran, as the U.S. maintains a full naval blockade on Iranian ports and is now blocking land routes.
“Both the United States and China have an interest in ensuring that energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz and that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon. We both feel that very strongly,” he underscored.
The president briefly touched on the ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine, with Trump looking to Xi to help bring the war to an end.
Trump announced Thursday that he will be hosting a press conference Friday at the White House to discuss details of his trip, in which he is expected to address trade deals as well as international security.
– – –
Sarah Roderick-Fitch is The Center Square’s Washington D.C. Bureau Chief. She has previously worked as an editor, and has been a contributing writer for several publications. In addition to writing and editing, Sarah spent nearly a decade working for non-profit, public policy organizations in the Washington, DC area.

sources.news_title: Trump, Xi, and Putin pledge to boost oil production
sources.text:
The leaders of the US, China, and Russia vowed to increase supplies of refined petroleum for the “benefit of all nations,” following a rare trilateral summit that yielded little in the way of meaningful breakthroughs.
The pledge, which barely moved oil prices, could prove difficult to bring to fruition amid ongoing wars in the Middle East and Ukraine that have choked off crude oil supplies.
Moscow’s refining capacity, in particular, has been damaged by Kyiv’s aerial bombardment, while the growing risk of US escalatory action against Iran threatens to further disrupt oil flows. The International Energy Agency warned this week that the Iran war’s disruptions had “permanently altered the appetite in many countries for imported oil,” The New York Times wrote.

sources.news_title: BOOM! Trump, Xi, and Putin Make History in Shenzhen — The “Ask” for Farmers and a Declaration Toward Peace
sources.text:
President Donald J. Trump departed Shenzhen on Thursday after a marathon of summit diplomacy that resulted in the first-ever face-to-face meeting between the leaders of the United States, China, and Russia. The day concluded with a written declaration toward peace, a direct challenge to the globalist establishment, and a reminder to Xi Jinping that the days of America getting shafted on trade are officially over.
While the mainstream media obsesses over palace intrigue, President Trump was busy rewriting the rules of engagement with two of the world's most adversarial powers. The three leaders stood shoulder-to-shoulder against a blue backdrop reading "China-Russia-US Shenzhen summit," presenting a visual that the corrupt Washington establishment said could never happen. Trump stood to Xi's left, Putin to his right. It was a picture of raw power—the kind that scares the hell out of war hawks and globalists who profit from endless conflict.
The "Ask": America First in Action
During his bilateral sit-down with Xi Jinping at Kylin Villa, President Trump did not mince words. Surrounded by the flags of both nations, Trump thanked Xi for an "incredible warm welcome" but immediately pivoted to the economic betrayal of the past.
"I'm going to ask him to do some more for our farmers," Trump stated, calling the old U.S.-China relationship "very lopsided."
That is not a suggestion. That is a demand. For too long, American farmers and manufacturers have been forced to eat the cost of bad trade deals signed by uniparty hacks who cared more about their corporate donors than the American worker. Trump told Xi directly that past presidents "didn't do their job." That is what strength looks like; it is the complete antithesis of the Biden-era weakness that invited aggression abroad and poverty at home.
Peace Through Strength, Not Surrender
The centerpiece of the day was the trilateral session, which the White House confirmed as the first of its kind. Trump, Xi, and Putin gathered in a room dripping with chandeliers to discuss the heavy issues the media said were unsolvable. Trump looked at the two leaders and declared, "we are really making history." He raised the issues of denuclearization and the war in Ukraine—not as a beggar, but as a negotiator representing the world's strongest economy.
Earlier in the day, Trump had a pull-aside with Putin, walking toward the Russian leader and calling him "my friend" while predicting "wonderful things" could come from the meeting. While the Left will scream at the optics, patriots understand the assignment. Talking to your adversaries prevents World War III. The three leaders signed a declaration committing the permanent Security Council members to strategic stability, stable energy flows, and UN reform. In short, Trump is draining the swamp on a global scale.
Trump also used his platform at the APEC plenary to tout the roaring American comeback. He laid bare the facts for the world to hear: inflation is running below two percent for the last three months, trade deals are coming, and America will not be suffocated by AI regulation that benefits China. "The United States has been a Pacific power for hundreds of years," Trump reminded the room. He pledged to block any bureaucratic red tape that stifles American industry, ensuring the "super intelligence" revolution is won by the Stars and Stripes, not the CCP.
As the President stepped onto Air Force One and the wheels went up, the contrast with the previous administration could not have been starker. Instead of weakness and apology tours, we have strength, dialogue, and results. The Shenzhen summit proves that when you put an American businessman in charge instead of a career politician, you get peace deals instead of forever wars and demands for farmers instead of empty rhetoric.

sources.news_title: Trump China trip: Iran and Ukraine not in 'peace declaration' and more takeaways
sources.text:
President Donald Trump is headed back to Washington after a historic trilateral meeting with presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia — the first-ever sitdown between the three global superpowers — with no tangible diplomatic breakthroughs in hand.
Following their meeting, the three leaders released what was described as a symbolic four-point “peace declaration,” focusing on reform at the United Nations, oil supply, nuclear risk reduction and opposition to what it called the International Criminal Court’s “jurisdiction abuse.”
ABC News has reached out to the ICC for comment.
The symbolic peace declaration made no mention of Russia’s war with Ukraine, which is in its fifth year, or the war with Iran. Both Russia and China have faced accusations by U.S. and European officials of providing satellite imagery and broader intelligence support to Iran, accusations both countries have denied.
Trump left Shenzhen without taking questions from reporters after the meeting but announced in a post on his social media platform while traveling back to Washington that he would hold a news conference at the White House on Friday.
Here are takeaways from Trump’s trip:
On denuclearization
The three leaders affirmed their commitment that nuclear war should never be fought but announced no commitments to reduce their respective nuclear arsenals.
Trump had insisted nuclear arms control be a central topic of the summit.
“As the world’s three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used,” Trump said in brief remarks ahead of the meeting. “The power is unbelievable, unthinkable.”
“It’s not an easy thing to do — give them up,” Trump said.
Trump also used the issue of nuclear proliferation to defend the U.S. war with Iran, repeating his assertion that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon.
“It’s also vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world. That’s what we’re doing in Iran. We’re not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon,” he said.
In a joint statement released following the meeting, the three leaders said they had an “in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation” and “committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security.”
Trump, Xi, and Putin said the three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
On Ukraine
The “peace declaration” released after the meeting made no mention of Russia’s war in Ukraine or the U.S.-led war in Iran.
“We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine, and we already have. President Putin and I have had a long discussion today for quite a while. That’s what pretty much what the discussion was about, and I think things are happening,” Trump said.
For his part, Putin briefly commented on his escalating war in Ukraine during opening remarks.
“Our countries have numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine. We discussed this yesterday with the Chairman of the People’s Republic of China and today at the initiative of the U.S. president, we devoted significant attention to this during our bilateral meeting,” the Russian president said, speaking through a translator.
On stable energy flows
The leaders also declared they plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products “for the benefit of all nations” while also reaffirming the importance of the stable flow of energy.
The oil market has been roiled in the nine months of the U.S.’s war with Iran, with the critical waterway through which a fifth of the world’s oil supplies has transited under constant threat. Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities have further exacerbated global energy flows.
There were no signs upon conclusion of their meeting that Trump secured any agreements from Xi or Putin to help solve the Iran conflict.
The International Criminal Court
Trump also highlighted that the three would discuss the International Criminal Court, the international body that works to uphold international law and prosecute war crimes. The Trump administration has targeted the ICC and its judges with sanctions and has sharply criticized the body.
“In another area of potential cooperation between us, I’ll be suggesting ways to protect our nation’s sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction,” Trump said in his opening remarks.
As part of the peace declaration, the three heads of state “recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction.”

by Reuters and Algemeiner Staff
Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US and Russian counterparts Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin agreed on a symbolic “peace declaration” at an unprecedented three-way summit on Thursday and reaffirmed that nuclear war should never be fought, but announced no plans for arms control talks long sought by Trump.
A joint declaration released by the world’s three biggest nuclear powers capped a three-day diplomatic swing by Trump through Asia that produced few tangible victories, despite his repeated boasts about making history and brokering peace.
Instead, the trip raised fresh questions among US allies about his increasingly close relationships with Xi, and with Putin, who continues to wage war with Ukraine.
The powers “reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought” and added that they would “conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation of nuclear weapons,” without giving a time frame.
But the statement made no mention of any negotiations on a trilateral nuclear arms reduction treaty, something Trump has pushed since his first term and that China has consistently rejected, arguing that its arsenal is much smaller than those of the other powers.
Daryl Kimball, executive director of the US-based Arms Control Association, called the reaffirmation that a nuclear war should not be fought “positive,” but added, “We need much more than rhetoric. We need action on disarmament diplomacy.”
Trump referred to nuclear weapons at the start of the meeting, saying: “It’s not an easy thing to do – give them up.”
The leaders also pledged to advance reforms of the United Nations, to increase supplies of fuel products for all countries, and to uphold the immunity enjoyed by state officials in international courts.
The declaration made no mention of Russia’s war in Ukraine, or Trump‘s conflict with Iran, and in a news conference afterwards, Putin acknowledged it did not set ambitious goals and added that nobody would be forced to comply with its decisions.
The reference to immunity of state officials came more than three years after the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Putin and other Russian officials over alleged war crimes in Ukraine. Moscow rejects the allegations.
“The pushback against international norms and courts is the most interesting aspect,” said Jonathan Eyal, international director at the Royal United Services Institute think-tank in London. “The big powers dictate, the small powers suffer.”
Eyal said Putin had been a winner from the summit and “gained credibility and escape from pariah status,” while Trump “gained a photo opportunity he didn’t need.”
Trump told NBC after the meeting that the summit “went great.”
“I think it was a 12. On a scale of zero to 10, I think it was a 12,” he said. “Fantastic relationships built.”
In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump said he was heading back to Washington and would hold a news conference at noon on Friday.
China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi said the three countries would maintain coordination at working level after the “peace summit.” He said the leaders had exchanged their strategic intentions in person and established a “new paradigm” for interaction among the powers.
Analysts said Trump came to Shenzhen seeking to bolster his standing after his Republicans lost control of Congress in midterm elections this month.
US Senator Charles Schumer, who leads Democrats in the Senate, called the trilateral summit “a historic embarrassment that people will remember long into the future.”
“It’s a betrayal of the United States by a president who loves nothing more than to bow down to our adversaries for a photo op,” he said.
The leaders met in a villa in wooded hills beside a lake in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Xi in his turn said: “History tells us that when major powers live in harmony, the world is at peace. When major powers clash, the world falls into turmoil.”
DIFFERENCES OVER UKRAINE, IRAN, AND TRADE
Putin, fresh from a setback in Ukraine after the crippling of a key bridge linking Crimea to Russia, said the three had “numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine.”
The meeting was a diplomatic coup for Putin, with Russia’s economy barely a 10th the size of China’s and most of its businesses barred from trading with the West by sanctions.
European allies met in Berlin on Thursday to show their support for Ukraine, indignant after Trump embraced Putin as a “friend” at the summit and at the absence of Europe from the Shenzhen discussions.
“A Yalta format will not bring peace,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told reporters. “The United States know without us there will not be peace.”
Putin rejected criticism comparing the summit to the 1945 Yalta Conference, where Soviet, US, and British leaders helped shape postwar Europe. He said Yalta had not divided the world into spheres of influence but “codified the existing reality.”
“In today’s conflicts, too, we will have to come to terms with the realities on the ground.”
On X, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said Shenzhen had not proven a latter-day “Yalta of Putin‘s dreams.”
“Meanwhile, Russia has practically lost its bridge to the real Yalta in occupied Ukrainian Crimea,” he said. “Time for him to wake up, get real, and end the war he can never win.”
The underlying diplomatic tensions could resurface in a few weeks when Trump hosts the Group of 20 summit at his golf resort in Florida, where he is expected to meet Xi again and could potentially cross paths with Putin.
Putin, whose presence would likely anger the United States’ European allies, told his news conference he would consider attending, having discussed it with Trump, but would need to take the situation in Russia into account.
Before the trilateral, Trump met Xi and Putin separately, referring to both as friends.
Trump told NBC he discussed artificial intelligence with Xi and they agreed that having guardrails was good.
FANFARE AND PAGEANTRY
Earlier, Trump highlighted the pomp surrounding his Shenzhen arrival, when Xi greeted him at the airport, the first time Xi has done so with any visiting leader since becoming president. This reciprocated Trump‘s gesture when Xi visited the US in September. The leaders also briefly hugged.
This contrasted with the more muted greeting of other leaders, including Putin. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi landed without any welcoming ceremony.
Japan’s relations with China have soured since Takaichi said last year that Japan could deploy its military if a Chinese move on Taiwan also threatened its territory.
On Taiwan, Xi told Trump the US must “do the right thing” to avoid major setbacks in their relationship.

sources.news_title: Xi, Putin and Trump commit to global stability in historic summit
sources.text:
Three world leaders have committed to working together to safeguard global security, stabilise energy supplies and reform the United Nations.
Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump made the commitment following their trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday.
In a joint declaration issued after the summit, the three leaders pledged to strengthen international cooperation amid mounting global security and geopolitical challenges.
The meeting brought together leaders of three major world powers with competing strategic interests and significant influence over international security, trade and the global balance of power.
Putin and Trump expressed appreciation to China for hosting the summit, which provided a platform for discussions on the international situation and the need to maintain strategic stability.

sources.news_title: Shenzhen Was No Yalta Conference
sources.text:
Shenzhen Was No Yalta Conference
For all the talk of a new world order, the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting produced little of substance.
Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief.
The highlights this week: The presidents of China, Russia, and the United States hold a historic trilateral summit in Shenzhen, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi receives a cold welcome in China, and fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s scandal continues.
Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief.
The highlights this week: The presidents of China, Russia, and the United States hold a historic trilateral summit in Shenzhen, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi receives a cold welcome in China, and fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s scandal continues.
Trilateral Meeting Concludes in Shenzhen
The first-ever trilateral meeting among the leaders of China, Russia, and the United States—held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) gathering this week in Shenzhen, China—was, as expected, little more than a photo opportunity.
Still, all three will be pleased with the pictures. U.S. President Donald Trump, smarting from his party’s overwhelming defeat in the midterm elections, gets to play statesman. Russian President Vladimir Putin gets to play peacemaker. And Chinese President Xi Jinping gets to play the man in charge—though nowadays that may be more accurate than not.
The official joint statement from the summit, issued by Chinese state news agency Xinhua, echoed themes that Xi has promoted throughout Trump’s second term: strategic stability, opposition to Cold War thinking and economic decoupling, and respect for the outcomes of World War II.
China and Russia routinely trot out that final point to justify their territorial claims today. The irony is rich for China, which was represented during the war by leaders of the Republic of China government, who later fled to Taiwan. (In Eastern Europe, meanwhile, the victorious power was the Soviet Union, not Russia.)
Before the meeting, there was talk that the Shenzhen trilateral might amount to a new Yalta Conference—the 1945 summit at which the three main victors of World War II divided up Europe.
This speculation drew on the long-simmering idea that the world might once again be carved into spheres of influence. But the idea that a new Yalta is possible at all is fundamentally misguided. Two of the three great powers today are bogged down in economically devastating wars of choice against smaller countries.
Crucially, it is clear that the world is not theirs to divide. Trump cannot force Ukraine to surrender or hand Taiwan to Beijing. Putin cannot restore Soviet grandeur by force. And China, for all its bluster, has yet to bring Taiwan to heel.
The Yalta fantasy also ignores how much weaker today’s great powers are than their 1945 counterparts. At the time, the Soviet military was the largest in the world, the U.S. economy was bigger than those of the rest of the developed world combined, and the diminished United Kingdom still ruled an empire that encompassed one-quarter of the global population.
Nor did the Yalta bargain of a world divided among superpowers hold. Rather than securing a lasting peace, it laid the groundwork for the Cold War and spawned bloodshed from Korea to Hungary within a few years. A grand bargain among China, Russia, and the United States today is even less likely to work.
For all the talk of a new world order, the summit produced little of substance. The three powers nominally agreed to engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks, but with no advance diplomatic work and significant differences among their arsenals, not much will come of it.
The joint statement did have one effect, though. The leaders’ condemnation of the International Criminal Court handed China and Russia ideological ammunition, reinforcing the autocratic disdain for international institutions and human rights that all countries are meant to uphold.
But Beijing should not mistake the summit for a license to keep the terms of U.S.-China talks strictly about power. With Democrats set to take control of key China-related committees in the U.S. Congress in January, issues involving democracy and political dissidents will take on renewed importance, no matter what Trump or Xi would prefer.
What We’re Following
Takaichi receives cold welcome. Hosting the APEC gathering gave China another opportunity to signal its displeasure with Japan. The bilateral relationship is still at a nadir, more than a year after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said a Chinese invasion of Taiwan could justify Japanese intervention.
As other leaders were greeted with fanfare, Takaichi was received at Shenzhen’s airport by a relatively low-ranking diplomat. I suspect there was also implicit misogyny at play: Chinese state media has denigrated Takaichi in sexist terms, as it did with former Taiwanese President Tsai Ing-wen.
Though Takaichi was largely sidelined at the APEC meeting, she did what she could to meet bilaterally with other leaders instead.
A magisterial China resource. Last month, scholar Endymion Wilkinson published the eighth edition of Chinese History: A New Manual, one of the most important books in the field of China studies. First published in 1973 as a relatively slim research guide of around 70,000 words, it now approaches 2 million and covers everything from Chinese cuisine to politics.
Wilkinson is now 85, but each new edition still contains substantial revisions and additions. The latest includes personal recollections from his stints in China: first as an English teacher at Peking University on the eve of the Cultural Revolution and later as the European Union’s ambassador from 1994 to 2001.
A remarkable work of erudition and dedication, the book remains a starting point for virtually any research into China.
FP’s Most Read This Week
- Lame-Duck Trump Heads to Asia by Rishi Iyengar
- The Middle East Is Finally on Its Own by Stephen M. Walt
- How Netanyahu Lost His Bet on Trump by Azriel Bermant
Tech and Business
Nvidia scandal updates. The fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s marital infidelities continues to widen, with the company facing legal scrutiny and a wider crackdown on U.S. chip exports. Huang had an affair with alleged Chinese asset Alice Huang; he resigned from his role last week and is set to testify before the U.S. Congress early next month.
Reporting suggests that Nvidia’s involvement in networks designed to evade U.S. export controls lies somewhere between active complicity and willful blindness. Alice Huang’s husband, who reportedly knew about the affair, also played a major part in building state-backed data centers designed to give China access to more computing power.
Alice Huang is now back in Beijing, beyond the reach of potential criminal charges in Singapore.
U.S. cybersecurity risks? As many tech services seemed to break in the last week, many people asked whether the outages were an ordinary screwup or a cyberattack. The consensus so far is that the problems were unrelated, caused by companies rushing to upgrade systems before the holidays.
But it’s worth remembering that China achieved deep penetration of U.S. infrastructure with Volt Typhoon, a state-sponsored hacking group, which was publicly exposed in 2024. The Trump administration dismantled the expert groups investigating Volt Typhoon early last year, and China could likely still shut down large parts of U.S. life if it chose to do so.

sources.news_title: Trump, Putin, and Xi Hold Historic Trilateral Summit on APEC Sidelines in Shenzhen
sources.text:
President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin sat down for a historic trilateral summit on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday.
The summit, which lasted 90 minutes, marked the first time the leaders of the three global powers ever held trilateral talks, a meeting that came amid soaring global tensions as the Russia-Ukraine war continues to rage and as there’s still no end in sight to the US-Iran war.
In a joint statement, the three leaders “reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought” and said that the “three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.”
The three leaders also vowed to reform “the UN so that the UN can respond more effectively to global challenges and conform to its fundamental mission of international peace and security” and said they would work to “increase the production and supply of refined petroleum.”
They also “recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction.”
In opening remarks, Trump said that as “presidents of three of the world’s largest countries, we have a special responsibility to maintain open, respectful, and productive dialogue on issues impacting not just our people but the entire planet.”
According to China’s statement on the talks, Xi said that history “tells us that when major countries live in harmony, the world enjoys peace; when major countries clash, the world falls into turmoil,” and expressed support for continued engagement.
“The three countries should maintain regular high-level exchanges, keep dialogue channels open at all levels, and establish crisis communication and prevention mechanisms to minimize miscalculation, keep differences under control, and prevent frictions from escalating,” the Chinese leader said.
In a separate bilateral meeting with Trump, Xi issued a warning on Taiwan as the US continues increasing diplomatic ties and weapons sales to the island. “On the question of Taiwan, the US side should keep doing the right thing and avoid major setbacks in China-US relations,” Xi said, according to the Chinese Foreign Ministry.
Trump also held a separate one-on-one meeting with Putin that lasted about 40 minutes. Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said it was a “good meeting” and that the talks mostly focused on the war in Ukraine.

sources.news_title: Trump, Xi & Putin Meeting May Be a First, But It's Not Progress
Trump, Xi, And Putin Pledge Expanded Oil Output As Climate Talks Quietly Erase Fossil Fuel Phase-Out Language
sources.text:
While global attention focused on a trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China, the leaders of the United States, China, and Russia jointly committed to flooding world markets with more refined petroleum.
A joint statement from the summit between Presidents Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin declared that “the three countries plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations.”
The pledge came as fuel prices surged globally, driven by the ongoing wars in Ukraine and Iran, adding economic urgency to a geopolitical alignment that has few modern precedents.
Roughly 5,000 miles west, at the United Nations climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, a revised draft of the summit’s final decision was quietly stripping out every reference to fossil fuels.
An earlier version of the text had demanded “accelerated action to phase out” oil, gas, and coal, language that now appears to have been abandoned entirely in the updated draft circulated to negotiators.
The new draft also removed references to “clean” electricity, a deletion that analysts noted could effectively permit countries to expand fossil fuel-based power generation to meet rising demand.
The dual developments represent a significant setback for climate advocates, who had hoped the Antalya conference would build on the landmark 2023 agreement – the only time a COP final decision had ever referenced fossil fuels – to “transition away” from them.
Saudi Arabia and other oil-producing states had pushed back hard against any restrictive language, making consensus on the earlier, stronger draft text politically unviable heading into the final days of the conference.
Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, who chairs the African group of negotiators at the talks, said the Shenzhen summit represented a direct contradiction of multilateral climate commitments, warning it would mark “hypocrisy in the whole process” if nations agreed to curb fossil fuels at one forum and reversed course at another.
Amoah stated bluntly that “if fossil [fuels] is something that we want to do away with as parties, let’s be honest to our commitment,” adding that he had not been briefed on the Shenzhen agreement before speaking to reporters.
One official present in Antalya, identified as Bowen, pushed back against the idea that the Shenzhen summit signaled disengagement from the climate process, noting that “China is here engaging constructively with us, very actively” and that Beijing was approaching the talks “in a spirit of helping us make it work.”
Bowen’s remarks made no mention of the United States, which is not formally represented at the Antalya conference, nor of Russia, leaving the scope of his defense notably narrow.
Most delegations that were approached for comment Thursday said they needed more time to review the revised draft text, declining to offer immediate reactions to the proposed rollback of fossil fuel language.

sources.news_title: Trump, Putin, Xi unveil historic ‘peace’ declaration, but major wars remain unresolved
sources.text:
President Donald Trump joined Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday in announcing a historic agreement to pursue nuclear talks, increase global oil supplies and reform international institutions.
The three leaders issued a four-point declaration following their unprecedented summit in Shenzhen, China, according to the White House. However, the agreement contains no binding nuclear weapons reductions, implementation deadlines or concrete plans to end ongoing wars in Ukraine and Iran.
Trump is scheduled to hold a press conference at the White House on Friday following his return from China. The president described his trip as “Great and Highly Consequential” and said he would also discuss trade agreements with Thailand, the Philippines and other countries in a Truth Social post Thursday.
China hosted the summit, with the American and Russian presidents thanking Beijing for organizing the meeting. The leaders discussed international security and maintaining strategic stability, according to the White House.
Perhaps the most significant development was a joint commitment to reducing the risk of nuclear conflict.
The three leaders reaffirmed that a nuclear war “cannot be won and must never be fought,” according to the White House.
Washington, Moscow and Beijing also pledged to begin discussions on preventing nuclear proliferation and reducing nuclear risks. However, the declaration does not specify when negotiations will begin or whether the countries intend to establish binding limits on their arsenals, according to the White House.
The announcement follows the Feb. 5 expiration of New START, the last major nuclear arms control treaty between Washington and Moscow. The agreement previously imposed limits on deployed American and Russian strategic nuclear weapons, according to the United Nations.
The trilateral commitment also brings China into discussions on nuclear risks as Beijing continues expanding its arsenal.
China possessed more than 600 operational nuclear warheads in mid-2024 and was projected to surpass 1,000 by 2030, according to the Department of War.
Beyond nuclear security, the three governments committed to reforming the United Nations to improve its ability to address international crises, according to the White House.
All three countries hold permanent seats on the U.N. Security Council and possess veto power over substantive resolutions. France and the United Kingdom hold the remaining permanent seats, according to the United Nations.
Reforming the United Nations could prove difficult even with cooperation from Washington, Moscow and Beijing. Amendments to the U.N. Charter require approval from two-thirds of the General Assembly and ratification by two-thirds of U.N. members, including all five permanent Security Council members, according to the United Nations.
The declaration also leaves unanswered whether the three countries intend to change Security Council membership, voting procedures or the veto powers held by permanent members.
The leaders also pledged to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products while maintaining stable global energy flows, according to the White House.
The provision specifically concerns refined petroleum products rather than crude oil production. Such products include gasoline, diesel and aviation fuel, which support civilian transportation, commercial activity and military operations, according to the Energy Information Administration.
However, the three governments did not specify whether increased supplies would come from expanded refining capacity, additional exports or changes to existing production. The declaration also provides no production targets, deadlines or mechanisms for determining whether the promised increases are achieved, according to the White House.
Another significant provision concerns the International Criminal Court (ICC), which the three governments warned against exceeding its jurisdiction.
The leaders emphasized national sovereignty, state consent and protections for government officials, arguing that international judicial institutions must respect those principles, according to the White House.
Notably, none of the three countries belongs to the ICC, which currently has 125 member states. The United States, Russia and China are absent from the court’s membership roster, according to the ICC.
The agreement’s emphasis on legal protections for government officials also raises questions about the court’s existing authority. Article 27 of the Rome Statute states that official government positions and associated immunities do not prevent prosecution before the court, according to the International Committee of the Red Cross.
Furthermore, countries do not necessarily escape ICC jurisdiction simply because they have not joined the court. The institution can exercise jurisdiction over qualifying crimes committed on the territory of member states, including those allegedly committed by foreign nationals, according to the ICC.
The ICC issued an arrest warrant for Putin in March 2023 over allegations involving the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children into Russia, according to the International Criminal Court.
The court also issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Israeli Defense Minister Yoav Gallant in Nov. 2024 over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, including the use of starvation as a method of warfare, according to the International Criminal Court.
Trump previously imposed sanctions on the ICC in February 2025, accusing the institution of improperly asserting jurisdiction over American and allied personnel, according to a White House executive order.
Despite the declaration’s emphasis on international peace, the document notably omits any direct reference to Russia’s war against Ukraine, the American-led war against Iran or tensions involving Taiwan.
The agreement also contains no ceasefire proposals, territorial settlements or enforceable nuclear disarmament measures.
For now, the declaration establishes broad diplomatic commitments between three competing global powers without resolving the military conflicts and strategic disputes that continue to divide them, according to the White House.

sources.news_title: The biggest takeaway from trilateral is the nuclear piece
sources.text:
The first trilateral meeting of Presidents Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin, held on November 19 in Shenzhen, was worth holding for one reason above all. The United States has a clear interest in reducing nuclear risks with both China and Russia, and the three leaders agreed to discuss how to do so.
Beyond that, the summit yielded little for Washington. Xi gained the prestige of convening the three powers, while Putin gained stature on the world stage even as Russia continues its brutal war against Ukraine.
The nuclear pledge deserves attention, however. Beijing has long resisted three-way arms-control negotiations, arguing that the United States and Russia should first reduce their much larger arsenals. China has discussed nuclear risks with both countries in the broader five-power process and held bilateral arms-control consultations with Washington in 2023. Beijing suspended further consultations in 2024, citing U.S. arms sales to Taiwan. What Shenzhen adds is Xi’s public commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and nonproliferation in a dedicated three-way format. That is a meaningful opening, especially since New START expired in February.
However, the joint declaration sets no timetable or agenda and contains no commitment to negotiate limits on arsenals.
The other results of the summit were thinner. The leaders endorsed U.N. reform and greater supplies of refined petroleum products without specifying what reforms they wanted or how much additional fuel they would supply. Beijing says they discussed Ukraine, the Middle East, and the Korean Peninsula, but the declaration identified no concrete next steps. Its language on immunity for state officials and alleged jurisdictional abuse by the International Criminal Court (ICC) had a clearer political payoff. It aligned with the Trump administration’s position and benefited Putin, who faces an ICC arrest warrant.
Xi also brought a familiar proposal into the three-way meeting by calling for crisis communication and prevention mechanisms. Although the joint declaration contained no agreement to establish them, Washington and Moscow should nevertheless take up the proposal and see whether Beijing will agree to practical steps, such as establishing and regularly testing emergency contacts.
On balance, Shenzhen was long on symbolism and promises and short on results that advance global stability or U.S. interests. That judgment could change if the three governments schedule nuclear talks and agree on measures that reduce the risk of miscalculation. The summit gave them an opening. Whether they use it is another matter. I won’t hold my breath.

The meeting at the government-owned lakeside Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit lasted for 90 minutes, much longer than the 60 minutes scheduled for the talks.
The three permanent members of the U.N. Security Council committed to reform of the U.N. to enable it to “respond more effectively to global challenges and conform to its fundamental mission of international peace and security.”
On the ICC they said they underscored that state consent principle and immunity for state officials were paramount and were in agreement that the court and other similar bodies “must not abuse their jurisdiction.”
The pledge on carbon fuels was, the leaders said, “for the benefit of all nations.”

US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping held the first three-way meeting between the leaders of the three powers in Shenzhen on Thursday, an encounter rich in symbolism that ended with a commitment to dialogue on reducing nuclear risks but no concrete measures.

The text also states that “the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”, upholds respect for the immunity of state officials and calls for reform of the United Nations. sources.news_title: Trump Made a Rookie Mistake at His “Historic” Summit With Putin and Xi
sources.text:
Sign up for the Slatest to get the most insightful analysis, criticism, and advice out there, delivered to your inbox daily.
As expected, nothing important happened at Thursday’s “historic” summit involving Presidents Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin, and Xi Jinping—the first time the leaders of the United States, Russia, and China have jointly met.
But don’t tell that to Trump. He thinks the summit had enormous significance. Shortly after his arrival in Shenzhen, China, where Xi took the unusual step of meeting him at the airport with great fanfare, a reporter asked him what he thought the “headline” coming out of the summit would be.
“I think I’ve already gotten that headline. Because the relationship that I have with China is a great one,” Trump replied. He added that Xi “has never gone to the airport to meet somebody. … That’s a big win for us.”
And there you have it. Trump is big on theatrics. The problem is that he often mistakes theatrics for reality. Xi’s greeting on the runway—whether a sign of genuine respect or an appeal to Trump’s ego—was a nice gesture. But it forecast nothing about the issues that summitry is meant to address and resolve. Trump doesn’t understand that. To him, everything is about Donald J. Trump—who seems to like him, who doesn’t. All the other world leaders recognize this, and as a result, he’s an easy mark for anyone who wants something from him.
The three leaders met at the end of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum.* Serious big-power summits go on for many hours, sometimes days. The Trump-Putin-Xi summit lasted an hour and a half. That’s hardly enough time to make opening statements and hear the translations.
In a post-summit statement, they announced agreement on four items: reform of the United Nations (no specifics), an increase in oil production (not exactly forward-thinking), further dialogue on reducing nuclear risk (no requirement to reduce their own nuclear arsenals), and sovereign immunity from international courts (an expression of shared contempt for international law).
In other words, there was no commitment to take action, or even to hold systematic talks, on anything.
Putin and Xi got something out of the event. Xi played host to an international conference, then got to sit as an equal with the world’s two largest nuclear powers. By simply attending the conference, Putin ended his pariah status, which has plagued him since he invaded Ukraine nearly five years ago, and then got to sit as an equal with the world’s two largest economic powers.
Trump, on the other hand, got nothing. He made the rookie’s mistake—after being president for six years—of setting high expectations in advance, hoping to discuss nuclear arms reduction and an end to the wars in Ukraine and Iran. Putin and Xi had no interest in any of those subjects.
Xi wants to continue building up his nuclear weapons until China’s arsenal is as large as those of the U.S. and Russia. Putin announced that, after Ukraine’s bombing of the Crimea bridge, he is halting all negotiations about that war (no big deal, as those negotiations have never been serious). Xi didn’t want to talk about Ukraine either, as he has long been providing Russia with weapons technology and buying its oil. Nor did Xi or Putin want to talk about the Iran war, as one or the other or both have been helping Tehran with trade, weapons, and intelligence.
Trump came to the summit with no outlined agenda and—after the failure of his massive bombing campaign in Iran and the crushing defeat of his party in the midterm elections—very little leverage. He was reduced to addressing each of the two dictators as “my friend,” even saying, “It’s an honor to be with Vladimir” and, to Xi, “it’s an honor to be with you, Mr. President.”
Trump no doubt boarded the plane back to Washington beaming and pumped up, his status as world leader reaffirmed by his mere presence at the Big Three’s table, free to ignore—even to dismiss with a sneer—his recent repudiation in a democratic election, an imposition that his good friends Vladimir and Xi don’t need to put up with.
Many presidents in Trump’s position—lame ducks whose party just lost control of Congress—have turned their focus toward foreign policy, where they enjoy more leeway. But at least most of them had productive goals in mind. Trump hasn’t articulated any, and as long as he has Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff as his global emissaries, he’s not likely to accomplish any, even if he did. How will he do the reboot? Will he flex his muscles and resume the bombing of Iran, realizing that he can’t cajole the Islamic Republic’s leaders to sign an agreement to his liking? Will he abandon Kyiv with an even more emphatic shrug, the better to help his friend Vladimir restore his sphere of influence? (Addressing the fear of Europeans that the trilateral summit might replicate the 1945 Yalta treaty, which divided up the continent for the subsequent Cold War, Putin said, “As far as a new Yalta goes, what was so bad about Yalta?”) Will he do the same for his friend Xi by hardening his indifference toward the fate of Taiwan?
The Yalta treaty formalized the positions of the Allied armies—the U.S., Britain, and Russia—at the end of World War II. Putin and Xi approached this meeting as another opportunity to reap, and to some extent share, the benefits of a world where American influence has declined. Trump is accelerating that decline. His fawning in Shenzhen further dramatized the trend, and, what’s worse, he clearly doesn’t see what’s going on.
Correction, Nov. 19, 2026: This story initially misidentified the conference that preceded the summit. It was a gathering of the 21-member Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, not the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

sources.news_title: Trump concludes China visit with historic trilateral meeting with Xi and Putin
sources.text:
SHENZHEN, China — President Donald Trump concluded his final day in China on Thursday with separate bilateral meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, followed by a historic first-ever trilateral summit of the three leaders at Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
The meetings covered trade, the war in Ukraine, nuclear risks, energy security through the Strait of Hormuz, and the role of international institutions. China and Russia later released a joint “China-Russia-U.S. Heads of State Declaration toward Peace,” outlining four points of agreement. Trump departed for the United States without a formal joint press appearance after the sessions.
Bilateral with Xi focuses on trade, farmers and shared interests
In his meeting with Xi, Trump highlighted progress on trade, saying the two sides had agreed to cut tariffs totaling $30 billion.
“Each side has agreed to cut tariffs, on $30 billion off trade, and we have split up the tariffs and done it in a very fair way,” Trump said. “Our farmers have done very well and I’ll be asking you to do some more for our farmers because China has an insatiable appetite, I can tell you that, and we can fill that appetite.”
Trump also pointed to shared interests on energy and Iran.
“Both the United States and China have an interest in ensuring that energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz and that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon. We both feel that very strongly on both points,” he said. He described his personal rapport with Xi as strong, noting the two had sat together for two hours the previous evening and calling their relationship “outstanding.”
Putin bilateral centers on Ukraine war
Trump’s subsequent bilateral discussion with Putin focused on the conflict in Ukraine. Ahead of Putin’s arrival, Trump said the leaders were looking to help end the fighting.
“We’re looking to both help with respect to the war with Russia and Ukraine, would like to see it ended. I think I can speak for both of us very much,” Trump said. He referenced the scale of casualties, noting “twenty five thousand mostly soldiers a month are being killed,” and indicated Putin would join later for the broader talks. Kremlin accounts described the atmosphere as positive and confirmed Ukraine was a central topic.
First-ever trilateral summit called historic
The day culminated in the trilateral session around a large round table, with the flags of the three nations displayed behind the leaders. Trump called the gathering unprecedented.
“Today so in that sense, and I think lots of other ways, we are really making history,” he said. “The three of us have a great deal to discuss.”
He stressed the value of direct engagement.
“We have a special responsibility to maintain open, respectful and productive dialogue on issues impacting not just our people, but the entire planet,” Trump said. “Too often past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements, and we feel the opposite.”
“No problems were ever solved under the old school refusing to talk about them. No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech,” he added.
On nuclear weapons, Trump underscored the unique position of the three countries.
“As the world’s three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used,” he said. “The power is unbelievable, unthinkable.” He added that reducing arsenals is difficult once countries possess them, but cooperation against proliferation remains vital, specifically citing Iran: “We’re not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”
Trump also raised concerns about international institutions.
“I’ll be suggesting ways to protect our nation’s sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction,” he said.
Putin told the gathering that the three countries share historical responsibilities.
“Our three states are the victors in World War 2, and we hold joint responsibility for maintaining international peace and security,” Putin said.
Joint declaration reaffirms nuclear principle
The White House released the “U.S.-Russia-China Heads of State Declaration toward Peace” later Thursday, confirming the four points agreed to by the leaders. According to the official U.S. text, the heads of state “had an in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation and committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security.”
The declaration states that as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, the three countries “committed to reform the UN so that the UN can respond more effectively to global challenges and conform to its fundamental mission of international peace and security.” It also says the nations “plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations” and “reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows.”
On international courts, the leaders “recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction.” Finally, they “reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought” and agreed the three countries “will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.”
No specific timelines, binding arms-control reductions, or explicit resolutions on Ukraine or other conflicts were detailed in the public statement. Xi described the meeting as constructive, according to Chinese accounts, and emphasized that major powers living in harmony supports global peace.
The sessions marked the centerpiece of Trump’s three-day Asia itinerary, which also included stops tied to the APEC gathering. Trump left Shenzhen for the return flight to the United States following the trilateral meeting.

Xi-Trump-Putin summit: What did it achieve?
November 19, 2026
Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday for an unprecedented trilateral summit in Shenzhen, bringing together the leaders of the world's three most powerful military powers amid heightened geopolitical tensions.
Xi hailed the talks as "groundbreaking," saying discussions ranged from global governance and denuclearization to the war in Ukraine and energy security.
The "peace declaration" released after their meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the US-led war in Iran.
Instead, the three leaders agreed to pursue reforms of the United Nations, limit the role of the International Criminal Court and reaffirm their commitment to avoiding nuclear war. They also pledged to boost supplies of refined petroleum products to address global energy challenges.
The tightly choreographed meeting fueled concerns that Beijing, Washington and Moscow could seek to reshape the international order around competing spheres of influence.
While Xi said the talks with Trump and Putin were "positive, constructive and fruitful," Trump heralded the gathering as "really making history."
Who gained the most from the meeting?
For Putin, the three-way talks, and his meetings with both leaders separately earlier, offered a chance to show the world that he was on par with the leaders of the US and China, despite Western efforts to isolate him since he launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Emma Chanlett-Avery, senior director for Political-Security Affairs at the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI), said Putin had the most to gain from the meeting as "he appeared on the world stage as one of the dominant players in the world."
Chim Lee, a senior analyst with The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU), echoed this view.
The meeting itself is a "major outcome for Russia," he told DW, pointing to Russian media coverage that has cast it as "reinforcing Russia's standing in the world."
Beijing reluctant to accept nuclear limits
The joint statement also said the leaders are committed to work to reduce nuclear risks and prevent nuclear proliferation.
The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New START, expired in February.
Trump has said he wants "a new, improved and modernized" deal that includes China.
But Beijing has so far been reluctant to accept limits as its estimated arsenal of around 500 warheads remains far smaller than those of Russia and the US.
Moscow and Washington are believed to possess more than 5,000 warheads each.
Lee said China is unlikely to participate in a trilateral institutionalized setting to control nuclear arms.
"The gap between China's nuclear arsenal and those of Russia and US is still quite large. From China's perspective, it doesn't seem to make a lot of sense to put the three powers in the same bucket in this area."
The expert believes Trump attended the meeting as he is "actively thinking about his legacy in the final two years in office."
"So, in this context, the idea of setting up a trilateral nuclear arms control arrangement would have been a very big achievement," Lee said.
But, in the end, the declaration said the countries would merely engage in "dialogue" on the issue, avoiding any explicit commitments to downsize their nuclear stockpiles.
A reluctant host?
China initially hesitated to organize the trilateral summit as it did not want to be explicitly tied to Russia's war in Ukraine and harm Beijing's efforts to present itself as a long-term force for global stability.
The Chinese government, which is working to rebalance economic ties with the EU, was also wary of appearing to form a G3 club with Washington and Moscow, which could alienate other global partners.
Chanlett-Avery said that China had some degree of discomfort in convening this meeting, worried about getting involved in Ukraine issues.
But Beijing eventually "managed to get the outcome they wanted" and kept the European conflict out of the meeting's focus, she noted.
"China was able to show off Shenzhen and all of its sparkling high-tech features. They convened a successful international meeting that grabbed lots of headlines," she added. "So, I think China probably came out feeling okay."
Warnings of a 'second Yalta'
Prior to the summit, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned of a "second Yalta," referring to the Yalta Conference held in Crimea in 1945.
That meeting saw the Allied powers decide on the post-war European order following the end of World War II.
In Shenzhen, Putin stressed that Russia, the US and China, as victors in World War II and veto-wielding members of the UN Security Council, bore a "joint responsibility for maintaining international peace."
But Ying-Yu Lin, Associate Professor at Graduate Institute of International Affairs and Strategic Studies at Taiwan's Tamkang University, said the Yalta comparison "is a bit of a stretch," given the vast differences between 1945 and now.
Will there be more such trilaterals?
Putin also said that all three leaders "agree that it's a useful format," and such meetings could take place again.
Lee, the EIU expert, said the trilateral setup "is unlikely to be just a one-off" and there will probably be more such meetings in the coming years.
"Especially from the US side to have this kind of setup, there will be some interest in maintaining warm relations with both China and Russia," he underlined.
