sources.text:
China, the United States and Russia issued a “Declaration toward Peace” after their leaders held an unprecedented summit, laying out common ambitions to overhaul the UN and keep the International Criminal Court in check.
Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met in China against a complex backdrop, with Russia’syears-long offensive in Ukraine grinding on, Trump bogged down in the Middle East and an ascendant China looking to strengthen its hand in East Asia.
“The three heads of state had an in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation and committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security,” a White House version of the statement said.
The powwow took place with Russia’s years-long offensive in Ukraine grinding on, Trump bogged down in the Middle East and an ascendant China looking to strengthen its hand in East Asia.
“We discussed the question of democracy. And what is democracy? It’s what? It’s the liberal order that certain circles put together and still now are trying to impose on the whole world,” Putin told a news conference in Shenzhen.
The three men made opening remarks touching on weighty topics from nuclear weapons to the war in Ukraine as they met around a large, dark round table with a pink flower arrangement at its centre.
The discussion behind closed doors in Kylin Villa ended after an hour and 20 minutes.
Trump said the leaders were “making history”, while Putin said they wrote a new “page in the history of diplomacy”.
“The three countries share a common perspective on safeguarding world peace,” Xi said.
On his way home to Washington, Trump called into a meeting of European leaders to discuss Ukraine and update them on his three-way summit.
Not all of those European leaders were impressed: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called the Trump-Xi-Putin talks a “photo op”, and French President Emmanuel Macron said it would not “lead to a reorganisation of the world”.
Trump said he would give a press conference on Friday about his “Great and Highly Consequential Trip” to China.
ICC, UN and oil
In their joint statement, the leaders “recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction”.
Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant, while Trump’s administration has vowed to dismantle the court “brick by brick”.
The leaders said they were “committed to reform the UN so that the UN can respond more effectively to global challenges and conform to its fundamental mission of international peace and security”.
The joint statement said the countries “plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations. They reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows”.
The summit stoked fears that the three powerful men want to divide the globe into spheres of influence, for example by making decisions impacting Ukraine over the heads of Kyiv or Europe.
But Trump said he wanted to make a deal on Ukraine “with Europe by his side”, according to special US envoy Jared Kushner.
Earlier, Trump and Putin held a meeting – their first since August 2025 – with the 80-year-old US President calling the Russian his “friend”. Putin responded in English: “Nice to meet you.”
Trump and Xi then came together – their third time this year – for one-on-one discussions, with the US leader highlighting a “very special relationship”.
Putin, 74, and Xi, 73, also held talks – their 50th meeting, the Chinese President said.
Beijing, Washington and Moscow previously gave different accounts of the agenda for the three-way meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit, a forum of 21 economies around the Pacific Rim.
Washington initially signalled that Ukraine was off the table, before Trump said the war would feature. Xi does not view the conflict as China’s problem to solve.
Washington had also flagged the Iran war and nuclear disarmament as topics of discussion, after a US-Russia bilateral treaty on atomic weapons expired in February.
Beijing has long maintained that the United States and Russia must reduce their giant nuclear arsenals before it agrees to talks on its smaller stockpile.
The final statement said that the countries “will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons”.
Breaking with decades of diplomatic protocol, Xi received Trump at the airport, with the men briefly hugging before a red-carpet greeting complete with cheering children and a flyover.
Critics warned that the optics from the meeting would be damaging for the US President – but a fillip to Xi and Putin.
The meeting “gives Putin a platform to legitimise his war of aggression over Ukraine with seemingly little repercussions”, said Lyle Morris at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
“Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin are playing Donald Trump like a cheap violin,” Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said.

sources.news_title: Trump-Xi-Putin summit in China: What the three leaders agreed on and what they left out — 5 key takeaways
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin held their first-ever trilateral meeting on Thursday (November 19), bringing together the leaders of three major global powers for talks on international peace, security and geopolitical challenges.
The meeting, which lasted over an hour, ended with a joint declaration outlining areas of agreement, including reforms to the United Nations, increased oil supplies and measures to reduce nuclear risks. However, the declaration made no direct mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the US-led war in Iran, raising questions about the substantive outcomes of the historic gathering.
The three countries also opposed what they described as the misuse of international jurisdiction by the International Criminal Court (ICC), arguing that state officials should enjoy immunity from prosecution, according to reports.
All three leaders sought to project a message of cooperation and shared responsibility for maintaining global stability.
Here are five key takeaways from the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting.
Hosting the first-ever meeting between the leaders of the US, China and Russia offered Xi Jinping an opportunity to strengthen Beijing's diplomatic standing on the global stage.
According to China's state-run Xinhua news agency, Xi described the discussions with Trump and Putin as positive and fruitful, saying the three countries shared common views on safeguarding world peace.
The Chinese leader emphasised that major powers should take the legitimate security concerns of all countries seriously and resolve differences through dialogue and cooperation.
“As long as dialogue does not stop, doors remain open, there is hope for peace,” Xi said.
However, the joint declaration avoided several contentious geopolitical issues, including China's claims over Taiwan.
Beijing has consistently maintained that Taiwan is part of its territory and has not ruled out using force to bring the democratically governed island under its control.
Trump described the gathering as an important moment in international diplomacy, suggesting that the three leaders could move beyond traditional approaches to dealing with geopolitical rivals.
The US President portrayed the discussions as the beginning of a broader diplomatic engagement that could potentially help address some of the world's most complicated conflicts.
“A lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start,” Trump told Putin during a bilateral meeting ahead of the trilateral discussions.
Iran was among the issues Trump said he discussed with Xi.
He reiterated that both Washington and Beijing wanted Iran to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a critical global energy shipping route that has become a major chokepoint amid the war.
Trump also said he and Xi agreed that Iran should not be allowed to acquire nuclear weapons.
However, there was no indication that China or Russia had committed to taking concrete steps to help resolve the Iran conflict.
The meeting also came at a challenging time for Trump's presidency, following Republican setbacks in the US midterm elections, widespread technology outages and escalating Iranian attacks on US allies.
For Putin, the meeting offered an opportunity to reinforce Russia's position as a major global power and demonstrate that Moscow remains an important player in international diplomacy.
His participation in the APEC summit in China, alongside separate meetings with Trump and Xi, provided a significant diplomatic opening for the Russian leader.
Putin last attended an APEC summit in 2017. His presence as an honoured guest at the gathering in Shenzhen was seen as a diplomatic boost for the Kremlin.
During the discussions, Putin emphasised the shared historical responsibility of the three countries as victors of World War II and founding members of the United Nations.
He said the three nations had a responsibility to maintain international peace and security and strengthen the global system of international law.
Putin also referred to the Ukraine conflict as one of the regional issues where the three countries shared common interests.
However, Russia's war in Ukraine was not the main focus of the trilateral discussions, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
The Kremlin subsequently released footage showing Xi escorting Putin to his car after the meeting, with the two leaders exchanging handshakes.
“I don't think anyone even expected things to go so well,” Putin told Xi as they parted ways.
Despite the emphasis on international peace and cooperation, the joint declaration did not directly address two of the most pressing geopolitical conflicts involving the three countries.
Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine and the US-led war in Iran were both absent from the final statement.
This was significant given that Moscow and Washington remain directly involved in the Ukraine conflict, while China and Russia have considerable influence over Iran.
Trump had indicated that Iran would feature in the discussions, particularly regarding the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and preventing Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons.
However, the meeting produced no publicly announced commitments from Beijing or Moscow to help resolve the conflict.
Similarly, although Putin raised Ukraine during the discussions, the three leaders did not announce any concrete agreement on ending the war.
The absence of specific commitments highlighted the gap between the diplomatic symbolism of the summit and its practical outcomes.
Another important area of convergence between Washington and Moscow was their opposition to the International Criminal Court.
The three countries reportedly agreed that state officials should enjoy immunity from prosecution and opposed what they described as the misuse of international legal jurisdiction.
The issue carries particular significance for Putin, who is subject to an ICC arrest warrant over alleged war crimes linked to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
The US, meanwhile, has opposed the ICC's arrest warrant against former Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The discussion highlighted an area where Trump and Putin share common ground despite their countries' differences over several international issues.
The leaders also agreed on the need to reform the United Nations, increase oil supplies and reduce nuclear risks. However, their declaration did not provide details about the proposed reforms or explain how the three countries would work together to implement them.
The first-ever meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin was significant for the diplomatic visibility it offered all three leaders.
Xi strengthened China's position as a diplomatic host, Trump presented the gathering as an opportunity to reshape global engagement, and Putin gained a platform to reinforce Russia's standing alongside Washington and Beijing.
Yet the absence of concrete agreements on Ukraine and Iran, two major conflicts affecting global security, underscored the limitations of the discussions.

sources.news_title: Shenzhen summit letdown and the limits of multipolarity
sources.text:
The United States, China and Russia emerged from their historic Shenzhen summit with a declaration for peace but no settlement for Ukraine or Iran, no binding nuclear reductions and no mechanism for resolving their most consequential strategic disputes.
A day earlier, Moscow hosted a political gathering drawing participants from across the Global South to advocate for a more equitable international order.
Together, the two events exposed multipolarity’s central contradiction: major powers want to preserve their privileges, while countries demanding greater influence remain divided over what should replace the existing order.
The November 19 summit brought together Chinese President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin for unprecedented trilateral talks.
Their joint Declaration toward Peace pledged cooperation on nuclear risks, United Nations reform, energy supplies and the immunity of state officials. The White House later restated the four commitments, underscoring the agreement’s narrow scope.
Shenzhen’s peace promises meet geopolitical reality
The declaration showed that Washington, Beijing and Moscow could identify common interests despite their strategic rivalry. Its omissions, however, were equally telling.
The leaders reaffirmed that nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought, committing to dialogue on nuclear-risk reduction and non-proliferation. This represented diplomatic engagement rather than a binding arms-control agreement.
The New START treaty’s expiration on February 5, 2026, removed the last bilateral treaty limits on American and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals.
Washington wants Beijing involved in future arms-control arrangements, while China remains reluctant to accept comparable obligations because its arsenal is substantially smaller than those of the United States and Russia.
Ukraine exposed another divide. Moscow continues to seek a settlement accommodating its security demands, while Kyiv and European governments insist that Ukraine’s sovereignty cannot be negotiated without its participation.
As Reuters reported, European foreign ministers warned against discussing Europe’s future security architecture with Russia before a Ukrainian ceasefire.
Ukraine was reportedly discussed during bilateral exchanges, but the final declaration contained no conflict-specific commitments specific to Ukraine or Iran.
The declaration’s treatment of international justice was equally revealing. It emphasized state-official immunities while warning that the International Criminal Court and similar institutions should not abuse their jurisdiction.
The provision was particularly notable given the ICC’s outstanding arrest warrant against Putin concerning alleged war crimes involving the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children, although the declaration did not address the case directly.
Economic disagreements also went unresolved. Despite expectations of progress, the summit produced no announcement extending the US–China trade truce, which expires on January 10, 2027.
The lack of a further extension mattered amid ongoing tariff disputes, semiconductor restrictions and competition over advanced technologies. It did not mean the existing truce had ended, but illustrated the limits of diplomacy in overcoming economic rivalry.
Each side took something from the meeting. For Beijing, hosting the talks reinforced China’s diplomatic centrality. Moscow gained international visibility despite Western efforts to isolate it over Ukraine. Washington maintained direct engagement and open channels with two major strategic competitors.
Yet the talks produced few concrete breakthroughs, underscoring the gap between diplomatic symbolism and real conflict resolution.
Moscow’s alternative vision of global power
The Moscow gathering the previous day showed the political appeal of a more representative international order, though its participants did not collectively speak for their national governments.
Where the Shenzhen summit brought together three permanent UN Security Council members, the Moscow gathering sought to rally countries frustrated by their limited influence over international institutions.
Russia’s ruling United Russia party hosted the Global South conference, presided over by former President Dmitry Medvedev and reportedly attended by approximately 300 representatives from 72 countries, including China, India, Iran, Turkey, Indonesia, Vietnam and countries across Africa and Latin America.
The gathering was part of Russia’s Movement for the Freedom of Nations, which advocates sovereignty, opposes unilateral sanctions and resists what Moscow describes as neocolonial practices.
According to United Russia’s account, discussions addressed economic cooperation, international representation and initiatives concerning the historical legacy of colonialism.
For Moscow, such platforms expand diplomatic networks and challenge Western efforts to limit Russian influence. Yet participation should not be confused with geopolitical alignment.
China’s deep economic ties with Western markets, India’s simultaneous partnerships with Moscow and Washington, and Turkey’s NATO membership show the limits of political convergence.
These countries may favor a more representative international system without supporting a unified geopolitical alliance.
The conference produced political initiatives rather than binding economic or security agreements among participating governments. Its significance lies in the demand for diplomatic alternatives, even as participants pursue competing national interests.
The limits of multipolarity
Shenzhen and Moscow reveal different visions of international influence. The great powers seek to manage strategic rivalries through direct negotiations, while emerging economies demand a voice in decisions affecting their security and prosperity.
Sanctions, technology restrictions, energy supplies and financial arrangements increasingly shape developing countries’ economic choices, often leaving them vulnerable to decisions made elsewhere.
For middle powers, diplomatic diversification offers flexibility, but strategic autonomy also requires economic resilience, credible institutions and sustainable commercial partnerships.
Coordinated negotiating positions among developing countries and greater representation in multilateral institutions could also strengthen their bargaining power, although regional disagreements complicate collective action.
Shenzhen showed that great powers can agree on the language of peace without accepting the compromises required to achieve it. Moscow revealed that countries seeking a more representative international order remain constrained by competing strategic interests.
A genuinely different world order will not be measured by how many powers sit at the negotiating table, but by whether those outside it can shape the decisions affecting their security, sovereignty and prosperity.

sources.news_title: What a sap: Trump lets himself get sweet-talked into total irrelevance
sources.text:
For many years, I was a fan of Big Brother, the perennial CBS summer reality show that I used to say demonstrated how gullible and stupid some people could be.
Then I realized I could be categorized the same way for watching the show.
If you ever watched, or still watch, season 6 stands out. That season featured a guy named Howie Gordon. He was, to me, a self-delusional egomaniac with cartoon-level bravado. He strutted around the house convinced he was a strategic genius.
When Howie finally won power as Head of Household, his rival Maggie and her tight-knit alliance stroked his ego, told him how brilliant he was, and talked him into nominating his own closest allies for eviction.
The foolhardy Howie blew up his own team’s majority while grinning for the cameras and bragging about what a mastermind he was. Meanwhile, his rivals laughed behind his back.
In Big Brother, the point of sweet-talking a vain houseguest is to get them to eliminate their own power and hand control of the game to you. That is precisely the scheme Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin pulled off in Shenzhen this week as they continue trying to push the United States off the global stage.
During this week’s trilateral summit between Donald Trump, Xi, and Putin, Trump tried to portray himself as some sort of stable-genius diplomat. Yet the 90-minute meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference ended with absolutely nothing that benefited the United States.
Instead, the world watched a visibly exhausted, gullible, and stupid American president fall hook, line, and sinker for cheap flattery. All Trump managed to do was hand two of America’s fiercest adversaries exactly what they wanted: a chance to make him look like a gullible and stupid sap.
Before Trump wobbled his buckling legs to the yacht-sized conference table, he was already humiliated. At the APEC plenary session, cameras once again caught “Sleepy Donald” with his eyes closed and bulbous head drooping while Xi delivered his keynote address.
When Trump finally woke up, he returned to acting like a starstruck contestant thrilled to be invited into the metaphorical Big Brother house. He pointed at Putin, beamed, and pathetically chirped, "Who is that? He’s my friend!" before gushing over their "great relationship."
Then he turned to fawn over Xi, who had rolled out military honors and flyovers when Trump arrived and greeted him with a Judas-like bro hug. The gullible and stupid Trump swooned over the pageantry.
Xi and Putin played their Head of Household roles like longtime watchers of the show. Like seasoned reality-TV schemers working a pliable nincompoop, they wily worked their way around “Dupe Donald.”
At that giant table, Xi placed Putin immediately to his right, which, for those not in the know, is the diplomatic seat of highest honor, while relegating Trump to a less important seat on the left. After nearly 90 minutes, Trump offered no joint press conference, took zero questions from reporters, and wobbled straight — oops, no, serpentine — back to his Qatari luxury plane, now known as Air Force One.
Meanwhile, Beijing and Moscow rolled out a four-point "Declaration Toward Peace" that Trump’s own lackluster press team didn’t release until later.
But it really didn’t matter, because the gist of the so-called declaration was as thin as it was empty. The two septuagenarians and one octogenarian signed off on vague platitudes about reforming the United Nations, boosting refined petroleum supplies, holding generic talks on nuclear risks, and rebuking the International Criminal Court for "abusing" its jurisdiction.
That last line was particularly horrific. It was an utter capitulation by Trump to Putin and a gift from Xi to a leader wanted by the ICC for war crimes in Ukraine.
Yet on the three really big-deal issues, Russia’s war in Ukraine, the unnecessary war in Iran, and some semblance of joint oversight of artificial intelligence, Trump walked away with nothing. He couldn't care less about Ukraine, wants to forget about Iran, and thinks there’s nothing wrong with letting AI run rampant.
I got a real kick out of how some were comparing the meeting in Shenzhen to the 1945 Yalta Conference, where an ailing, exhausted Franklin D. Roosevelt sat beside Joseph Stalin and Winston Churchill to map out the postwar world.
Sure, the physical comparison is tempting, given the glaring questions surrounding Trump’s slouching stamina. Yet even on his absolute worst day, FDR was better than Trump on Trump’s best days, which are few and far between.
More to the point, Yalta was a grueling wartime negotiation among allies hammering out world-altering terms. Shenzhen wasn't Yalta, not at all, not even close.
Xi and Putin know full well the implications of the midterm elections in the U.S. They know their patsy Trump is now a weakened president facing two years of potential gridlock, subpoenas, and investigations into his corruption.
On the flip side, Xi and Putin know they have a two-year window to press their Head of Household advantage and continue their push to make the U.S. irrelevant by exploiting Trump’s ego, gullibility, and stupidity.
After the meeting, standing beside Xi, Putin told Russian media, "I don't think anyone even expected everything to go so well."
For Moscow and Beijing, it really did. Putin and Xi, who cemented himself as the indispensable global power broker, rolled over Trump, and made him look even weaker; however, the obtuse Trump left still convinced he was the smartest guy at the table.
In the end, Xi and Putin don’t need to defeat Donald Trump. They just need to keep telling him how brilliant he is while he hands away America’s stature. They’re playing the game, Trump is playing the dimwitted fool, as they seek to get the United States evicted from the Big Brother house.

It also included representatives from the 21 Pacific Rim member economies: Australia, Brunei Darussalam, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, China, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Peru, the Philippines, Russia, Singapore, Taiwan (caleld “Chinese Taipei” on the official list), Thailand, the United States, and Vietnam.
The three leaders affirmed the importance of stable energy flows during the meeting, which Xi described as “groundbreaking” and Trump called “really making history” in his opening remarks, according to The Guardian.

Dialogue on reducing nuclear risks

sources.news_title: Trump, Xi, Putin conclude historic summit, but what did the talks actually achieve?
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin concluded their historic trilateral summit in Shenzhen on Thursday, and issued a joint declaration emphasizing strategic stability, international security, and nuclear nonproliferation. The meeting, held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, brought together the leaders of three of the world’s most powerful countries for discussions about global security and the future of their relations.
One could argue that this meeting was important. After all, the three leaders were brought together in the same room – an act symbolic of global order. However, was there anything concrete that came out of this meeting? What might change, and what are the likely ramifications?
According to the BBC, the meeting lasted approximately 90 minutes. That’s not a lot of time when one considers that each comment had to be translated into multiple languages.
The three presidents departed without making statements to the press. Putin appeared pleased with the outcome, telling Xi as he departed: “Thank you for organizing this. I don’t think anyone even expected everything to go so well.”
China’s official Xinhua news agency reported that Xi described the summit as “positive, constructive, and fruitful.” Xi said that the three countries shared a commitment to safeguarding world peace and strengthening communication and cooperation.
What is the China-Russia-US Heads of State Declaration toward Peace?
The meeting produced a four-point declaration titled the China-Russia-US Heads of State Declaration toward Peace. The document addressed the reform of the United Nations, energy security, international judicial institutions, and nuclear weapons.
Interestingly, China, Russia, and the US all appear to be concerned with the ICC. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently slammed the ICC in a speech at the Federalist Society.
China said that the three countries were committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security. Its generalized language does not indicate any particular outcomes.
As permanent members of the UN Security Council, the three countries also agreed on the need to reform the organization so that it could respond more effectively to global challenges.
The leaders also agreed to increase the production and “supply of refined petroleum products,” and emphasized the importance of “stable energy flows.” This comes amid concerns about energy security, primarily related to the Iranian conflict. China and Russia want to see the conflict scaled back, and both have worked with Iran. Prior to the US-Israel strikes, China had a 25-year deal with Iran prior. Russia, for its part, helped Tehran secure the 2015 Iran deal.
A third provision of the joint declaration addressed the jurisdiction of international courts. The declaration stated that the leaders recognized the importance of state consent and the immunities enjoyed by state officials. They agreed that “the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction.”
The fourth provision concerned nuclear weapons. The three leaders reaffirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.” They also committed to dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing nuclear proliferation.
The declaration did not announce specific nuclear arms reductions or establish a timetable for negotiations. However, it provided a framework for continued discussions among the three nuclear powers.
Xi outlines principles for relations between major powers
Xi called for a new approach to relations between major powers. The Chinese leader outlined four principles for relations between major powers: mutual respect, peaceful coexistence, cooperation, and dialogue. Xi also said that countries should respect each other’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, and political systems. He emphasized the importance of recognizing the core interests and major concerns of other countries.
One could read this as criticism of the US interfering in the Middle East by attacking China.
According to Xinhua, Xi warned against interference in “domestic affairs.” The report noted that Xi said, “On major sensitive issues concerning one another, it is important to communicate in advance, try to see things from one another’s perspective, act with caution, and in particular, not to challenge the red lines of one another.”
Xi argued that China, Russia, and the US should view one another as partners rather than adversaries. He warned against falling into the “Thucydides Trap,” a term used to describe the danger of conflict between established and rising powers.
In ancient Greece, the Athenians arrogantly challenged a Sparta-led alliance and, in the end, lost the war. The war was devastating for both sides, however, and led to a larger decline. If China and the US came into conflict, it would likely harm both countries immensely. This is the point that Xi appears to be making.
China’s leader linked this argument to the legacy of World War II, describing the three countries as major victors of the conflict with a responsibility to preserve the postwar international order. On nuclear weapons, Xi went further than the language of the joint declaration. He called for their eventual elimination, describing them as a “Sword of Damocles” hanging over humanity.
Xi also emphasized economic cooperation. He said that the three countries could combine their strengths in natural resources, manufacturing, and consumption to expand trade and economic opportunities. It is interesting how much the Chinese leader used Western terminology from the Classical era to discuss the modern world.
At the moment, China’s goal is to ease tensions and reduce the chances for escalation in the Middle East. It also wants to prepare for any future “misunderstandings.” For now, China seems to prefer diplomacy. However, it is keeping tabs on what will come next and whether the US will make any missteps.

sources.news_title: Trump, Xi and Putin Back UN Reform, Oil Boost and Nuclear Talks at Summit
sources.text:
Trump, Xi and Putin Back UN Reform, Oil Boost and Nuclear Talks at Summit
In a bid to address the current global energy crisis generated by the Iran war, the declaration expressed commitment to increase the production and supply for the benefit of all nations.
Beijing: The presidents of the US, China and Russia issued a "Declaration Towards Peace" after their historic meeting on Thursday, calling for UN reforms, increased petroleum production and supply, dialogue to reduce nuclear risks and an end to the alleged abuse of jurisdiction by the ICC and similar bodies.
A four-point declaration issued after the unprecedented trilateral meeting between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin held on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China's Shenzhen city outlined consensus on critical global issues while avoiding mention of concerns over AI and calls for its international governance.
The declaration - issued at the end of the 90-minute meeting, the first-ever by the top leaders of the three major countries - stated that they had an in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation and committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security.
Significantly for India, which has been vocal in calling for UN reforms, the three presidents, whose countries are the permanent members of the UN Security Council, expressed commitment to reform the world body, which is increasingly coming under criticism for its ability to prevent global conflicts.
"As permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, China, Russia, and the United States committed to reform the UN so that the UN can respond more effectively to global challenges and conform to its fundamental mission of international peace and security," the declaration said.
Trump has been a vocal critic of the UN, accusing it of inefficiency, bureaucratic excess, political bias and failure to deliver results on major international conflicts.
In a bid to address the current global energy crisis generated by the Iran war, the declaration expressed commitment to increase the production and supply for the benefit of all nations.
"The three countries plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations. They reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows," it said.
It was regarded as a major gain for Russia and relief for bulk importers of its oil, especially China and India, facing persistent threats of sanctions from the Trump administration against countries importing Russian oil.
The three Presidents came down heavily against the International Criminal Court (ICC) and similar bodies, warning that they must not abuse their jurisdiction.
"The three heads of state recognised that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction," it said.
The ICC is a permanent international court based in The Hague, Netherlands, under the Rome Statute adopted in 1998, which came into force in 2002.
The US, China, Russia, besides India and Israel, are not signatories, limiting its universal reach.
The ICC issued an arrest warrant against Putin in 2023 over allegations of human rights violations in Ukraine and against Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu. Currently, it is prosecuting former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte over alleged crimes against humanity.
The three Presidents also agreed to conduct dialogue to reduce the risks and proliferation of nuclear weapons. The US, Russia and China have a large arsenal of nuclear weapons.
"The three heads of state reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. The three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons," the joint declaration said.
The Russian and US heads of state expressed appreciation to China for hosting this historic trilateral Summit, it said.
"First of all, when it comes to history and historical importance: no such meetings had taken place before, and now it has happened. This is undoubtedly a page in diplomatic history," Putin was quoted as saying by the state-run TASS news agency.
Xi, who hosted the meeting, called it a "milestone event" and referred to the three countries' experience as allies during World War II.
As the main victors of World War II, China, Russia and the US should steadfastly safeguard the post-war international order, Xi said.
Xi said that China, Russia and the United States should continue to encourage parties to a conflict to sit down and talk, and settle disputes through political and diplomatic means, state-run Xinhua news agency reported.
He said that nuclear weapons, the Sword of Damocles that hangs over humanity, should be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of nuclear weapons.
He said that the three countries should strengthen economic cooperation and trade, combine their respective strengths as major countries in resources, manufacturing and consumption, so as to make the pie of cooperation bigger and achieve a win-win and all-win outcome.
China, Russia and the United States should be partners and friends, he said, adding that they should not go for conflict or confrontation among themselves, but should hold the line on peaceful coexistence and make efforts to avoid the Thucydides Trap, which means a new power rising to challenge the existing power.
Putin said Russia, China, and the US are capable of making a significant contribution to strengthening global stability if they cooperate in a constructive manner as partners.
Putin, who held a bilateral meeting with Trump earlier, said that during the meeting at the initiative of the US leader, significant attention was devoted to the conflict in Ukraine.
"We discussed this [the Ukrainian conflict] yesterday with the Chinese president, and today, at the initiative of the US president, we devoted a great deal of attention to it during our bilateral meeting," Putin said at the start of the trilateral summit, TASS reported.
Later, he told the media that the trilateral meeting was a serious endeavour and it was agreed that the format was a useful one but no overly ambitious goals had been set.
He added there was no agreement to regularly hold meetings in that format, BBC reported.
On stopping conflict with Ukraine, he questioned the idea that Russia is the aggressor, citing attacks on the Crimea bridge and Russian energy facilities.
Putin said it is up to the Ukrainian side to put an end to the war and to make compromises.
A TASS report said Putin was given the "seat of highest honour" during the trilateral meeting with Presidents Xi and Trump.
In a report in which it summarises "the main" takeaways from the "first in history" meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the US, TASS said, "to his [Xi's] right-hand side, which in diplomatic protocol is the seat of highest honour, sat Putin; to his left sat Trump."
Trump defended the trilateral meeting, saying that he is engaging China and Russia. "Too often, past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," he said.
"No problems were ever solved under the old school refusing to talk about them. No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement," he said.
( Source : PTI )

sources.news_title: What the four-point declaration by Putin, Xi and Trump really means
sources.text:
The full text of the declaration adopted following a trilateral meeting between the presidents of Russia, China and the United States — Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump — has been published. The document consists of four points and contains no detailed roadmaps. What can we make of them?
The declaration states that:
As permanent members of the UN Security Council, the parties reaffirm their commitment to reforming the United Nations so that the organisation can respond more effectively to global challenges and fulfil its founding mission of maintaining international peace and security.
There is no talk of abolishing the veto. All three powers formally support expanding the representation of developing countries from Africa, Asia and Latin America on the Security Council. The United States supports granting permanent seats to countries such as Germany, Japan and India. Russia opposes expanding the Security Council to include Germany and Japan, while supporting India and Brazil. China, for its part, takes a cautious approach to permanent membership for Japan and India.
The three countries plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations. They have reaffirmed the importance of stable energy supplies.
Russia, China and the United States occupy very different positions in the global energy market, so each interprets the concept of "stable energy supplies" in its own way. For Russia, this means removing barriers such as the price cap and sanctions against its tanker fleet and oil refineries. For the United States, the priority is to ensure that everyone buys American oil, even if they do not want to. China, meanwhile, is an importer. Its main concern is preserving its sources of oil — avoiding a war in the Persian Gulf and sanctions against Russia.
The leaders of the three countries note that the principle of state consent and respect for the immunities of state officials are of fundamental importance. They agree that the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their powers.
Neither Russia, China nor the United States is a party to the Rome Statute. For EU countries, however, support for the ICC is a cornerstone of their foreign policy and the concept of a "rules-based international order". When three of the five permanent members of the UN Security Council openly accuse the court of "abusing its powers", this calls its legitimacy into question — and, consequently, challenges the very idea of a "rules-based order". This is the only point on which there is genuine agreement.
The leaders of the three countries reaffirm that there can be no winners in a nuclear war and that it must never be fought. The three countries will engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
The parties have established a common political framework — "risk reduction" — but avoided the issue of actually reducing their nuclear arsenals, where they have deep disagreements. For China, this is a diplomatic victory: it has agreed to a trilateral dialogue format without taking on any commitments to limit the expansion of its nuclear capabilities. For the United States and Russia, it is a way to restart frozen channels of communication on strategic stability in a new trilateral format.
Although the leaders addressed the settlement of the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East before the negotiations began, neither issue is mentioned explicitly in the final text of the declaration. Leaving these conflicts out of the document made it possible to establish consensus in areas where agreement was achievable. This does not mean, however, that no decisions were made behind closed doors. We will learn about them through the actions of the parties.
The summit succeeded as a political signal: the leaders of the world's three major powers sat down at the same table and reduced the risk of uncontrolled escalation. But it is too early to speak of a breakthrough in humanity's progress towards a stable multipolar world.

sources.news_title: Trump’s 'farce' on full display as 'big win' flops on world stage
sources.text:
On Thursday, as President Donald Trump’s high-stakes trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin came to a close, one of the world’s top experts on authoritarianism pointed out a looming irony: that the very thing Trump came away bragging about achieved little more than handing “useful propaganda” to the United States’ main adversaries. According to renowned historian and Atlantic contributor Anne Applebaum, while the media has suggested lofty goals for the summit, it was mostly an opportunity for the three attending leaders to “mask their political failures.”
The meeting between Trump, Putin, and Xi has been repeatedly compared to the Yalta summit of 1945, in which President Franklin Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, and Soviet dictator Josef Stalin met to decide the fate of post-war Europe and how its zones of influence would be divided. According to Applebaum, the summit is mostly remembered not for building peace, but for forcing Eastern Europeans – whose leaders were not even in the room – into Soviet occupation and repression for decades to come. Now as Trump’s “inconsequential” summit has ended, argues Applebaum, in which “no serious agreement was signed,” it’s become clear what was actually accomplished: political theater.
“The meeting was brief, almost substance-free and carefully choreographed for the maximum benefit of the Chinese hosts,” writes Applebaum, “Its true purpose was not to end any wars — and certainly not to end Russia’s bloody invasion of Ukraine — but to produce propaganda photographs and video clips that each of the three leaders will now use to mask their political failures.”
According to Applebaum, that was “certainly Trump’s main goal,” who made it clear that his priority was not policy, but pageantry. As he told Fox News, the most significant moment was “the greeting yesterday, which in the history of China has never happened.” As Applebaum explains, Xi Jinping, aware of how easy it is to manipulate the American president, had met Trump at the airport. “This is a highly respected, this is a great president, one of the great presidents of China — and he’s never gone to the airport to meet somebody,” Trump blustered, rambling about “the fanfare, the beauty, the pageantry, the thousands of people, the young children, the soldiers, the whole thing,” adding, “that’s a big win for us. It’s a big win for China too.” Then, writes Applebaum, “The White House published a video clip, seemingly created to promote Chinese communism, showing all of that fanfare and putting Trump at the center of it — a big win for China indeed, and maybe a big win for Trump’s post-midterm ego, although hardly a big win for the United States.”
She explains why “the meeting also created useful propaganda” for Putin. The war he said would last three days has gone on for almost five years, inflicting 1.5 million casualties on Russia so far, while the country’s infrastructure has been devastated. Now, writes Applebaum, “Putin will use the Shenzhen meeting to tell Russians that their country is still a superpower, still allowed to sit in the same room as the Americans and the Chinese, still important on the world stage even as Russian power, influence, and prosperity dramatically shrink.” And for host Xi, the meeting broadcast his authority to the world. “With Trump’s cooperation, he telegraphed American decline, Chinese power, and Russian subservience,” explains Applebaum. “Even as the Chinese economy is experiencing a real-estate slump, manufacturing losses, and chronic unemployment, he made China look like the only serious country in the room. The American president was babbling about airport greetings. Russia is bankrupt without Chinese support. But Xi, safe in the knowledge that he has successfully obtained the American chip technology his military and industry need, was the master of ceremonies.”
In the end, Applebaum concludes, the so-called “Yalta 2.0” summit proved the old adage: “History does repeat itself — the first time as tragedy, the second time as farce.”

sources.news_title: Trump, Xi and Putin’s historic summit: Diplomacy or power play? 5 key takeaways
sources.text:
Behind the smiles, competing interests test prospects for cooperation after China talks
Dubai: Three of the world’s most powerful leaders sat around the same table, exchanged warm words and promised greater cooperation. But behind the historic meeting between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin lay a more complicated question: Was the summit a genuine step towards peace or an exercise in global power politics?
The 81-minute meeting in Shenzhen produced a joint declaration on international security, energy supplies and nuclear risks. Yet its significance may lie less in what was agreed than in what each leader hoped to achieve.
CNN reported that officials had expected few major breakthroughs. The meeting itself, rather than any binding agreement, was the central diplomatic achievement.
For Trump, the summit offered an opportunity to demonstrate his influence on the world stage following Republican losses in the US midterm elections.
He has struggled to deliver on promises to end the Ukraine war, while the prolonged confrontation with Iran has increased economic and political pressure at home.
Trump has sought closer personal relationships with both Xi and Putin, believing direct engagement can help overcome entrenched disagreements.
“I think as long as you and I are in charge of things, we’ll never have a problem,” he told Xi, according to CNN.
But personal diplomacy has yet to resolve the conflicts confronting Washington.
For Xi, hosting the unprecedented summit placed China at the centre of global diplomacy.
The meeting allowed Beijing to present itself as a major international power capable of bringing together Washington and Moscow despite their competing interests.
According to The New York Times, China secured the prestige of hosting the talks without accepting binding restrictions on its nuclear arsenal or endorsing a specific Ukraine peace plan.
Xi also avoided commitments that could complicate Beijing’s relationships with Russia and Iran.
His message was that major powers should cooperate rather than confront one another.
“History tells us that when great powers are at peace, the world is secure; when great powers clash, the world is in chaos,” Xi said.
For Putin, the summit marked a prominent return to international diplomacy after years of isolation by Western countries over Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Appearing alongside Trump and Xi reinforced Moscow’s claim to a central role in shaping international security.
The meeting also revived comparisons with the 1945 Yalta conference, when the Allied powers helped determine Europe’s postwar future.
Asked about the possibility of another Yalta, Putin responded: “What was so bad about Yalta?” according to The New York Times.
He argued that present-day conflicts would ultimately require recognition of realities on the ground.
But Putin’s subsequent refusal to negotiate with Ukraine following strikes on the Crimean Bridge exposed the limits of the summit’s peace rhetoric.
The meeting also highlighted the complex relationship between the three countries.
China and Russia have strengthened their strategic partnership, while Trump has attempted to improve relations with both governments despite disputes over trade, technology and security.
AFP and AP reported that the declaration contained broad commitments but no detailed framework for ending either the Ukraine or Iran conflict.
Neither Ukraine nor Iran participated in the trilateral discussions, raising questions about how far the three powers could advance peace without the countries directly involved.
For now, the summit has opened a channel for dialogue. Whether that produces meaningful agreements will depend on negotiations beyond Shenzhen.
In Kyiv, where Russian drones struck the city as the three leaders met in China, Ukrainians expressed anger at discussions about their country's future without their participation.
“What they want is to divide the whole world... they are all creating evil,” Gennadiy Bystrukhin, 68, told AFP, branding Trump, Xi and Putin “three losers”. One person was killed in the drone attacks, which also reportedly damaged the Dutch embassy and a landmark cathedral.
Oleg Obukhovsky, a 49-year-old Ukrainian war veteran, dismissed the summit's significance. “They are deciding nothing,” he told AFP. “This is not the Yalta Conference.” Referring to the conflicts confronting the three leaders, he added: “Trump has Iran. Xi has Taiwan. What can they possibly decide? It's nonsense.”
The central question remains whether the three leaders can turn their historic diplomatic engagement into practical cooperation — or whether competing national interests will ultimately prevail..
A diplomatic first, but limited agreements: Trump, Xi and Putin held their first trilateral summit, issuing a declaration covering energy, nuclear risks and international cooperation. No binding peace agreement emerged.
Trump seeks progress on two wars: The US president wants movement on Ukraine and Iran, but the meeting produced no announced ceasefire, timetable or peace framework for either conflict.
Xi strengthens China’s diplomatic profile: Hosting the summit allowed Beijing to present itself as a major global power without accepting significant new commitments on nuclear arms or Ukraine.
Putin returns to centre stage: The Russian president appeared alongside the US and Chinese leaders despite Western efforts to isolate him. His subsequent threat of retaliation over the Crimean Bridge highlighted continuing tensions.
The next steps matter more than the photographs: The declaration opens the possibility of further talks, but its significance will depend on whether the three governments establish concrete negotiations and deliver measurable results.

sources.news_title: Trump, Xi and Putin release 'peace declaration' from unprecedented summit
sources.text:
Trump, Xi and Putin release 'peace declaration' from unprecedented summit
Summary
U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed on a symbolic peace declaration in Shenzhen on Thursday, but announced no plans for nuclear arms-control talks. They said nuclear war must never be fought and pledged dialogue on nuclear risks without setting a timetable. The declaration also called for United Nations reforms and increased fuel supplies, but did not mention the wars in Ukraine or Iran. Putin said the statement set no ambitious goals and would not force countries to comply.
Key Facts
- The declaration said the three powers would conduct dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing nuclear proliferation, but gave no time frame.
- China has consistently rejected trilateral nuclear arms-reduction talks, arguing that its arsenal is much smaller than those of the United States and Russia.
- The leaders pledged to uphold state officials’ immunity in international courts, more than three years after the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Putin and other Russian officials over alleged war crimes in Ukraine; Moscow rejects the allegations.
- Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said the three countries would maintain coordination at working level after the summit.
- Trump said he and Xi agreed that having guardrails for artificial intelligence was good.
SHENZHEN, China — Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US and Russian counterparts Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin agreed on a symbolic "peace declaration" at an unprecedented three-way summit on Thursday and reaffirmed that nuclear war should never be fought, but announced no plans for arms control talks long sought by Trump.
A joint declaration released by the world's three biggest nuclear powers capped a three-day diplomatic swing by Trump through Asia that produced few tangible victories, despite his repeated boasts about making history and brokering peace.
Instead, the trip raised fresh questions among US allies about his increasingly close relationships with Xi, and with Putin, who continues to wage war with Ukraine.
The powers "reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and added that they would "conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation of nuclear weapons," without giving a time frame.
But the statement made no mention of any negotiations on a trilateral nuclear arms reduction treaty, something Trump has pushed since his first term and that China has consistently rejected, arguing that its arsenal is much smaller than those of the other powers.
Daryl Kimball, executive director of the US-based Arms Control Association, called the reaffirmation that a nuclear war should not be fought "positive," but added, "We need much more than rhetoric. We need action on disarmament diplomacy."
Trump referred to nuclear weapons at the start of the meeting, saying: "It’s not an easy thing to do – give them up."
The leaders also pledged to advance reforms of the United Nations, to increase supplies of fuel products for all countries and to uphold the immunity enjoyed by state officials in international courts.
The declaration made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine, or Trump's conflict with Iran, and in a news conference afterwards, Putin acknowledged it did not set ambitious goals and added that
nobody would be forced to comply with its decisions.
The reference to immunity of state officials came more than three years after the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Putin and other Russian officials over alleged war crimes in Ukraine. Moscow rejects the allegations.
"The pushback against international norms and courts is the most interesting aspect," said Jonathan Eyal, international director at the Royal United Services Institute think-tank in London. "The big powers dictate, the small powers suffer."
Eyal said Putin had been a winner from the summit and "gained credibility and escape from pariah status", while Trump "gained a photo opportunity he didn't need."
Trump told NBC after the meeting that the summit "went great."
"I think it was a 12. On a scale of zero to 10, I think it was a 12," he said. "Fantastic relationships built."
In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump said he was heading back to Washington and would hold a news conference at noon on Friday.
China's Foreign Minister Wang Yi said the three countries would maintain coordination at working level after the "peace summit." He said the leaders had exchanged their strategic intentions in person and established a "new paradigm" for interaction among the powers.
Analysts said Trump came to Shenzhen seeking to bolster his standing after his Republicans lost control of Congress in midterm elections this month.
US Senator Charles Schumer, who leads Democrats in the Senate, called the trilateral summit "a historic embarrassment that people will remember long into the future."
"It's a betrayal of the United States by a president who loves nothing more than to bow down to our adversaries for a photo op," he said.
The leaders met in a villa in wooded hills beside a lake in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen.
"We are really making history," Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. "No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement."
Xi in his turn said: "History tells us that when major powers live in harmony, the world is at peace. When major powers clash, the world falls into turmoil."
Differences over Ukraine, Iran and trade
Putin, fresh from a setback in Ukraine after the crippling of a key bridge linking Crimea to Russia, said the three had "numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine".
The meeting was a diplomatic coup for Putin, with Russia’s economy barely a 10th the size of China's and most of its businesses barred from trading with the West by sanctions.
European allies met in Berlin on Thursday to show their support for Ukraine, indignant after Trump embraced Putin as a "friend" at the summit and at the absence of Europe from the Shenzhen discussions.
"A Yalta format will not bring peace," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told reporters. "The United States know without us there will not be peace."
Putin rejected criticism comparing the summit to the 1945 Yalta Conference, where Soviet, US and British leaders helped shape postwar Europe. He said Yalta had not divided the world into spheres of influence but "codified the existing reality."
"In today's conflicts, too, we will have to come to terms with the realities on the ground."

Trump, Xi Jinping & Putin Issue 'Declaration Towards Peace'; Agree On UN Reforms, Oil Supply And Nuclear Risk
The presidents of the US, China and Russia issued a "Declaration Towards Peace" after their historic meeting on Thursday, calling for UN reforms, increased petroleum production and supply, dialogue to reduce nuclear risks and an end to the alleged abuse of jurisdiction by the ICC and similar bodies.
AI-generated summary, reviewed by editors
A four-point declaration issued after the unprecedented trilateral meeting between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin held on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China's Shenzhen city outlined consensus on critical global issues while avoiding mention of concerns over AI and calls for its international governance.
The declaration - issued at the end of the 90-minute meeting, the first-ever by the top leaders of the three major countries - stated that they had an in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation and committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security.
Significantly for India, which has been vocal in calling for UN reforms, the three presidents, whose countries are the permanent members of the UN Security Council, expressed commitment to reform the world body, which is increasingly coming under criticism for its ability to prevent global conflicts.
"As permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, China, Russia, and the United States committed to reform the UN so that the UN can respond more effectively to global challenges and conform to its fundamental mission of international peace and security," the declaration said.
Trump has been a vocal critic of the UN, accusing it of inefficiency, bureaucratic excess, political bias and failure to deliver results on major international conflicts. In a bid to address the current global energy crisis generated by the Iran war, the declaration expressed commitment to increase the production and supply for the benefit of all nations.
"The three countries plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations. They reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows," it said.
It was regarded as a major gain for Russia and relief for bulk importers of its oil, especially China and India, facing persistent threats of sanctions from the Trump administration against countries importing Russian oil.
The three Presidents came down heavily against the International Criminal Court (ICC) and similar bodies, warning that they must not abuse their jurisdiction. "The three heads of state recognised that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction," it said.
The ICC is a permanent international court based in The Hague, Netherlands, under the Rome Statute adopted in 1998, which came into force in 2002.
The US, China, Russia, besides India and Israel, are not signatories, limiting its universal reach. The ICC issued an arrest warrant against Putin in 2023 over allegations of human rights violations in Ukraine and against Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu.
Currently, it is prosecuting former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte over alleged crimes against humanity. The three Presidents also agreed to conduct dialogue to reduce the risks and proliferation of nuclear weapons.
The US, Russia and China have a large arsenal of nuclear weapons. "The three heads of state reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. The three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons," the joint declaration said.
The Russian and US heads of state expressed appreciation to China for hosting this historic trilateral Summit, it said. "First of all, when it comes to history and historical importance: no such meetings had taken place before, and now it has happened. This is undoubtedly a page in diplomatic history," Putin was quoted as saying by the state-run TASS news agency. Xi, who hosted the meeting, called it a "milestone event" and referred to the three countries' experience as allies during World War II.
As the main victors of World War II, China, Russia and the US should steadfastly safeguard the post-war international order, Xi said. Xi said that China, Russia and the United States should continue to encourage parties to a conflict to sit down and talk, and settle disputes through political and diplomatic means, state-run Xinhua news agency reported.
He said that nuclear weapons, the Sword of Damocles that hangs over humanity, should be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of nuclear weapons.
He said that the three countries should strengthen economic cooperation and trade, combine their respective strengths as major countries in resources, manufacturing and consumption, so as to make the pie of cooperation bigger and achieve a win-win and all-win outcome.
China, Russia and the United States should be partners and friends, he said, adding that they should not go for conflict or confrontation among themselves, but should hold the line on peaceful coexistence and make efforts to avoid the Thucydides Trap, which means a new power rising to challenge the existing power.
Putin said Russia, China, and the US are capable of making a significant contribution to strengthening global stability if they cooperate in a constructive manner as partners. Putin, who held a bilateral meeting with Trump earlier, said that during the meeting at the initiative of the US leader, significant attention was devoted to the conflict in Ukraine.
"We discussed this [the Ukrainian conflict] yesterday with the Chinese president, and today, at the initiative of the US president, we devoted a great deal of attention to it during our bilateral meeting," Putin said at the start of the trilateral summit, TASS reported. Later, he told the media that the trilateral meeting was a serious endeavour and it was agreed that the format was a useful one but no overly ambitious goals had been set.
He added there was no agreement to regularly hold meetings in that format, BBC reported. On stopping conflict with Ukraine, he questioned the idea that Russia is the aggressor, citing attacks on the Crimea bridge and Russian energy facilities.
Putin said it is up to the Ukrainian side to put an end to the war and to make compromises. A TASS report said Putin was given the "seat of highest honour" during the trilateral meeting with Presidents Xi and Trump.
In a report in which it summarises "the main" takeaways from the "first in history" meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the US, TASS said, "to his [Xi's] right-hand side, which in diplomatic protocol is the seat of highest honour, sat Putin; to his left sat Trump."
Trump defended the trilateral meeting, saying that he is engaging China and Russia. "Too often, past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," he said. "No problems were ever solved under the old school refusing to talk about them. No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement," he said.

sources.news_title: At historic summit, Xi and Putin share global stage with weakened Trump
sources.text:
SHENZHEN, China — As President Donald Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin met for a rare trilateral summit Thursday, they brought three different agendas — and three competing visions of the international order.
Never before had the leaders of the United States, Russia and China sat together without other counterparts. The meeting offered an opportunity for two authoritarian leaders to reinforce their standing on the world stage, sitting around a table with a politically weakened American president whose ambitions may exceed his leverage.
Yet for all its carefully choreographed displays of unity, the less-than-90-minute summit produced no major breakthroughs on the issues that mattered most to the three leaders. The meeting did not advance peace in Ukraine, though the leaders hinted in a joint statement published by Chinese media that the United States might start lifting some of the energy sanctions on Russia that it imposed after Putin’s 2022 invasion. And Trump’s push to persuade Moscow and Beijing to reduce their nuclear arsenals yielded only an agreement to begin a dialogue.
Trump in his opening remarks said the leaders were “really making history” by diverging from an era of diplomacy in which leaders avoided talking to their adversaries.
“No problems were ever solved under the old school, refusing to talk about them,” said Trump, speaking in a grand room with a mountain landscape painting and a large pink floral arrangement. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech. Together, we’re choosing a different course.”
But the first formal trilateral meeting of the three men highlighted the complexity of the emerging multipolar global order, with China rising as a strategic competitor to the United States.
The summit at a secluded, lakeside villa away from the bustling center of this tech capital was largely a victory for Xi, who wanted to leverage the event to showcase his role as a convener of global powers. He focused his opening remarks on China’s role in fostering international peace and stability, speaking of the special responsibilities the leaders have in a “global village” and urging them to “abandon Cold War thinking.”
He appeared to successfully avoid being drawn into direct negotiations over the Ukraine war or making concessions on nuclear arms. China possesses a much smaller nuclear arsenal than either the U.S. or Russia and has made clear it does not want to be drawn into arms-control talks until it can catch up. But he appeared to be open to establishing a crisis line among the countries, saying they needed “crisis communication and prevention mechanisms to ensure that misjudgments are minimized.”
Trump, a lame-duck president who has expressed concerns about nuclear proliferation since the 1970s, said the leaders of the countries with the three largest nuclear arsenals were “uniquely positioned” to reduce the number of nuclear weapons in the world. But he increasingly has less leverage as both Putin and Xi eye a future without Trump in the White House. Trump has not publicly commented on the meeting since it concluded.
Putin had seen an opportunity to discuss ending the war in Ukraine on his terms. But in his public remarks, he did not raise Moscow’s demands that NATO scale back its military presence in Europe. Putin sought to portray Russia as a geopolitical peer of the U.S. and China, saying the countries shared a mutual responsibility to “preserve and strengthen” the system of international law.
The leaders agreed in their joint statement that immunity for state officials is “of fundamental importance” and said the International Criminal Court must not abuse its authority. Multiple U.S. presidents have resisted the ICC’s authority, but Trump has been especially confrontational in his approach. His administration has imposed sanctions on the court following its arrest warrants for top Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, over the war in Gaza. That opposition provides common ground with Putin, who is subject to an ICC arrest warrant over alleged war crimes in Ukraine.
The leaders also committed to “promoting reform of the United Nations to enable it to respond more effectively to global challenges” and to increasing the production and supply of refined petroleum, as wars in Ukraine and the Middle East strain global oil supplies.
Before the meeting began, Trump appeared more focused on the optics of the event than the policy outcomes. In a Fox News interview ahead of the summit, he called the trip a “win” for the U.S. and China because of the “respect” Xi displayed when greeting him at the airport. Trump said he appreciated “the fanfare, the beauty, the pageantry, the thousands of people, the young children, the soldiers, the whole thing.”
Trump also said that it was beneficial for him to meet with Xi and Putin together because the two leaders “work together” and “have a relationship.” He suggested that part of the reason he wanted to spend time with them wasn’t strictly about geopolitical necessity.
“Can I tell you? They both like Trump. Now, what happens after me? That I can’t tell you,” he told Fox News.
From an economic or even a geopolitical perspective, Russia’s presence had an anachronistic air. Russia’s economy is one-eighth that of China and one-eleventh that of the United States. It isn’t a player in artificial intelligence or other advanced technologies. Its ability to boost allies outside its borders has turned out to be minimal in Venezuela, Iran and Syria in recent years, as it remains bogged down in Ukraine.
Russia has sought to frame the three-way meeting as a “new, modern Yalta,” inviting comparisons between Thursday’s summit and the eight-day conference in February 1945 where President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin discussed the postwar future of Germany and Europe.
That meeting helped shape the political division of postwar Europe and laid important foundations for the emerging Cold War. It also came to symbolize the pitfalls of allowing powerful countries to make decisions affecting other nations without their consent. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned against a “Yalta 2.0.”
“Big countries always think that they can make decisions about the future of all the world,” Zelenskyy told NBC, adding that it was “a huge mistake” not to involve smaller countries in those decisions.
But the leaders’ joint statements did not address the futures of Taiwan or Ukraine.
The trilateral meeting capped Trump’s three-day sprint through Asia, which included a stop in Manila.
Before heading to the session, Trump had a one-on-one meeting with Putin for about 40 minutes. He also separately had lunch with Xi, along with Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
In both meetings, he touted his personal relationships with his chief rivals, calling Putin a “friend” and touting his “outstanding personal relationship” with Xi.
Putin arrived first to their bilateral session and beamed at Trump as he walked in. The two men pumped hands as Trump told him “nice to see you,” then whispered something in Putin’s ear. Trump, who currently does not have his own press secretary, also patted Russian press secretary Dmitry Peskov on the arm and said, “You’re doing a great job.”
Rubio and Bessent, each of whom have pursued tough policies against Russia, stood unsmiling at Trump’s side, although a tight smile briefly crossed Rubio’s face as he leaned in to shake hands with the Russian leader.
“We’ve had a great relationship for many years,” Trump said before cameras were ushered out of the room. “We know each other for a long time, and I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start.”
Trump has always reveled in the showmanship of leader-to-leader diplomacy, especially when he has been able to talk alongside authoritarian leaders like Xi and Putin.
The White House released a sleekly edited video of Xi walking down a red carpet to greet Trump at the airport. The video highlighted the dancers, soldiers and tightly choreographed ceremony that took place as Air Force One landed.
Trump expressed gratitude that Xi broke protocol and greeted him at the airport, a gesture that reciprocated what he did when Xi came to the U.S.
On issues including control of advanced AI chips, tariffs and Chinese export controls on rare earth minerals, the warm displays between Trump and Xi masked rising tensions between rivals.
China has threatened countermeasures in response to the new U.S. restrictions on advanced AI chip exports. The Trump administration tightened the controls following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s admission that he had an affair with a woman who was allegedly a Chinese spy and an executive at a company engaged in smuggling Nvidia chips to China.
But Trump, who appeared to be increasingly focused on his dwindling time in office, did not appear concerned by those headwinds.
“We have a very special relationship and I think as long as you and I are in charge of things, we will never have a problem,” Trump said to Xi. “We’re never going to have a problem.”
---
Birnbaum reported from Washington. Joshua Yang and Cleve R. Wootson Jr. in Shenzhen contributed to this report.
