sources.text:
The Chinese, Russian and American presidents walked into their unprecedented summit with different aims.
In the end, Xi Jinping emerged serene, Vladimir Putin could feel emboldened and Donald Trump would likely claim success whatever happened, analysts said.
Here we break down what each leader can take home from Shenzhen:
Xi: the 'pivotal actor'
China's president had an opportunity to place his country on par with the US at the crux of global diplomacy and project an image of calm control over proceedings.
But there were risks too, such as Beijing's stance on Russia's war in Ukraine, which it has declined to condemn despite Western criticism that it tacitly supports Moscow.
At first glance, Mr Xi seemed to have walked the tightrope well.
"Xi positioned himself at the centre of the event, the pivotal actor and convener of great powers. The optics will bolster Xi's political standing," said Ryan Hass, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution.
A "declaration toward peace" published by the three countries after the meeting reflected several of China's long-standing positions, including its desire to reform multinational institutions such as the United Nations.
"By reaching strategic consensus... (the countries) can catalyse broader multilateral cooperation and guide the reshaping of global order and values," said Wang Yiwei, director of the Institute of International Affairs at Beijing's Renmin University of China.
Trump: much style, little substance
The US leader came into the summit needing a win, following a disastrous performance in the midterm elections that has left him facing two years as a lame-duck president.
He got off to a promising start when Mr Xi broke with decades of diplomatic protocol to welcome him personally in an elaborate ceremony at the airport in Shenzhen.
But it was unclear whether Mr Trump had scored any significant political victories beyond a photo opportunity with two men he has long lavished with praise.
It was notable that "there was no new agreement" between the powers, said Chong Ja Ian, an associate professor at the National University of Singapore.
The format "suggests the creation of conditions where Beijing, Moscow, and Washington call the shots for the rest of the world... (and) given Beijing's close ties with Moscow, they could potentially put Washington on the back foot", he added.
Prior to his trip, the US president had said he hoped for substantive discussions on nuclear weapons controls.
Read more: Zelensky in Berlin for summit of Ukraine allies
But the declaration said the countries would merely engage in "dialogue" on the issue, a vague term that does not commit them explicitly to stronger cuts.
"President Trump will claim political victory no matter what the outcome of the meeting," said Peter Loge, director of George Washington University's School of Media and Public Affairs.
"Whether or not anyone else agrees is an open question."
Putin: a seat at the table
Mr Putin would normally have entered the meeting as a junior partner, given Russia's economy and population are far smaller than China and the US.
But his war in Ukraine and apparently warm ties with Mr Xi and Mr Trump have positioned him as a far more consequential geopolitical actor.
He already scored a win by sidelining Ukraine and its European allies from any conversation on ending the conflict.
Chim Lee, a senior analyst with The Economist Intelligence Unit, said the formalisation of a three-way summit played further into Mr Putin's hands.
"The US and Russia have both been interested in having this trilateral meeting, and the China side has apparently been relatively reluctant," he said.
"The fact that China affirms its value means that this set-up is very likely to continue," giving Mr Trump less of an incentive to disrupt ties with China and Russia, he added.
Wu Xinbo, dean at the Institute of International Studies at Shanghai's Fudan University, said that the format showed the United States "can no longer dictate international affairs" and must treat both Russia and China "as equals".

Trump has long believed his ability to create personal connections gives him a diplomatic edge. The summit took place against the backdrop of Russia’s prolonged military offensive in Ukraine, instability in the Middle East following Trump’s attacks on Iran, and China’s growing influence in East Asia.

Xi, in his remarks, said the three nations shared a common position on protecting global peace.
The joint declaration also addressed the activities of international judicial institutions, stating that the International Criminal Court and similar bodies must not misuse their jurisdiction.
The position is particularly significant given that Putin is wanted under an arrest warrant issued by the ICC, while Trump’s administration has pledged to dismantle the court.
The statement further emphasised the need to respect state sovereignty and the diplomatic immunity of government officials.
It said the three countries recognised the importance of obtaining state consent and respecting the protections granted to officials while carrying out their diplomatic responsibilities. They also pledged to support reforms within the United Nations.
Before the summit, Putin said discussions would cover food and energy security, areas that have been affected by the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran.
In the joint declaration, the countries expressed their intention to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products, while stressing the need to maintain stable energy flows.
The unprecedented gathering has also raised concerns that the three powerful nations could seek to establish separate spheres of influence across the world, potentially making decisions affecting countries such as Ukraine without involving Kyiv or European governments.

Trump subsequently met Xi for one-on-one discussions, marking their third meeting this year. The US president described their relationship as very special.

The format "suggests the creation of conditions where Beijing, Moscow, and Washington call the shots for the rest of the world... (and) given Beijing's close ties with Moscow, they could potentially put Washington on the back foot", he added.
Prior to his trip, the US president had said he hoped for substantive discussions on nuclear weapons controls.
But the declaration said the countries would merely engage in "dialogue" on the issue, a vague term that does not commit them explicitly to stronger cuts.
"President Trump will claim political victory no matter what the outcome of the meeting," Peter Loge, director of George Washington University's School of Media and Public Affairs, told AFP.
"Whether or not anyone else agrees is an open question."
Putin: a seat at the table
Putin would normally have entered the meeting as a junior partner, given Russia's economy and population are far smaller than China and the United States.
But his war in Ukraine and apparently warm ties with Xi and Trump have positioned him as a far more consequential geopolitical actor.
He already scored a win by sidelining Ukraine and its European allies from any conversation on ending the conflict.
Chim Lee, a senior analyst with The Economist Intelligence Unit, said the formalisation of a three-way summit played further into Putin's hands.
"The US and Russia have both been interested in having this trilateral meeting, and the China side has apparently been relatively reluctant," he told AFP.
"The fact that China affirms its value means that this set-up is very likely to continue," giving Trump less of an incentive to disrupt ties with China and Russia, he added.
Wu Xinbo, dean at the Institute of International Studies at Shanghai's Fudan University, told AFP that the format showed the United States "can no longer dictate international affairs" -- and must treat both Russia and China "as equals".

sources.news_title: A New International Order? Xi, Trump & Putin Hold Historic Trilateral Summit in China
sources.text:
Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted his U.S. and Russian counterparts for a historic trilateral summit on Thursday, with the leaders of the three biggest nuclear superpowers meeting for about 90 minutes in Shenzhen. Afterward, the countries published a “peace declaration” that affirmed “nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.” The declaration also announced a commitment to increase petroleum production, called for reforms at the United Nations and urged the International Criminal Court and similar bodies to “not abuse their jurisdiction.”
While in China, President Donald Trump also had a separate meeting with President Vladimir Putin to discuss the war in Ukraine, though it’s unclear if they made any progress.
“It’s a significant post-1945 moment, which was the last time that we had great summits,” says Scott Lucas, professor of international politics at University College Dublin. “What is the most important takeaway … is an ascendant China. It was China that really set the terms of what was said.”
Transcript
NERMEEN SHAIKH: We begin today’s show looking at today’s historic trilateral summit in China between Chinese President Xi Jinping, President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin. The three leaders met for about 90 minutes.
After the meeting, Chinese state media issued what it described as a, quote, “peace declaration” by the Chinese, Russian and U.S. leaders. The four-point declaration called for reforms at the United Nations and said the three leaders, quote, “concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction.” The three countries are not signatories to the ICC. The ICC has issued an arrest warrant for Putin for war crimes committed in Ukraine.
The declaration also states, quote, “The three countries plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations.”
In addition, the declaration states, quote, “The three countries will engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing nuclear proliferation.”
AMY GOODMAN: Prior to the closed-door meeting, the three leaders shared brief remarks. This is Chinese President Xi Jinping.
PRESIDENT XI JINPING: [translated] This is the first time the leaders of our three countries have come together. It is a historic meeting. We will discuss how to safeguard world peace and promote strategic stability and relations among major powers. …
The world is undergoing rapid changes unseen in a century. The world is not peaceful, and challenges reveal true leadership. As major world powers and permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, our three nations should lead by example, collaborate to address global challenges, jointly safeguard world peace and stability, and make more significant contributions to the progress of humanity.
AMY GOODMAN: Russian President Vladimir Putin also spoke before the trilateral meeting in China.
PRESIDENT VLADIMIR PUTIN: [translated] For my part, I am convinced that Russia, China and the United States, and our respective peoples, are capable of making a significant contribution to strengthening global security and stability, provided they engage in constructive, partnership-based cooperation rooted in mutual respect, equality and a balance of interests.
NERMEEN SHAIKH: And this is President Trump speaking in China before the trilateral meeting.
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: As presidents of three of the world’s largest countries, we have a special responsibility to maintain open, respectful and productive dialogue on issues impacting not just our people, but the entire planet. Too often past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements. And we feel the opposite, and we think that we are sure about that. No problems were ever solved under the old school refusing to talk about them, so no peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech.
AMY GOODMAN: Well, we’re joined right now by Scott Lucas. He’s a professor of international politics at University College Dublin’s Clinton Institute.
Professor Lucas, thanks so much for being with us. First, if you can just talk about the significance of this moment, of these three world leaders coming together for the first time ever in China, President Trump, the Russian President Vladimir Putin, as well as the Chinese President Xi Jinping?
SCOTT LUCAS: Well, Amy, I think it’s a significant post-1945 moment, which was, you know, the last time that we had great summits, including discussing the future of China, in part because you’re looking at a changed international order. You’re looking at a United States which is no longer the leader of that post-1945 system. You’re looking at a Russia having succeeded the Soviet Union, which is very much tied down by this struggling invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year, isolated, in some part, economically and politically because of that invasion, struggling to escape that isolation. And you’re looking at, I think, what is the most important takeaway, both symbolically and in real terms, from the summit, which is an ascendant China.
It was China that really set the terms of what was said throughout this, beyond Ukraine, talking more about the global situation in a couple of ways. They did that symbolically by putting Xi right at the center, as you saw at that table, between Putin and Trump. China now is a great power. But they also did it with the specific terms that they put forward: strategic stability, unity, technology and innovation, and perhaps most striking, free trade — given that, of course, the United States had premised its post-1945 position on precisely that, but you have a Trump administration doing something much differently.
There’s a lot of specific takeaways, especially because Donald — because Putin’s priority was Ukraine, but this was a summit where you had Trump coming there for ego and the photo opportunity, Putin because of the problems with his invasion and trying to get an alliance with Trump to force Ukraine’s surrender, and China there for strategy, a political, economic and military free hand in pursuing its alternative system.
NERMEEN SHAIKH: Well, Professor Lucas, could you comment specifically on some of the remarks that were made by these leaders, what we mentioned in our introduction on the International Criminal Court, as well as — you know, we’re speaking to you — we’re here at COP31 at the U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey — this pledge that they would all increase petroleum production?
SCOTT LUCAS: So, one of the features where we are now, with the post-1945 system breaking, perhaps broken, is the dismissal of international law. And that is what you saw, on camera, before that closed-door meeting.
Vladimir Putin is wanted on war crimes charges, specifically the deportation of Ukrainian children, by the International Criminal Court. He does not want to face those charges. Donald Trump, who wants a friendship with Vladimir Putin, who will be shown in that vivid embrace of Putin — “He is my friend” — was there to carry out Putin’s wishes by saying the International Criminal Court should have no credibility — not even that its decisions can be questioned, it has no credibility. So, that is where we are, between two of the three leading powers, that there is no regard for the International Criminal Court. And the Chinese, of course, have sort of a different approach, because they’re looking for a different type of international system.
I think whether you’re at COP31 dealing with specific questions of climate change, or you’re dealing with specific questions of war crimes or broader questions of justice, this is a crisis moment for international law and for the ICC.
NERMEEN SHAIKH: And could you comment also on the fact that this meeting comes so soon after Jensen Huang, the chief of Nvidia, was forced to step down after reports of his affair with an alleged Chinese spy, in addition to two others in his company? Do you think that’s significant at all? And would it have come up?
SCOTT LUCAS: I don’t think it would have come up directly, but I think it’s part of the important backdrop at work here, which is, on the one hand, China is working from a position of leverage — of course, we’ve known this for quite some time — with its possession of rare earth minerals, with its dominance in terms of magnets. But, of course, it needs chips.
On the other side, you have a Trump administration which is almost in chaos right now for two very important reasons. First of all, American companies, in this case Nvidia, allegedly, was taking 20% of its revenue from China, despite saying that none of it came from there. Now, that’s a specific gap regarding where you are in terms of AI and technology in the U.S.-versus-China relationship. And that is magnified by the revelation that the Commerce Department did not enforce more than 100 recommended export controls on China-linked firms.
So, on the one hand, you have China, which has a very clear policy where it wants to go with tech and AI and with innovation and with control of resources, and you have a Trump administration that’s scrambling and divided over where exactly its position is right now in terms of the relationship with China. Open supply of chips? Export controls? Something in between? Where does it go next?
AMY GOODMAN: I also wanted to ask you — at the same time that they’re meeting in Shenzhen in China, Putin and Xi and Trump, you have Jared Kushner and Witkoff meeting with President Zelensky, with other European representatives. The significance of this and what this means?
SCOTT LUCAS: There are two different agendas right now in terms of where we go next regarding that invasion of Ukraine. The Russian agenda is to push Ukraine to the side — don’t discuss a ceasefire, don’t discuss security guarantees for Kyiv, don’t discuss freezing the frontlines; instead, call for a Europe-wide security architecture, by which the Russians mean security guarantees for us, and NATO withdrawing to its 1997 position, which not only means, of course, that Ukraine is exposed. It means that there’s no NATO, effectively, in the Baltic states or in Poland.
On the other hand, you have Ukraine and Europe that are saying, “No. Before you discuss a European-wide security arrangement, you need to have a specific commitment to a ceasefire on the current frontlines. You need to have an agreement that Russia will not get more territory. And you need to have security guarantees for Kyiv, so we don’t have a repeat of this aggression.”
The problem that we have right now is, is that the Russians are trying to impose their agenda by putting Donald Trump in their pocket. How are they doing that? You saw part of it today from Putin’s rhetoric, and from Trump supporting that rhetoric. But perhaps more seriously, you have it through the Russians putting tens of billions of dollars of proposed economic deals on the table, including some deals that would benefit friends and family of Donald Trump and his envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, and saying, “You can get all these deals, provided this invasion is halted on our terms.”
AMY GOODMAN: Let me ask you something, and this last question: On the one hand, you have President Trump announcing there shouldn’t be regulation of SI, what he calls superintelligence, but also, will this set a new template for the international order, major powers meeting amongst themselves, ignoring the U.N. Security Council and other forums? We just have a minute, Professor Lucas.
SCOTT LUCAS: First of all, Trump’s statement, supported by some of the people in the technological industry, is: “Look, don’t restrict us. Don’t do anything to restrict what we’re doing with AI.” More broadly, what you’re seeing here is this isn’t a question of international order. International order has broken down because certain countries and certain leaders don’t believe in international order. I think that’s true of Vladimir Putin. And with regret, I think that’s also true of Donald Trump and his inner circle. But I think the country that benefits from that lack of respect for international order, and we saw it today, is China.
AMY GOODMAN: Professor Scott Lucas teaches international politics at the Clinton Institute, University College Dublin.
Coming up, we’re going to go here to Turkey to summarize what’s happening at the U.N. climate summit, in the plenaries, but also outside, where all sorts of groups are protesting all the issues that are being discussed here. Stay with us.
[break]
AMY GOODMAN: “The Fire of Antalya,” performed at the COP31 opening ceremony.

sources.news_title: Putin defends his 'Yalta', as 3-way summit draws parallels to post-war carve-up
sources.text:
Putin defends his ‘Yalta’, as 3-way summit draws parallels to post-war carve-up
Nov 19 - Vladimir Putin defended a comparison between his summit with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping on Thursday and a conference at the end of World War Two reviled by Eastern Europeans, denying that either event aimed to carve the world into spheres of influence.
Some of Ukraine's allies had expressed concern that Thursday's three-way meeting between the leaders of Russia, the United States and China would be an attempt to replicate the Yalta Conference between the Soviet Union, Britain and the US that set terms for the global order after World War Two.
That 1945 summit is scorned in much of Eastern Europe as a betrayal, because it is widely seen as having ratified Moscow's dominance over countries occupied by Soviet troops at the time, which remained under Communist control through the Cold War.
Asked about the comparison by a reporter, Putin rejected the suggestion that there was anything wrong with either event.
"I want to emphasise this, and I want it to be perfectly clear: there was no division of the world into 'spheres of influence' at Yalta. Yalta simply acknowledged the realities that had emerged in the wake of the Second World War. What else were they supposed to do — keep the war going?" he asked.
"Yalta merely codified the existing reality. And in today’s conflicts, too, we will have to come to terms with the realities on the ground."
With Russian forces controlling about a fifth of Ukraine, Putin has frequently used the phrase "realities on the ground" to press his demands for peace terms that Kyiv says would amount to its capitulation.
'NOT THE YALTA OF PUTIN'S DREAMS'
The echoes of Yalta have special resonance for Ukraine and its European allies, which fear a scenario in which Trump and Putin might seek to impose a settlement on Moscow's terms without them at the table.
Ukraine's foreign minister mocked the comparison, noting that a Ukrainian attack had just knocked out the Crimean Bridge, which connects Russia to the peninsula it seized from Ukraine, site of the resort town that hosted the 1945 conference.
"Shenzhen is not the Yalta of Putin's dreams. Meanwhile, Russia has practically lost its bridge to the real Yalta in occupied Ukrainian Crimea," Andrii Sybiha wrote on X. "Time for him to wake up, get real, and end the war he can never win."
Putin, at his press conference, said the Yalta Conference had "formalised the victory over Nazism" and something similar would be welcome now, a clear allusion to his demand for the "denazification" of Ukraine. Ukraine rejects that as a baseless slur and bogus justification for Putin's 2022 invasion.
Ahead of the Shenzhen meeting, the Kremlin had said that attempts to compare it to Yalta were "games of political scientists". Some historians have also played down comparisons.
While the earlier event brought together three leaders on the verge of final victory in World War Two, two of those taking part on Thursday are still bogged down in unresolved crises: Putin in Ukraine and Trump in Iran.
And while Yalta lasted eight days and still resonates eight decades later, Shenzhen was over in less than two hours, with a five-paragraph "peace declaration" whose lasting historical significance has yet to be seen. REUTERS

sources.news_title: Trump meets Xi and Putin: What did the historic summit achieve?
Trump Declared History in Shenzhen. The Summit’s Statement Skipped Two Wars.
sources.text:
Before sitting down with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping for three-way talks in Shenzhen, Donald Trump called Xi his “friend” and spoke of a shared interest in reopening the Strait of Hormuz. In this C-SPAN clip, Trump delivers his opening remarks at the one-on-one meeting, where warm words about U.S.-China relations met the reality of an ongoing war in Iran.
Donald Trump pointed at Vladimir Putin as he arrived for their meeting in Shenzhen on Thursday. “Who’s that?” he asked. Then he answered his own question. “He’s my friend.”
“We look forward to our meeting,” Trump said after greeting the Russian president. “We have had a great relationship for many years — we’ve known each other for a long time, and I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this or at least start.”
The Kremlin said Putin emerged from the meeting in an “excellent mood.” Trump also called Chinese President Xi Jinping his “friend” and told the two leaders as their three-way talks began that they were “really making history.” Then came the declaration. It managed to discuss world peace without naming either of the wars Trump said he had raised.
The first meeting of its kind among the leaders of the United States, China and Russia took place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. The Associated Press, citing Russian officials and Chinese state media, reported that the three agreed to pursue U.N. reforms, boost fuel supplies and continue talks on reducing nuclear risks. No major breakthrough was announced.
Ukraine was the main topic of Trump’s one-on-one meeting with Putin, according to Kremlin foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov, whose remarks CNN reported via Russia’s state news agency TASS. Putin also brought up the war during the three-way talks. By the time the declaration came out, the subject had disappeared.
In Berlin, meanwhile, Ukraine’s allies were gathering for talks of their own. Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, were expected to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European leaders. Kushner said the discussions would cover what a settlement might look like and how Ukraine’s security might be assured after the war. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk had a shorter response to Trump calling Xi and Putin his friends. “God, protect us from such friends,” he wrote.
The omission of Iran was just as telling. In his separate meeting with Xi, Trump spoke of a shared interest in reopening the Strait of Hormuz. The summit’s declaration touched on fuel supplies, leaving out the U.S. war that made reopening the strait a diplomatic priority. Washington wants oil moving again while its own war remains unresolved.
There was a serious reason for the three leaders to sit down. New START, the last nuclear arms treaty between Washington and Moscow, expired in February. Trump wants a successor that includes China, whose arsenal, the AP reported, remains considerably smaller than either the American or Russian stockpile. What limits are Washington and Moscow prepared to accept on their much larger arsenals, and what would Beijing get in return for joining them? Shenzhen produced an agreement to keep talking about nuclear risk. The work of negotiating actual limits still lies ahead.
A first meeting can open a door. What matters now is whether the governments walk through it. That means sustained arms talks with verifiable limits on the table, negotiations in which Ukrainians have a say over their own future, and an American policy toward Iran that addresses the war as urgently as it addresses the flow of oil. Trump already has the photograph. The people living through these wars are still waiting for a reason to remember the summit.

sources.news_title: Trump Spends Entire Summit Fangirling Over Putin
sources.text:
Trump Has Super Normal Reaction to Seeing Authoritarian Dictator Putin
Donald Trump could not stop fangirling over his Russian counterpart.
Vyacheslav PROKOFYEV/AFP/Getty Images
Donald Trump isn’t even trying to hide his affinity for Russia anymore.
The U.S. president was all buddy-buddy with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, celebrating the authoritarian warmonger every chance he got.
Upon first seeing Putin, Trump walked over and rhetorically asked, “Who is he?” while pointing at the Russian leader. Then he answered his own question: “He’s my friend.” The two shook hands, whispered in each other’s ears, and then prepared to sit down.
Trump points to Putin and says “he’s my friend” before walking over and shaking his hand. https://t.co/IztoWA4Qih
The two were similarly cozy during a photo op later that day, where Trump arrived first. As Putin approached, Trump looked toward him and clapped, shaking Putin’s hand when he arrived and pulling him in to pat Putin on the back.
I didn’t realize Trump did a small clap for Putin when he saw him earlier. https://t.co/0w5eLtqgmc
The pair’s conviviality was a stunning public display—particularly as Russia continues to batter and barrage Ukraine. But Trump has spent much of his political career kowtowing to Moscow. Last year, he not only invited Putin to the U.S. for the first time in a decade but also had U.S. service members literally roll out a red carpet for the Russian dictator.
This year, Trump waived practically all of the new sanctions the U.S. put in place on Russia, brokered an eyebrow-raising deal to buy diesel from Moscow, and seemingly played a role in a military intelligence lapse that opened up Kyiv to attack last month.
But overall, the U.S. president has little to show for the profound international recognition he’s offered the Kremlin. Discussions between Trump, Putin, and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Shenzhen summit, for instance, largely sidestepped the topic of Ukraine, despite massive U.S. investments in the region.
Nonetheless, Trump took the opportunity to show the world just how enthusiastic he was about America’s long-standing adversary.
“We are really making history,” Trump said as the meeting began. “Today marks the first-ever trilateral meeting between our countries, and it’s an honor to be with you, Vladimir.”
Trump, 80, Fully Falls Asleep During International Summit
Donald Trump decided that APEC was the perfect time for a televised nap.
Ng Han Guan/Getty Images
Grandpa’s napping again!
President Donald Trump appeared to fall asleep during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s speech at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit Wednesday, closing his eyes and falling forward in his chair as Jinping spoke about global trade.
EMBARRASSING on the world stage: Donald Trump falls asleep during the APEC summit in China https://t.co/yTmBWYIHxh
Trump has struggled to keep his eyes open at a series of public events in recent months, dozing off during a health care announcement at the White House, an Oval Office press conference on fraud, another announcing a new steel plant in Iowa, a roundtable on cybercrime, and the signing ceremony for his executive order changing the childhood vaccine schedule, as well as after getting excited about Russian President Vladimir Putin’s birthday, and repeatedly during the 9/11 memorial event at the Pentagon. This, plus his strange walking pattern and the needle marks on his hands, has medical experts concerned. The man’s health is not trending upward.
The president’s allies, however, insist that he’s doing just fine. Wrote White House communications director Stephen Cheung on X Thursday: “Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth.” (No, you cannot.)
“This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung wrote, lying.
Peace Negotiator Jared Kushner Is Using War to Make Bank
The president’s son-in-law holds a major stake in a key defense contractor.
Jared Kushner, right, hugs Guenter Sautter, the foreign and security policy adviser to the German chancellor.
Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP/Getty Images
Jared Kushner, right, hugs Guenter Sautter, the foreign and security policy adviser to the German chancellor.
Jared Kushner failed to disclose his significant financial stake in a company directly profiting from the wars he was sent to mediate.
Kushner’s private equity firm Affinity Partners failed to disclose its $32 million stake in Arxis, a Connecticut-based defense contractor, The Atlantic reported Wednesday. The company produces “mission-critical” components of F-35 fighter jets, Navy destroyers, nuclear submarines, and anti-missile systems—the exact kind of assets that have been deployed in the conflicts in the Middle East and Russia-Ukraine, where Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law, has served as a negotiator for the White House.
Affinity Partners purchased its stake in Arxis after Trump was reelected, but the purchase was not disclosed to the Securities and Exchange Commission until November 5, just two days after the midterm elections. Per SEC rules, investment managers that own more than $100 million in certain kinds of securities must disclose them within 45 days. But when Affinity filed its required paperwork in mid-August, the company made no mention of Arxis. Three months later, Affinity amended the form to include information about the defense contractor. Is it possible that Trump’s billionaire son-in-law was concerned that his blatant war profiteering could impact the midterm elections?
In its latest quarterly report, Arxis said that it got a “significant portion” of its revenue from suppliers and contractors with the U.S. government, specifically the Department of Defense, and noted that “rising geopolitical tensions” promised accelerated investments in global defense spending. For years Arxis had lost money, but after Trump returned to office, it was suddenly able to turn a profit. Last year, the company made $1.6 billion, and around 47 percent came from defense and space spending.
This is far from the first time that Kushner has been accused of blatant self-dealing in his service to Trump. He used used peace negotiations with Russia to concoct a multibillion-dollar deal to benefit this business partners, invested in a firm that saw massive gains from Israel’s ongoing military campaign in Gaza, and used his gig as special envoy as an opportunity to try to raise funds from foreign governments and individuals in the Middle East.
Last month, Kushner was accused of overseeing foreign slush funds filled and managed by the leaders of the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, and Israel and getting paid $50 million by the UAE to get former Secretary of State Rex Tillerson fired. Kushner has denied these allegations.
Google’s Attempt to Force Schools to Use Its AI Tools Is Backfiring
Three of the biggest school districts in the U.S. are weighing turning away from Google Search.
Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images
A growing number of schools across the country are looking for search engine alternatives in lieu of Google’s AI ultimatum.
The company announced earlier this month that it plans to turn off search engine access as soon as next year for K-12 schools that toggle off its AI tools, claiming the decision is necessary based on the technologies’ recent fusion. But educators were not satisfied by that.
Some of the country’s largest school districts—including in Los Angeles, New York, and Chicago—are considering doing away with Google altogether.
“If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options,” Kamar H. Samuels, the chancellor of New York City schools, said in a statement. “We refuse to accept the false binary Google has laid out.”
Potential options include DuckDuckGo and Microsoft’s Bing, both of which offer users the option to disable AI-generated answers. Google, meanwhile, has only offered school districts more ways to interact with AI, such as AI Mode and AI Overview, which provides users with chatbot search functions and summarized results, reported The New York Times.
“We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers,” Google told the Times in a statement Wednesday, disclosing that the company would turn off its Gemini AI program and search engine for schools “until schools decide which services to enable.”
Studies conducted over the last several months have indicated that the risks attached to the use of AI in schools outweigh the potential benefits. A January report by the Brookings Institution’s Center for Universal Education found that AI can “undermine children’s foundational development,” and that “the damages it has already caused are daunting.”
New skill development and problem-solving abilities are among the chief concerns when it comes to early-age AI dependence. Children can easily fall into a catch-22 in which they continually offload their work onto the AI, diminishing their self-confidence and self-reliance in the process, according to the Brookings Institution report.
“When kids use generative AI that tells them what the answer is,” Rebecca Winthrop, one of the report’s authors, told NPR in January, “they are not thinking for themselves. They’re not learning to parse truth from fiction. They’re not learning to understand what makes a good argument. They’re not learning about different perspectives in the world because they’re actually not engaging in the material.”
Cops Detained Teens at Gunpoint After AI Misidentified Bag of Chips
A lawsuit reveals the police and school principal then joked about the incident.
Sergio Flores/Bloomberg/Getty Images
After school on October 20, 2025, 16-year-old Taki Allen was waiting with three friends outside Kenwood High School in Baltimore County, Maryland, for a ride home from football practice. Allen was eating a bag of Doritos. Suddenly, at least six Baltimore County Police Department vehicles arrived at the scene, and officers leapt out, guns drawn, forcing the boys to the ground and searching them.
The teens hadn’t done anything wrong. But Omnilert Gun Detect, an artificial intelligence weapon-detection system that scans security footage for firearms, had used the school cameras to misidentify Allen’s bag of chips as a gun.
Allen and his classmates Yui-Osa Ogbeide, Devon Thompson Jr., and Keith Winfield III are all Black. The Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law filed a lawsuit on their behalf Tuesday against the police department, the Baltimore County board of education, school administrators, and several individual officers.
“The encounter was terrifying and life-threatening,” the lawsuit says. “With armed police encircling them for no apparent reason, each student feared for his life and the lives of his friends.”
After failing to find anything in the search, one police officer reportedly told the students, “AI is not the best,” and another said, “Fucking Omnilerts.” As the officers were leaving, another said, “Hey, thanks for not running away, that would have been a real problem.”
The lawsuit showed that the principal texted school staff and administrators after the police left to laugh about the incident.
The lawsuit also points out that the Omnilert Gun Detect system was patented in 2022, “barely a year” before it was implemented in Baltimore County schools. After it identified Allen’s doritos as a firearm, it sent a text message to a group of school administrators and police, who reviewed the alert and canceled it. But 10 minutes later, the school principal sent a screenshot of the footage in the security alert to a co-worker, who sent it to the police department, who then responded at the scene.
The Omnilert Gun Detect parent company, Omnilert LLC, has claimed that the AI system “distinguishes guns from inert objects such as cell phones, hand tools, common office objects and more” in order to “diminish false positives.” Maryland’s Office of the Inspector General for Education, however, found that 99 percent of alerts in Baltimore County schools have been false positives.
“These students were failed not only by a technology that is prone to false alerts, but also by the very adults meant to keep them safe when we send them to school. Instead of this protection, they were met with guns and traumatized,” Damon Hewitt, president and executive director of the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law said. “And it could have been even worse.”

sources.news_title: MichaelSavage.com – Trump knocks ‘old school’ diplomacy at historic but brisk 80-minute summit with Xi, Putin
sources.text:
SHENZHEN, China — President Trump slammed the “old school” of American diplomacy as he kicked off a historic but brief trilateral summit with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping. It was the first-ever trilateral summit among the leaders of China, Russia and the US — and Trump entered the discussion emphasizing his interest in a pact to reduce nuclear arms. The discussion lasted just 80 minutes, including 10 minutes of opening remarks to the media. A four-point joint declaration released afterward pledged more “dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.”
The declaration, which was released by China and Russia and not immediately confirmed by the White House, also called for unspecified reforms to the United Nations, more oil production and condemned the International Criminal Court, which has indicted Putin for war crimes in Ukraine. “No problems were ever solved under the old school refusing to talk about them,” Trump said in his opening remarks alongside the world’s most powerful dictators, whom he met with separately and pronounced his “friends” earlier Thursday. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech,” Trump added as the summit started about two hours later than planned.

sources.news_title: Trump, Xi, Putin wrap up historic summit with nuclear arms control on agenda
sources.text:
The leaders of the United States, China and Russia concluded their first-ever trilateral summit in Shenzhen on Thursday, with nuclear arms control and regional conflicts high on the agenda amid deepening geopolitical and technological competition among the world’s major powers.
U.S. President Donald Trump met Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for more than an hour on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, describing the gathering as a historic diplomatic occasion.
“As the world’s three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used,” Trump said in his opening remarks.
Xi called for the prohibition and destruction of nuclear weapons and the establishment of a world free of them, according to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.
The summit marked the first leader-level talks on nuclear arms control since New START expired in February. Its lapse ended the last remaining bilateral nuclear treaty between Washington and Moscow, raising concerns about an unrestricted arms race.
Trump has called for a new agreement that would bring Beijing into nuclear arms control negotiations. China, however, has long maintained that Washington and Moscow should substantially reduce their stockpiles before asking it to accept limitations on its comparatively smaller arsenal.
China is estimated to possess more than 600 nuclear warheads, while the United States and Russia hold more than 5,000 each.
“Once you have the nuclear weapons, it’s very hard not to have them,” Trump said. “So it’s not an easy thing to do, give them up.”
Xi also proposed regular high-level exchanges and the creation of a crisis communication mechanism among the three powers to help manage tensions.
No concrete agreement on nuclear arms control was immediately announced following the summit.
The White House released a statement that said the three leaders “reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.”
The statement also said that the three countries would hold dialogues on preventing the spread of nuclear weapons and minimizing nuclear risks.
Taiwan’s security concerns
Ahead of Thursday’s trilateral meeting, Taiwan’s government downplayed expectations that the island would feature prominently in discussions among the three leaders.
“From what we know, Taiwan is not the focus,” Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) spokesperson Liang Wen-chieh told a news briefing in Taipei.
Liang said the discussions were more likely to prioritize securing a ceasefire in Ukraine and addressing Iran’s nuclear program.
“Even if Taiwan is mentioned, it will be a relatively peripheral issue,” he said.
Liang also expressed doubts about whether the three leaders could reach substantive agreements given their competing interests and the limited time available for negotiations.
“The three parties want different things, and their priorities are also different,” he said.
Taiwan nevertheless featured in a separate bilateral meeting between Trump and Xi earlier on Thursday, their third face-to-face meeting this year.
Xi told Trump that Washington should “stick to doing the right thing” on Taiwan to avoid major setbacks in relations between the two countries, China’s official Xinhua News Agency reported.
According to Xinhua, Trump told Xi that the United States “does not support Taiwan independence.”
The White House had not released its own account of the bilateral meeting at the time of Xinhua’s report.
During the trilateral summit, Xi also called on major powers to respect each other’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and core interests, warning against crossing red lines on sensitive issues.
Taiwan, which joined APEC in 1991 under the name Chinese Taipei, is represented at this year’s summit by Acer founder and honorary chairman Stan Shih, appointed by President Lai Ching-te to attend on his behalf.
Competition over artificial intelligence
The summit took place against a backdrop of mounting technological rivalry between Washington and Beijing, particularly over artificial intelligence (AI) and access to advanced semiconductors.
Trump has held off on imposing tougher restrictions on China’s access to advanced chips used to develop AI models, indicating that additional measures could aggravate bilateral tensions.
Xi urged Washington and Moscow to work with Beijing to maintain stable global supply chains and called on the three powers to “abandon Cold War mentality, not pursue decoupling and breaking chains.”
Competition over emerging technologies has become a major point of friction between the world’s two largest economies, alongside disagreements over trade and access to strategically important raw materials.
U.S. officials have accused Beijing of failing to fully implement commitments made during a Trump-Xi meeting last year, including pledges to purchase more American agricultural products and ease export restrictions on rare earth minerals used in electronics manufacturing.
A trade truce reached last year following successive tariff increases is due to expire on Jan. 10, 2027, adding another source of uncertainty to bilateral relations.

sources.news_title: Putin, Trump and Xi Call for UN Reform, Nuclear Dialogue in ‘Declaration on Peace’
sources.text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping adopted a joint declaration on peace following their trilateral meeting in Shenzhen on Thursday, Nov. 19.
The four-point document, released by China’s state news agency Xinhua, outlines commitments to reform the United Nations (UN), expand energy supplies and hold discussions on nuclear risks.

The statement made no mention of Ukraine.
The three leaders, whose countries are permanent members of the UN Security Council, said they would work to make the organization more effective in responding to global challenges and maintaining international peace and security.
They also pledged to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products, citing the importance of stable energy flows.
Another aspect addresses international legal jurisdictions. The leaders said respect for state consent and the immunities of government officials was essential, adding that the International Criminal Court (ICC) and similar bodies should not abuse their jurisdiction.
The final point of the declaration commits three countries to dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the increase of nuclear weapons. The leaders mentioned that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.
The Shenzhen meeting was the first trilateral summit between Trump, Putin and Xi, held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
The White House initially said Russia’s war against Ukraine would not be discussed, identifying nuclear arms reduction and the war in Iran as priorities. However, Trump later said he wanted to raise the Ukraine conflict with both Putin and Xi.
Moscow had sought to use the summit to discuss possible settlements of the war. Putin reportedly proposed the trilateral format during the telephone conversation with Trump on Oct. 9.
Ukraine, meantime, warned against decisions being made without its participation. President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv and European governments shared the position that questions concerning Ukraine must be decided with Ukraine involved.

sources.news_title: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping issue joint 'peace declaration' in first ever meeting together
sources.text:
The first-ever meeting of U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Chinese President Xi Jinping concluded Thursday in Shenzhen, China, with the three leaders issuing a joint “peace declaration” after talks that covered total nuclear disarmament and the war in Ukraine.
The historic trilateral session, held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit at the Kylin Villa, lasted roughly an hour and a half. Trump departed immediately afterward, heading to the airport to board Air Force One for the return flight to the United States. Yet minutes after the gathering ended, Putin shifted to a far more confrontational stance in a press briefing, promising a “much more painful response” to Ukraine following recent strikes on a bridge linking Russia and Crimea.
Putin warned that Russia would not tolerate any form of military ties between Ukraine and Europe or the deployment of troops as part of any deal to end the conflict. He insisted the bridge targeted by Kyiv served exclusively civilian purposes, rejecting claims that it carried military equipment or petroleum products. At the same time, he stated that Ukraine has a right to its own security—but not at the expense of Russia’s—and suggested Trump appeared genuinely committed to ending the war.
European leaders had previously voiced concern that the meeting could sideline them from negotiations. Putin claimed Moscow remained ready to continue talks but demanded that European officials travel to Russia, something they have refused to do since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022. “The American side is urging us to agree to the involvement of the Europeans … Through diplomatic channels, we suggested to the Europeans to come to Moscow. And after that we will decide in what format the talks can continue,” he said.
Around the large round table, the leaders of the world’s largest nuclear powers delivered opening remarks. Trump declared, “I’m delighted that this trip has also given us the opportunity for this first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China, and today, so in that sense, and I think in lots of other ways, we are really making history.”
He later added, “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech,” framing the session as a chance to explore new approaches. Trump specifically highlighted nuclear weapons, arguing the three countries were “uniquely positioned” to discuss reducing their arsenals and lowering the risk of their use.
The other leaders did not address the topic, even as China has rapidly expanded its stockpile, tripling it to 620 warheads according to the Pentagon’s latest assessment.
Putin opened by praising Xi for hosting the meeting and casting the three nations as sharing responsibility for international peace, citing their roles as World War II victors and founders of the United Nations.
He pointed to potential common ground on food and energy security, regional conflicts including Ukraine, and efforts against terrorism and transnational crime, stating the countries could advance global peace through “mutual respect, equality, and a balance of interests.”
Trump was accompanied by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. A brief bilateral meeting between Trump and Putin preceded the trilateral session.
Video showed Putin appearing uneasy at first, but the atmosphere shifted when Trump entered, pointed at him, and told those present, “Who is he? He’s my friend.” Trump later told reporters, “We have had a great relationship for many years — we’ve known each other for a long time, and I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this or at least start.”
While the leaders announced their joint peace declaration, its precise contents were not immediately clear, and the White House has not released a readout of the closed-door discussions.
The gathering of the three nuclear powers was widely viewed as unlikely to yield major breakthroughs given deep divisions over Ukraine, Iran, nuclear weapons, and trade. Whether any tangible progress occurred behind closed doors remains unknown.

He said the victory in World War Two brought the three countries together, while safeguarding the purposes and principles of the United Nations Charter and upholding international peace are their shared responsibilities.
In a statement, the White House said the three heads of state had an in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation and committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security.
Washington added that the three countries planned to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the "benefit of all nations".

sources.news_title: No major breakthroughs as Trump, Xi and Putin sit down for historic meeting
sources.text:
Three leaders who view their nations as the world’s superpowers sat around a table together for the first time on Thursday to talk about reducing nuclear risks and resolving conflicts – a step they applauded as historic though they did not agree to any major breakthroughs.
US President Donald Trump, China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin offered smiles and friendly handshakes, ending their talks at a villa in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen by agreeing on points including UN reforms and a vow to get more fuel to the market.
It remains to be seen if the gathering could mark a pivot in world history – or become a quickly forgotten photo op.
The leaders made only brief remarks at the beginning and did not take questions afterward, releasing a short statement that did not mention the wars in Ukraine or Iran, two issues that Trump said he raised with the leaders in separate one-on-ones earlier in the day.
The agreements were modest, but the rhetoric was not.
“We are really making history,” Mr Trump said. “The United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk of those weapons being used.”
Mr Xi earlier said the meeting would focus on “promoting world peace”. Mr Putin, for his part, said the countries “hold joint responsibility for maintaining international peace”.
After the meeting, Mr Xi called it positive, constructive and fruitful, while Mr Putin described the talks as open and candid.
The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New Start, expired in February, and Mr Trump has said he wants “a new, improved and modernised” deal that includes China.
But China has less motivation to accept limits given that its arsenal of more than 600 warheads is far smaller than the more than 5,000 warheads believed to be in each of the US and Russian stockpiles.
Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, said the meeting could at best start a process that would eventually lead to a sustained set of talks for reducing nuclear arsenals.
“We need more than diplomatic theatre and photo opportunities between Xi, Putin and Trump,” Kimball said. “And one meeting will not likely produce dramatic breakthroughs.”
The leaders also talked about Iran and trade.
The US president earlier had a separate one-on-one with Mr Xi, their third substantial meeting this year.
Mr Trump said they had a shared interest in having oil shipped through the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil shipments from the Middle East that was repeatedly shut because of attacks in the Iran war. Mr Trump suggested he would push Mr Xi to buy more agricultural products from America.
Mr Xi said that relations between the U.S. and China have been “generally stable and improved” during Mr Trump’s presidency.
The official Chinese news agency Xinhua reported that Mr Xi discussed Taiwan with Mr Trump and said the two countries needed to improve communication on economic and trade issues.
Mr Trump also added a separate sit-down with Mr Putin, marking the first time the leaders have met for talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal on Russia’s war in Ukraine.
“Wonderful things can come out of this – or at least start,” Mr Trump said, calling Mr Putin “my friend”.
The US president also added that the trio would talk about ways to “protect our nation’s sovereignty from rogue, globalist organisations such as the International Criminal Court”.
In their joint statement, the three countries took aim at the court, saying state officials should enjoy immunity from its prosecutions and warning that it should not abuse its jurisdiction.
Mr Putin is wanted by the court, and Mr Trump’s administration has imposed sanctions on ICC officials and the institution itself as part of a campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the United States and its allies, including Israel.

sources.news_title: Trump, Xi and Putin Agree on Oil, Nuclear Risks and UN Reform: 5 Key Takeaways
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to pursue United Nations reform, increase refined petroleum production and supply, and hold talks on reducing nuclear risks at their trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday.
The four-point declaration also addressed the International Criminal Court (ICC), emphasizing state consent and respect for government officials' immunity. However, it didn't establish specific production targets, nuclear arms-reduction measures or implementation deadlines.
The declaration made no mention of Ukraine, although Putin said the war was discussed during his separate meeting with Trump. Here are five key takeaways from the summit.
1. Nuclear Risk Dialogue, but No Arms-Reduction Targets
The declaration called on the three countries to pursue dialogue to reduce nuclear risks and prevent nuclear proliferation. It stated that "a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought." The declaration didn't include nuclear arms-reduction targets or a timetable for negotiations.
Xi described nuclear weapons as a "sword of Damocles hanging over humanity" and called for them to be "completely banned and completely destroyed." The scale of the three countries' nuclear arsenals underscores the significance of the issue. The Federation of American Scientists' 2026 estimates put the United States' total nuclear inventory at about 5,042 warheads, Russia's at 5,420 and China's at 620.
2. Oil Supply Pledge Leaves Production Details Open
The three countries agreed to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations. The declaration didn't specify how much additional fuel would be produced, how the supply would be distributed or when the commitment would take effect. It also provided no production quotas or implementation schedule.
The pledge signals an effort by the three countries to coordinate on energy supply at a time when disruptions to global oil flows have heightened concerns about market stability, and its impact will depend on how the governments translate the broad commitment into practical measures.
3. UN Reform Gets Support, Without a Concrete Plan
The declaration expressed support for reform of the United Nations, an institution in which all three countries hold permanent seats on the Security Council, and the leaders didn't set out specific changes to the council, propose a timetable or explain how they would approach questions such as its membership and decision-making powers.
The issue remains contentious because changes to the Security Council's composition or voting rules could affect the influence of its five permanent members, which include the United States, China and Russia. Any major reform would require broad support among UN member states.
4. Declaration Challenges ICC Jurisdiction
The leaders also addressed the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court, emphasizing the importance of state consent and immunity for government officials. The declaration argued that the ICC and similar international bodies shouldn't abuse their jurisdiction. The position reflects longstanding objections by governments that reject the court's authority in cases where they haven't accepted its jurisdiction.
In March 2023, the ICC issued an arrest warrant for the Russian president over alleged unlawful deportation and transfer of children from occupied areas of Ukraine to Russia. The warrant concerns allegations and isn't a criminal conviction.
5. Ukraine Was Excluded From the Joint Declaration
Putin said he discussed the Ukraine conflict with Trump during their separate bilateral meeting, but the issue was not addressed in the three leaders' joint declaration. The absence of Ukraine from the joint statement also means the declaration didn't establish a trilateral position on the war or set out a joint plan for ending it.

sources.text:
By Lucretia Hughes
SHENZHEN, China — In an unprecedented diplomatic gathering, the leaders of three of the world’s most powerful nations met Thursday as President Donald Trump joined Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping for historic discussions involving nuclear weapons, international security and ongoing global conflicts.
The meeting, held in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, brought together the leaders of three nations whose military capabilities, economic influence and geopolitical relationships play significant roles in shaping international affairs.
The summit marked the first formal three-way meeting of its kind involving the sitting leaders of the United States, Russia and China.
Three World Powers at One Table
Trump described the gathering as a historic opportunity to pursue diplomacy among nations that have frequently found themselves on opposing sides of international disputes.
“We are really making history,” Trump said during opening remarks.
The president emphasized the importance of maintaining communication between powerful nations, particularly when disagreements involve military conflicts and nuclear weapons.
“No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement,” Trump said.
Putin also acknowledged the importance of cooperation, pointing to shared interests in resolving regional conflicts, including the ongoing war in Ukraine.
Xi emphasized the importance of peaceful relations among major powers and encouraged cooperation in addressing global challenges.
The three countries collectively possess some of the world’s largest military capabilities, with the United States and Russia maintaining the two largest nuclear arsenals.
Nuclear Weapons and Global Security Take Center Stage
One of the central issues surrounding the summit was nuclear arms control.
The last remaining nuclear arms limitation treaty between the United States and Russia expired in February, raising concerns about the future of international agreements designed to restrict nuclear weapons.
Trump has expressed interest in establishing a broader nuclear agreement that includes China.
However, Beijing has historically resisted participating in the same nuclear arms reduction framework as Washington and Moscow, arguing that its arsenal is substantially smaller.
During Thursday’s meeting, the leaders discussed the importance of reducing nuclear risks.
Following the summit, Chinese and Russian officials released a declaration stating that the three countries reaffirmed the principle that nuclear war must never be fought.
The declaration also called for continued international dialogue on nuclear security.
Although the statement represents a diplomatic commitment, it does not establish a new binding nuclear arms reduction treaty.
Ukraine, Iran and International Conflicts
The gathering also provided an opportunity to discuss ongoing international conflicts.
Russia’s war in Ukraine remains a major source of tension between Moscow and Western governments.
Trump has repeatedly expressed his desire to negotiate an end to the conflict, while Putin has maintained Russia’s position on its security interests.
The conflict involving Iran was another issue Trump identified as a subject of discussion.
However, the declaration released following the meeting did not establish specific agreements to end either conflict.
Questions remain about whether Thursday’s discussions will produce additional negotiations or concrete diplomatic progress.
Leaders Release Joint Declaration
Following the meeting, China and Russia released what they described as a declaration agreed upon by the three leaders.
According to Reuters and the Associated Press, the document addressed several areas of international cooperation, including nuclear security, reforms to the United Nations and energy supplies.
The declaration also included language supporting immunity for state officials in international courts, an issue that has generated controversy in international legal proceedings.
The document did not announce a comprehensive peace agreement or a resolution to the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran.
The leaders concluded their discussions after more than an hour.
A Historic Moment With Uncertain Outcomes
The significance of Thursday’s meeting extends beyond the discussions themselves.
The United States, Russia and China have competing interests involving military strategy, international trade, territorial disputes and diplomatic influence.
Despite those differences, the gathering demonstrated a willingness among the three governments to engage directly at the highest level.
Supporters of high-level diplomacy argue that communication between competing nuclear powers can reduce misunderstandings and create opportunities for negotiations.
Critics caution that diplomatic meetings do not necessarily translate into meaningful policy changes, particularly when participating governments remain divided over major international conflicts.
For the United States, the meeting also raises questions about future relationships with traditional allies and the role Washington intends to play in shaping international security agreements.
What Comes Next?
The summit concluded without a comprehensive agreement resolving the major conflicts discussed.
Nevertheless, the declaration provides a framework for continued dialogue on nuclear risks and other international issues.
Whether the discussions lead to additional negotiations, formal agreements or changes in international relations remains uncertain.
For now, the meeting represents a significant moment in modern diplomacy: the leaders of the United States, Russia and China sitting together to discuss issues that affect the security and stability of nations around the world.
Three world powers met at one table. The question now is whether their discussions will produce lasting diplomatic progress.

SHENZHEN, China — President Trump opened a historic but tightly timed trilateral summit with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping by criticizing what he called the “old school” approach to American diplomacy.
The meeting marked the first trilateral summit involving the leaders of the United States, Russia and China. Trump entered the talks signaling that reducing nuclear arsenals would be a central priority.
The session lasted 80 minutes, including 10 minutes of opening comments delivered in front of the media.
A four-point joint statement issued afterward called for expanded “dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.”
The declaration, released by China and Russia but not immediately confirmed by the White House, also urged unspecified reforms at the United Nations, encouraged increased oil production and condemned the International Criminal Court, which has indicted Putin on alleged war-crimes charges related to Ukraine.
“No problems were ever solved under the old school refusing to talk about them,” Trump said during opening remarks alongside the leaders of China and Russia, whom he had met separately earlier Thursday and referred to as his “friends.”
“No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech,” Trump added as the summit began roughly two hours behind schedule.
“Together, we are choosing a different course. A historic summit offers us the chance to seek out new opportunities and approaches on a range of very important issues.”
Trump presented nuclear disarmament as the summit’s main focus, while also identifying three additional subjects: ending the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and working together against what he called “rogue globalist organizations,” including the ICC, in defense of national sovereignty.
An administration official had characterized the nuclear discussions beforehand as an initial step, rather than negotiations expected to produce an immediate agreement.
“As the world’s three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used,” Trump said.
“The power is unbelievable, unthinkable.”
Speaking with Fox News on Thursday morning, Trump said the three countries “only need about 10” nuclear weapons each and argued that “you don’t need 4,000.”

Putin, who has been indicted by the ICC over alleged war crimes in Ukraine, described the three leaders as stewards of global peace in his opening remarks.
“We hold joint responsibility for maintaining international peace,” Putin told Trump, who launched the Iran war in February, and Xi, whose military expansion has fueled concerns that China could eventually attempt to seize Taiwan.
“Our task [is] to preserve and strengthen the system of international law,” Putin said, despite Russia’s attempt to capture Ukrainian territory, a conflict that has resulted in hundreds of thousands of deaths.

Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have issued a joint declaration following their first official three-way summit in Shenzhen, China. The three leaders pledged to uphold strategic stability and international security, discussed energy cooperation and reaffirmed that a nuclear war must never be fought. However, their meeting has also raised concerns about a possible new division of global spheres of influence, with Europe once again left out of discussions on Ukraine.
The 90-minute meeting took place on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen. It ended at 11 am Hungarian time, after which the three presidents released a joint statement outlining the main areas of agreement.
According to the BBC, the declaration focuses on maintaining strategic stability and international security, improving energy security and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons. The leaders also addressed the immunity of state officials and the role of international institutions.
Four key points of the joint declaration
The statement sets out four main areas of cooperation:
- UN reform: As permanent members of the UN Security Council, China, Russia and the United States pledged to promote reforms that would enable the organisation to respond more effectively to global challenges and fulfil its central mission of maintaining international peace and security.
- Energy security: The three countries intend to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products, while stressing the importance of maintaining stable energy flows.
- International legal institutions: The leaders recognised the importance of the principle of national consent and respect for the immunity of state officials. They agreed that the International Criminal Court (ICC) and similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction.
- Nuclear weapons: The three presidents reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. They also confirmed that dialogue is underway to reduce nuclear risks and prevent the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
Xi Jinping reportedly described nuclear weapons as a sword of Damocles hanging over humanity, according to Chinese state media. He also called for their complete prohibition and destruction.

Leaders praise the meeting, but Ukraine remains a sensitive issue
The three presidents all appeared satisfied with the outcome of the meeting. According to China’s state broadcaster CCTV, Xi described the talks as “positive, constructive and highly productive”, stressing the importance of protecting the hard-won peace.
The Chinese president said the major powers must respect one another’s legitimate security concerns and work together to address global challenges.
“As long as dialogue continues and the doors remain open, there is hope for peace,” Xi said, according to Chinese state media.
Putin also expressed satisfaction. In a video released by the Kremlin after the meeting, the Russian president can be seen saying goodbye to Xi as he leaves the summit venue.
“Thank you for organising this. I don’t think anyone expected everything to go so well,” Putin said.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov described the atmosphere as positive, while Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov claimed that Ukraine had not been the central topic of the discussions.
However, Trump made clear that he would welcome discussions on the war. At the beginning of the meeting, he said that dialogue was essential to achieving peace and expressed his wish to see the conflict come to an end.
“I would like to see this war end,” the US president said.
Trump also described the summit as an honour and thanked Xi for the warm welcome. He argued that previous leaders had too often avoided talking to countries with which they disagreed.
“We think differently. (…) Peace has never been achieved without the possibility of dialogue,” he said.
Fears of a new division of global influence
Despite the positive tone of the meeting, the summit has raised concerns that the three leaders could be laying the groundwork for a new division of the world into spheres of influence, sometimes described as a possible “Yalta 2.0”.
The comparison refers to the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the United States, the Soviet Union and the United Kingdom discussed the post-war order in Europe.
One of the main concerns is that Trump and Putin once again discussed the war in Ukraine without European leaders at the table. The meeting also took place against the backdrop of growing tensions over Taiwan, which Beijing considers part of its territory.
According to Chinese sources, Xi told Trump that Washington must handle the Taiwan issue appropriately if it wants to avoid damaging relations with Beijing, HVG reported. Although the United States does not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, it remains an important arms supplier to the island.
China has rejected comparisons between the summit and the Yalta Conference, arguing that such interpretations reflect outdated Cold War thinking. Beijing says it supports a multipolar international order rather than a world divided between a handful of dominant powers.
Nevertheless, concerns about the emergence of competing spheres of influence persist. Trump’s approach to the Americas, sometimes referred to as the “Donroe Doctrine”, reflects Washington’s ambition to maintain a dominant position in North and South America. Russia, meanwhile, continues to seek influence in Ukraine and other former Soviet republics, while China is expanding its position in Asia and Africa.
The situation is not identical to that of 1945, however. The European Union remains a major economic power, and several middle powers continue to support an international order based on international law.
Australia calls on Putin to end the war
Not everyone at the APEC summit shared the conciliatory tone of the three leaders.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese directly called on Putin to end Russia’s war against Ukraine during the organisation’s plenary session.
“The two main causes of disruptions to trade are the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, and we must do everything we can to bring them to an end,” Albanese said.
He then addressed the Russian president directly: “And I say this very clearly to President Putin: end the war, end it now.”
They signed a “Peace Declaration” after which Putin and Trump said “War is Peace and Ignorance Is Strength” all of which was applauded by their cheerleader Viktor Orban.
