SHENZHEN, China (AP) — Three leaders who view their nations as the world's superpowers sat around a table together for the first time on Thursday to talk about reducing nuclear risks and resolving conflicts — a step they applauded as historic though they did not agree to any major breakthroughs.
U.S. President Donald Trump, China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin offered smiles and friendly handshakes, ending their talks at a villa in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen by agreeing on points including U.N. reforms and a vow to get more fuel to the market. It remains to be seen if the gathering could mark a pivot in world history — or become a quickly forgotten photo op.
The leaders made only brief remarks at the beginning and didn't take questions afterward, releasing a short statement that did not mention the wars in Ukraine or Iran, two issues that Trump said he raised with the leaders in separate one-on-ones earlier in the day.
The agreements were modest, but the rhetoric was not.
“We are really making history,” Trump said. “The United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk of those weapons being used."
Xi earlier said the meeting would focus on “promoting world peace.” Putin, for his part, said the countries “hold joint responsibility for maintaining international peace.”
After the meeting, Xi called it positive, constructive and fruitful, while Putin described the trilateral talks as open and candid, calling the format “useful and substantive.”
“It is a serious collaborative work,” he said in response to a question about whether this format is something other than just an image of three leaders coming together.
The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New START, expired in February, and Trump has said he wants “a new, improved and modernized” deal that includes China. But China has less motivation to accept limits given that its arsenal of more than 600 warheads is far smaller than the more than 5,000 warheads believed to be in each of the U.S. and Russian stockpiles.
Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, said the meeting could at best start a process that would eventually lead to a sustained set of talks for reducing nuclear arsenals.
“We need more than diplomatic theater and photo opportunities between Xi, Putin and Trump,” Kimball said. “And one meeting will not likely produce dramatic breakthroughs.”
The leaders also talked about Iran and trade
The U.S. president earlier had a separate one-on-one with Xi, their third substantial meeting this year.
Trump said they had a shared interest in having oil shipped through the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil shipments from the Middle East that was repeatedly shut because of attacks in the Iran war. Trump suggested he would push Xi to buy more agricultural products from America.
Xi said that relations between the U.S. and China have been “generally stable and improved” during Trump's presidency. The official Chinese news agency Xinhua reported that Xi discussed Taiwan with Trump and said the two countries needed to improve communication on economic and trade issues.
Trump also added a separate sit-down with Putin, marking the first time the leaders have met for talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal on Russia’s war in Ukraine.
“Wonderful things can come out of this — or at least start,” Trump said, calling Putin “my friend."
Trump has frequently boasted of his rapport with Putin, as relations between the U.S. and Ukraine appear to have cratered recently. Trump rejected new Russia sanctions, while Kyiv was undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war.
The U.S. president also added that the trio would talk about ways to “protect our nations' sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court."
In their joint statement, the three countries took aim at the court, saying state officials should enjoy immunity from its prosecutions and warning that it should not abuse its jurisdiction. Putin is wanted by the court, and Trump’s administration has imposed sanctions on ICC officials and the institution itself as part of a campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the United States and its allies, including Israel.

sources.text:
At a lakeside villa in Shenzhen on Thursday, Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin produced a joint "Declaration toward Peace" at a trilateral summit that Russians would like us to think was Yalta 2.0. But the only war these unlikely peaceniks mention—and there are plenty to choose from—is a nuclear one that hasn’t even happened.
Not Ukraine, where Russia’s full-scale invasion nears its fifth anniversary. Not Iran, where Washington and Tehran have settled into a frozen war of rival blockades around the Strait of Hormuz. Gaza and Sudan go unnamed, as does Taiwan, where the threat of one hangs overhead, sometimes literally as Chinese jets practice for an invasion.
What the three not-so-great men did agree on fits on an index card. And, like most index cards, it probably belongs in the trash.
Read More on Analysis
The U.N. should be reformed by the countries that hold its veto. The world needs more refined fuel. International courts should mind their own business. And nuclear war is bad, a view Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev inked together 41 years ago this week.
This is not a peace plan. It’s not even a Yalta-style carve-up into spheres of influence, which, grim as it is, would at least be tangible. Instead, it flatters three large egos belonging to men who agree on little except that none of them should answer to anyone: not to courts; not to countries without a U.N. veto; not to treaty limits; not even really to their allies. Nearly every commitment shields the signatories from accountability, tries to vibe more fuel into existence, or recycles an ancient vow.
Call them what you like. The three amigos! The three musketeers! The three little pigs! Here’s their dodgy declaration, as distributed by China and Russia, Dissected.
"China-Russia-U. S. Heads of State Declaration toward Peace"
"Toward" is doing a great deal of work, unless they mean tanks rolling forward. Peace through strength, right? Putin and Trump both raised Ukraine in the room. None of it reached the page. Even the 1987 Reagan-Gorbachev summit statement named Afghanistan, the Iran-Iraq War, and Cambodia. Volodymyr Zelensky feared Shenzhen might produce a Ukraine deal struck behind Kyiv’s back. But it delivered nothing on Ukraine at all.
"The Russian and U.S. heads of state expressed appreciation to China for hosting this historic trilateral Summit."
How sweet. The most concrete commitment in the declaration is a thank-you note, and Putin owes Xi plenty. China is propping up his war in Ukraine, and, really, Russia has no business pretending it’s a great power. He should have been there to serve Xi and Trump tea.
"The three heads of state had an in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation and committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security."
The in-depth exchange lasted about 90 minutes. As for "maintaining" strategic stability, there’s less to maintain than there was. The war in Ukraine thunders on. Russia wages hybrid war against NATO allies. The U.S. and Israel upended what was left of Middle East stability when they took on Iran in February. Meanwhile, the Iranian regime is still the Iranian regime. And New START, the last treaty limiting U.S. and Russian strategic nuclear forces, expired on Feb. 5, leaving the world’s two largest arsenals uncapped for the first time in more than half-a-century. Sorry, what were we maintaining again?
"As permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, China, Russia, and the United States committed to reform the U.N. so that the U.N. can respond more effectively to global challenges and conform to its fundamental mission of international peace and security."
Three of the five veto holders agree that the U.N. needs fixing, without saying what is broken. "Reform" seems to mean a U.N. even less able to constrain permanent members more interested in war and insecurity.
"The three countries plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations."
Look, everyone wants cheap gas. Americans wanted it before the midterms and got Trump’s war in Iran and $6 diesel instead. China, too, lost a key oil supplier when the U.S. blockaded Iran. Russia’s oil industry, which funds its war in Ukraine, is under constant attack. So what does this mean in practice? Will China press Iran into a war-ending deal that lifts the blockade? Will Trump again ease sanctions so Russia can sell more oil? Will he punish Ukraine for defending itself by striking Russian refineries? And how does OPEC feel about all this?
"They reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows."
Some flows are more stable than others. The U.S. and Iran both maintain blockades around the Strait of Hormuz, once the conduit for a fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas. On October 26, a U.N. commission of inquiry concluded that Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s energy grid, which have cut power and heat to millions through freezing winters, amounted to war crimes and crimes against humanity. Less than a month later, Russia put its name to this. Go figure.
"The three heads of state recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance…"
"Paramount" will come as news to Nicolás Maduro, erstwhile ally of China and Russia. U.S. forces captured him in a raid on Caracas on January 3 and spirited him to New York, where he is asking a federal judge to throw out the charges on grounds of head-of-state immunity. Washington says it stopped recognizing him as Venezuela’s legitimate president in 2019. But a principle that applies only to leaders you recognize is not paramount. It is conditional. Did Trump really agree to this?
"…and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction."
None of the three countries belongs to the court, but one of the leaders is wanted by it: the ICC issued a warrant for Putin in March 2023 over the unlawful abduction of Ukrainian children. Before the meeting, Trump said the court "has gotten out of control." All three leaders may fear the ICC and "similar bodies" will "abuse their jurisdiction." But many people fear those three leaders will abuse their power, which is precisely why institutions like the ICC are needed.
"The three heads of state reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought."
"Reaffirmed" is the right word for a sentence with a long, long résumé. Reagan and Gorbachev signed it in Geneva in 1985. The leaders of the five permanent Security Council members repeated it on January 3, 2022. Fifty-two days later, Russia invaded Ukraine and began hinting at nuclear use. In Shenzhen, Xi called for nuclear weapons to be banned and eliminated, as he has before, even as China’s arsenal has grown to more than 600 warheads. Trump last year ordered the Pentagon to resume nuclear testing "on an equal basis" with China and Russia, and a senior State Department official has not ruled out the first full-scale U.S. underground test since 1992. Three leaders who agree nuclear war is futile and verboten all seem to be pushing the world closer to it.
"The three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons."
A dialogue is not a negotiation, or a commitment to anything but jaw-jaw, and this one has no date, venue, or agenda. In 1987, Reagan and Gorbachev welcomed an agreement to set up Nuclear Risk Reduction Centers in both capitals. In 2026, the risk-reduction offer is a conversation. China has little reason to accept limits while its arsenal is a fraction of the more than 5,000 warheads each held by the U.S. and Russia, and Trump conceded in Shenzhen that giving up nukes is "not an easy thing to do." On proliferation, Trump told the room the U.S. would not let Iran acquire a nuclear weapon, and it went to war with Iran in February for that very reason. Yet China and Russia have used trade and more to support Tehran during that war. Sometimes, it takes more than talk to stop nuclear proliferation.

SHENZHEN, China — Three leaders who view their nations as the world's superpowers sat around a table together for the first time on Thursday to talk about reducing nuclear risks and resolving conflicts — a step they applauded as historic though they did not agree to any major breakthroughs.
U.S. President Donald Trump, China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin offered smiles and friendly handshakes, ending their talks at a villa in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen by agreeing on points including U.N. reforms and a vow to get more fuel to the market. It remains to be seen if the gathering could mark a pivot in world history — or become a quickly forgotten photo op.
The leaders made only brief remarks at the beginning and didn't take questions afterward, releasing a short statement that did not mention the wars in Ukraine or Iran, two issues that Trump said he raised with the leaders in separate one-on-ones earlier in the day.
The agreements were modest, but the rhetoric was not.
"We are really making history," Trump said. "The United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk of those weapons being used."
Xi earlier said the meeting would focus on "promoting world peace." Putin, for his part, said the countries "hold joint responsibility for maintaining international peace."
After the meeting, Xi called it positive, constructive and fruitful, while Putin described the talks as open and candid.
The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New START, expired in February, and Trump has said he wants "a new, improved and modernized" deal that includes China. But China has less motivation to accept limits given that its arsenal of more than 600 warheads is far smaller than the more than 5,000 warheads believed to be in each of the U.S. and Russian stockpiles.
Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, said the meeting could at best start a process that would eventually lead to a sustained set of talks for reducing nuclear arsenals.
"We need more than diplomatic theater and photo opportunities between Xi, Putin and Trump," Kimball said. "And one meeting will not likely produce dramatic breakthroughs."
The U.S. president earlier had a separate one-on-one with Xi, their third substantial meeting this year.
Trump said they had a shared interest in having oil shipped through the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil shipments from the Middle East that was repeatedly shut because of attacks in the Iran war. Trump suggested he would push Xi to buy more agricultural products from America.
Xi said that relations between the U.S. and China have been "generally stable and improved" during Trump's presidency. The official Chinese news agency Xinhua reported that Xi discussed Taiwan with Trump and said the two countries needed to improve communication on economic and trade issues.
Trump also added a separate sit-down with Putin, marking the first time the leaders have met for talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal on Russia's war in Ukraine.
"Wonderful things can come out of this — or at least start," Trump said, calling Putin "my friend."
Trump has frequently boasted of his rapport with Putin, as relations between the U.S. and Ukraine appear to have cratered recently. Trump rejected new Russia sanctions, while Kyiv was undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war.
The U.S. president also added that the trio would talk about ways to "protect our nation's sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court."
In their joint statement, the three countries took aim at the court, saying state officials should enjoy immunity from its prosecutions and warning that it should not abuse its jurisdiction. Putin is wanted by the court, and Trump's administration has imposed sanctions on ICC officials and the institution itself as part of a campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the United States and its allies, including Israel.
The U.S. president's ambitions recall an era of great power politics when wealthier countries felt entitled to decide the fate of seemingly lesser nations. Trump is negotiating with China and Russia without the involvement of Ukraine — or allies like Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Japan and South Korea that also have stakes in the outcome of any talks.
Trump has long believed his ability to create personal connections gives him a diplomatic edge. Xi made a symbolic gesture of friendship Wednesday by taking the unusual step of greeting Air Force One on the tarmac, and the two leaders turned their handshake into a one-armed hug.
But for all the compliments the U.S. president has showered on the two autocrats, the warmth has not always been mutual — and Trump does not always appear to have the same deep relationship based on common interests that Xi and Putin share.
On Wednesday at APEC, Xi greeted Putin by calling him "my old friend." The Russian leader responded by declaring Xi to be his "dear friend." China has helped economically support Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, providing Putin with a financial lifeline after the U.S. and its allies imposed new sanctions.
By contrast, when Xi came to the White House for a state visit in September, he was far more restrained with Trump, saying they had built a "personal rapport and stayed in touch." Trump and Xi have one more meeting planned this year, at the G20 summit in Florida in December.
There were also signs of friction Thursday in the U.S.-China relationship despite Trump's praise of Xi.
Chinese officials blocked a Bloomberg reporter, Annmarie Hordern, from the trilateral meeting after she asked a question at the earlier Trump-Xi session.

The ICC previously issued an arrest warrant against Putin and Russian official Maria Lvova-Belova in 2023 over alleged war crimes in the Russia-Ukraine war.
The three leaders held a more than 80-minute meeting in Shenzhen, China, the summit’s host city. Trump called the ICC a “rogue globalist organization” that has “gotten out of control” during his remarks.

Key Takeaways:

- The pledge could affect tight fuel markets because the U.S. and Russia are major oil producers while China is the largest crude importer.
- The joint statement provided no details on implementation, while production constraints in the U.S., Russia and China could complicate efforts to increase fuel supplies.
The leaders of the U.S., China and Russia agreed to boost the supply of fuels in a world that has seen prices surge as a result of wars being waged by two of the three military superpowers.
President Xi Jinping hosted what he called a “groundbreaking” discussion with Presidents Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin Nov. 19 in Shenzhen, China. The discussion spanned issues from Ukraine and denuclearization to the management of major-power disputes.
The unprecedented trilateral meeting had alarmed world capitals and raised concerns about carving up spheres of influence by the three military giants. For their part, the trio agreed in a joint statement to reform the United Nations, curtail the International Criminal Court and avoid nuclear war.
They also “plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations” and reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows. The statement didn’t spell out what that would entail.
Oil and diesel prices lost ground in morning trading in London. Brent, which initially was little changed after the news, slipped to as low as $91.21. Diesel’s premium over crude, a key measure of market strength, slipped as low as $57.61 a barrel, down from as high as $61 earlier in the session.
‘Making History’
Xi warned at the start of the meeting that major-power rivalry breeds global instability and called for regular exchanges between China, Russia and the US. The meeting, held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, lasted roughly an hour and a half.
Putin, Xi and Trump talk at the Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19. (Mark Schiefelbein/AP)
At the start of the gathering, Trump said, “We are really making history.” He added that the three have a special responsibility to maintain open dialogue, and said they would discuss issues including nuclear weapons and the Ukraine war.
“No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech,” Trump said. “Together, we are choosing a different course.”
Putin highlighted that the trio all represent victorious nations of World War II, and bear the task of preserving and strengthening the system of international law established at that time. The International Criminal Court issued an arrest order for Russia’s leader in 2023.
Energy and food
The Russian president said the group should also should discuss food and energy security. Costs of both agriculture and energy products have soared in recent years thanks to the disruptions in trade caused by the war in Ukraine and Trump’s February 2026 attacks on Iran.

The impact of the three-way agreement to boost refined products at one level is meaningful, given that it comes from two of the world’s largest oil producers — the U.S. and Russia — and the world’s biggest crude importer: China. But what exactly the three can do isn’t immediately clear.
In the U.S., crude oil processing rates are the highest for the time of year in three decades. Russia can produce much more fuel, but that will require Ukraine to stop attacking its refineries. Meantime, China’s crude oil imports remain far below pre-war levels. To boost fuel supplies, Beijing would likely need to start buying more crude.
Much of the world has been skeptical about the idea of the heads of the three nations being able to reduce international risks. Concerns about the optics of the meeting were all the more acute in western capitals, where Putin is widely regarded as a pariah due to Russia’s war on Ukraine, and many object to his being feted on such a global stage.
‘My friend’
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that U.S. negotiators will debrief allies meeting in Berlin on the outcome of the talks in China.
Trump, who regularly refers to his warm personal relations with foreign leaders as driving policy outcomes, shrugged off any such concerns earlier Nov. 19, telling Fox News that he was meeting with Xi and Putin at the same time “because they work together, have a relationship.” He referred to the warm greeting he received from Xi on Nov. 18, describing their relationship as “great,” and later called Putin “my friend.”
“It’s an honor to be with Vladimir,” Trump said at the start of the trilateral.
Both Xi and Trump raised the issue of reducing nuclear risks, though Putin avoided the topic in his remarks. The Kremlin has been resorting to nuclear saber-rattling recently among setbacks on the battlefield in Ukraine.
China’s official Xinhua News Agency said the host leader’s talking points in the meeting included a call for establishing a world free of nuclear weapons.
Nuclear risk
Trump said of such weapons that “it’s very hard to give them up as a leader of a country.” Even so, the three leaders are “uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used,” he said.
The U.S. and Russia together have some 86% of the world’s nuclear weapons, with China a distant third but its numbers rising, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, SIPRI. That’s left Beijing with little incentive to engage in reduction.
Xi’s talking points included a recommendation that the three countries maintain regular high-level exchanges, and ensure smooth dialogue channels at all levels. The three nations should act cautiously and avoid crossing the other sides’ red lines. In his opening remarks, Xi called the gathering “of groundbreaking significance.”
The inclusion of language on the ICC in the joint statement follows regular blasts of that body by the Trump administration. The ICC, of which the U.S. isn’t a member, has issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, a longtime Trump ally, based on his war in Gaza.
Yalta comparison
While the trilateral encounter has drawn parallels with Yalta in 1945, when the heads of the three dominant military powers of the day — the U.S., U.K. and Soviet Union — met to discuss the end of World War II and the post-war future, expectations of concrete results have been low.

Today’s Russia is very much the junior partner, with an economy less than one-seventh China’s size and an even smaller fraction of America’s.
Nevertheless, Putin appeared emboldened by his inclusion in the various meetings in Shenzhen. He used a speech to APEC business leaders on Nov. 18 to rail against “failed attempts” to isolate Russia and claiming that his nation was emerging stronger.
Putin left his bilateral meeting with Trump in “excellent spirits,” Russia’s state-run Tass news service said, citing Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov.
The trilateral has been called historic and unprecedented and “it really is,” Dennis Wilder, an ex-CIA official who is now a senior fellow at Georgetown University, told Bloomberg TV. “In terms of outcomes, the meeting really is the message.”

The three world leaders also stated that they wanted to reform the United Nations to protect diplomatic immunity and boost the supply and production of refined petroleum products.
“The three heads of state engaged in an in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation and committed themselves to upholding strategic stability and international security,” AFP quoted the statement as saying.

sources.news_title: Trump, Xi, Putin issue ‘peace declaration’ after meeting at Apec summit
sources.text:
Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US and Russian counterparts, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin agreed on a “peace declaration” at their unprecedented three-way meeting on Thursday, in which they reaffirmed that a nuclear war should never be fought, China and Russia said.
The declaration capped Trump’s three-day diplomatic swing through Asia that produced few tangible victories, despite his repeated boasts about making history and brokering peace.
Instead, the trip raised fresh questions among US allies about his increasingly close relationship with Putin, who continues to wage war with Ukraine.
In the declaration, the three leaders also pledged to advance reforms of the United Nations, to increase supplies of refined petroleum products for all countries and to uphold the immunity enjoyed by state officials in international courts.
The International Criminal Court in The Hague has issued arrest warrants for Putin and five other Russian officials.
Putin and Russia’s children’s commissioner, Maria Lvova-Belova, are accused of the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children, while the other warrants relate to alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Moscow rejects the allegations.
“The pushback against international norms and courts is the most interesting aspect. The big powers dictate; the small powers suffer,” said Jonathan Eyal, international director at the RUSI think-tank in London.
Eyal added that Putin “gained credibility and escape from pariah status”, while Trump “gained a photo opportunity he didn’t need”.
The document was released by Chinese state news agency Xinhua and by the Kremlin. Trump departed on his flight back to the US without making any comment after the meeting.
Earlier, the leaders of the world’s biggest nuclear powers, sitting at a round table in a villa nestled among wooded hills beside a lake in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, described their meeting as historic.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting before journalists were sent away. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Differences over Ukraine, Iran and trade
Putin, fresh from a setback in his war against Ukraine after the crippling of a key bridge linking Crimea to Russia, said the three countries had “numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine”.
The meeting was a diplomatic coup for Putin, with Russia’s economy barely a 10th the size of China’s and most of its businesses barred from trading with the West by sanctions.
The meeting ended a few hours before Ukraine and the leaders of its main European allies were due to meet Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Berlin.
Unlike Trump and Putin, Xi did not make a direct reference to Ukraine, but said: “History tells us that when major powers live in harmony, the world is at peace. When major powers clash, the world falls into turmoil”.
The three countries have deep differences over Ukraine, Iran, nuclear weapons and trade, casting doubts about a durable outcome. Their meeting on the sidelines of an Asia-Pacific summit has unnerved smaller countries that fear their interests might be disregarded.
The Kylin Villa, where they met, has a long history of sensitive diplomatic encounters. Its past visitors include former North Korean leader Kim Jong-il, Xi’s father Xi Zhongxun, and envoys of the Dalai Lama.
Before the trilateral, Trump met Xi and Putin separately, referring to both as friends.
Fanfare and pageantry
Speaking to Fox News earlier, Trump highlighted the pomp surrounding his arrival for the summit, which contrasted with the more muted greeting of other leaders, including Putin. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi landed without any welcoming ceremony.
Japan’s relations with China have soured since Takaichi’s remarks in 2025, when she said Japan could deploy its military if a Chinese move on Taiwan also threatened its territory.
Takaichi, who cut an isolated figure throughout the summit, said Tokyo’s position on Taiwan had not changed since 1972.
On Taiwan, Xi told Trump the US must “do the right thing” to avoid major setbacks in their relationship.
Xi greeted Trump at the airport, the first time he has done so with any visiting leader since becoming president, reciprocating his counterpart’s gesture at Joint Base Andrews in September, when they last met. The leaders also briefly hugged.
“This is a great president, one of the great presidents of China, and he’s never gone to the airport to meet somebody,” Trump said, calling that a “win” for both China and the US.
“And not only that, the fanfare, the beauty, the pageantry, the thousands of people, the young children, the soldiers, the whole thing.”
Tough nuclear arms discussion
Trump had insisted nuclear arms control be a central topic of the summit, despite China’s repeated objections in the past to joining talks with Washington and Moscow, which have far larger nuclear arsenals.
“It’s not an easy thing to do — give them up,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of their meeting.
Trump and Xi met after an extension of their trade truce this month, but also amid growing tension over reports of Nvidia chips being diverted to China through Southeast Asia, raising questions about the effectiveness of US export curbs and the future of Chinese access to advanced technology.

sources.news_title: Trump Slams “Old School” Diplomacy and Tells Xi and Putin the World Only Needs About Ten Nukes Each
sources.text:
President Trump just spent eighty minutes in a room in Shenzhen with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin and told them the quiet part out loud. The old way of American diplomacy never solved anything because it refused to talk about the hard problems. Then he floated the idea that the three biggest nuclear powers on earth each only need about ten bombs.
That is not the language of Foggy Bottom. It is the language of a man who has already watched New START expire and watched China race to catch up while the State Department issued press releases. The New York Post reported the first-ever trilateral summit between the leaders of the United States, Russia, and China.
It started two hours late, included ten minutes of cameras, and produced a four-point joint declaration from Beijing and Moscow that the White House has not yet fully owned. The declaration calls for more dialogue on nuclear risks, unspecified United Nations reforms, more oil production, and condemnation of the International Criminal Court that has indicted Putin.
Trump’s own words in the room were sharper. “No problems were ever solved under the old school refusing to talk about them,” he said. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech.” He framed the meeting as a chance for the three largest nuclear powers “to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used.” Later, on Fox News, he got specific.
The United States has about 4,000. Russia has about 3,800. China has 400 or 500 and is “going hot and heavy.” Then the line that will either age well or become a cautionary tale: you only need about ten.
As the world’s three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth.
Xi agreed in principle that nuclear weapons “should be comprehensively banned and thoroughly destroyed.” Putin called the three men guardians of world peace and said their peoples can strengthen security if they “cooperate constructively.”
Both of those statements are easy to make when your country is still building. China’s stockpile is smaller on paper, which is exactly why Beijing has spent years refusing to join the kind of verifiable cuts Washington and Moscow have already done. An administration official called the nuclear conversation a preliminary step, not a deal. That is the honest reading.
Scripture is clear that the desire for peace is not the same as the achievement of it. “If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.”
That verse from Romans does not require pretending an adversary has stopped expanding its arsenal or stopped exporting the fentanyl that has killed roughly half a million Americans during Xi’s time in power. Trump and Xi also discussed trade and that fentanyl flow. Separate meetings happened earlier. Trump offered his hand. Xi took the forearm on the escalator after a tarmac hug. Putin got a joke about “Who is he?” followed by “He’s my friend.” Optics matter less than whether the warheads actually come down.
The rest of the agenda was equally large and equally unfinished. Trump raised ending the wars in Iran and Ukraine and working against “rogue globalist organizations” such as the ICC in the name of national sovereignty. China and Russia’s declaration hits the ICC and calls for more oil. Those are not the same as a ceasefire or a verifiable nuclear reduction.
Meanwhile Chinese officials barred a Bloomberg reporter from the trilateral after she shouted a question at Trump about the ousted Nvidia CEO and an alleged Chinese spy. The White House tried to reverse it. Beijing called her conduct “extremely rude.” That is the same country talking about open dialogue on nuclear weapons.
None of this means the meeting was worthless. The old school Trump dismissed really did treat engagement with adversaries as a moral concession rather than a tool. Talking is not surrendering. But neither is a photo opportunity a treaty.
The power of these weapons is, as Trump put it, “unbelievable, unthinkable.” That is why the United States has maintained a large arsenal for decades and why any serious reduction requires inspections, verification, and a Chinese stockpile that stops growing first. Until those pieces exist, “about ten” remains a provocative goal, not a plan.
The three leaders left Shenzhen with a joint statement drafted by two of them and a president who has spent years arguing that strength and directness beat process for its own sake. History will judge whether the bombs actually get smaller or whether the conversation simply continues while the numbers go the other direction.
For now the record shows Trump said the quiet part, put the largest nuclear powers in the same room, and refused to pretend the old diplomatic habits had worked. That is more than most summits deliver. It is still not a finished deal.
Two Storms, One Harvest
Every food crisis in living memory has been a one-shock event. The 2008 price spike was a commodity bubble. The 2020 shortages were a logistics failure. The 2022 grain scare was a war on one exporter’s ports. Each time, the system bent, adjusted, and recovered, and each time the experts assured us afterward that global markets are simply too big and too diversified to fail.
What nobody in Washington seems eager to discuss is that 2026 is shaping up to be something the modern food system has never actually faced. Two independent shocks, one climatic and one geopolitical, are converging on the same harvest cycle at the same time. Not sequentially. Simultaneously.
Start with the weather. The Pacific Ocean is currently building toward what forecasters now openly call a record event. NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center puts the odds of at least a strong El Niño near 88 percent, with roughly two in three odds it reaches “very strong” status, the tier reserved for perhaps three or four events in the entire satellite era. Every major global model now projects a median peak in Super El Niño territory, and most of them project it exceeding the 2015-16 event, which until now held the modern record. Sea surface anomalies were already brushing the super threshold in mid-July, months before these events normally peak. The atmosphere has already shifted into El Niño mode, and the event is forecast to crest in late fall and early winter.
This is not about “climate change.” It’s about the standard cycles of weather, and the cycle we’re currently in is one that has likely devastated societies in the past. We’re better prepared as a society today, but not all Americans are equally prepared.
Serious households have started doing the quiet math on their own. Grocery bills tell part of the story, and the forecast maps tell the rest, which is why long-term food storage has moved from fringe hobby to mainstream line item in the family budget, with established suppliers like Heaven’s Harvest seeing demand from people who five years ago would have rolled their eyes at the idea. That instinct is not paranoia. It is pattern recognition, and the pattern is worth walking through carefully.

The Fertilizer Clock Is Already Running
While the Pacific warms, the second shock has been unfolding in the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict with Iran turned the world’s most important energy chokepoint into a contested waterway, and the consequences reach far beyond the gas pump. Roughly a third of global fertilizer trade moves through Hormuz, and the disruption sent urea prices up 86 percent year over year by March, with a 53 percent jump in a single month.
The World Bank projects energy prices rising about 24 percent in 2026 and fertilizer about 31 percent. By its own accounting, fertilizer prices ran 35 percent higher in the first five months of this year than the same period last year.
Here is the mechanism the nightly news will not explain. Fertilizer is not a grocery item. It is a time-delayed input. The nitrogen a farmer in Iowa or Punjab could not afford to apply this spring does not show up as a problem this spring. It shows up as a thinner harvest six to twelve months later.
The World Bank’s own food security brief concedes that the effects of reduced applications earlier this season “are likely to become visible only later in harvest outcomes.” Translate that from institutional language into plain English and it means this. The damage is already done, it is already in the ground, and we are simply waiting for it to arrive on the shelf.
Now check the calendar. Six to twelve months from the spring planting season lands us squarely in late 2026 and early 2027. Which is precisely when the strongest El Niño in the instrumental record is forecast to peak, bringing its signature droughts to Southeast Asia, Australia, southern Africa, northern Brazil, and South Asia, the very regions that grow the world’s rice, sugar, and oilseeds.
The World Bank warns openly that a strong El Niño “could disrupt multiple crop belts simultaneously” on top of the conflict-driven input costs. Their baseline projection assumes the Middle East disruptions ease by autumn. What in the last two years of Middle East history suggests that assumption is safe?
The System Has No Slack Left
The comfortable answer is that global markets always adjust. But adjustment requires slack, and the slack is gone. Global cereal production is expected to decline from last year’s records even before El Niño does its work. The UN World Food Programme, hardly a den of right-wing preppers, is calling this the most significant disruption to its supply chains since Covid and the invasion of Ukraine, and its supply chain director put the stakes bluntly.
Today’s supply chain challenges are tomorrow’s hunger crisis.
There is also a political dimension that markets cannot price. When food gets scarce, governments do not behave like economists. They behave like politicians. Export bans, hoarding mandates, and panic buying at the national level turned the modest rice shortfall of 2008 into a global crisis, and analysts are already warning that import-dependent nations are the first dominoes.
The 2015-16 Super El Niño, a far weaker event than what is now forecast, threw tens of millions into food stress across Africa and Asia. This one is projected to be stronger, and it arrives with fertilizer already rationed by price and shipping lanes already contested by missiles.
What Joseph Knew
Scripture does not treat preparation for lean years as faithlessness. It treats it as wisdom delivered in advance to those willing to act on it.
Behold, there come seven years of great plenty throughout all the land of Egypt: And there shall arise after them seven years of famine; and all the plenty shall be forgotten in the land of Egypt.
Joseph did not respond to that warning with a hashtag or a committee. He stored grain during the years of abundance, and when the famine came, Egypt stood while its neighbors begged. The lesson is not that famine is certain. It is that the time to prepare is precisely when preparation still looks optional.
Nobody who filled a pantry in a year of plenty has ever regretted it, and nobody standing in an empty aisle has ever been glad he waited for certainty.
None of this calls for panic, and panic is the enemy of sound judgment anyway. It calls for the same unglamorous prudence our grandparents considered ordinary. Keep some cash margin, know your local growers, and put real food in deep storage while it is cheap and available, because the entire arc of this story is that cheap and available is a closing window.

sources.news_title: Trump, Xi, Putin Declare Peace, Skip Ukraine and Iran
sources.text:
The leaders of the United States, China and Russia met together for the first time on Thursday, holding about 90 minutes of talks at Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit and emerging with a four-point declaration, published first by Chinese state media and the Kremlin, that says a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. The document commits President Donald Trump, President Xi Jinping and President Vladimir Putin to United Nations reform, to higher production and supply of refined petroleum products, to dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation, and to respect for the immunity of state officials. It says nothing about the two wars Trump had said he would raise, in Ukraine and Iran, and it sets no numbers on warheads, fuel volumes or deadlines. The talks were reportedly held without aides in the room, and Trump left Shenzhen afterward.
The leaders spoke briefly before reporters were sent out. Trump told his counterparts, "We are really making history," and said earlier American presidents had avoided talking to nations they disagreed with, a habit he said he was reversing. He said the three countries were uniquely positioned to cut the world's nuclear arsenals, acknowledged that persuading governments to give up their weapons is not easy, and pressed for arms control to be central to the day. He also told Xi and Putin that the United States would not allow Iran to obtain a nuclear weapon, and said he had already spoken at length with Putin about Ukraine. Xi called the meeting groundbreaking and said that when major powers live in harmony the world is at peace, and that when they clash it falls into turmoil, according to Chinese state media. He urged the three countries to keep encouraging the parties to conflicts to sit down and talk, but did not name Ukraine or Iran in the remarks that were released. Putin said the three countries share responsibility for international peace and could contribute significantly to global stability if they cooperate constructively as partners. Afterward Xi described the meeting as positive, constructive and fruitful, and Putin told reporters the discussion was open, free and useful, covering United Nations reform, security issues and nuclear nonproliferation. Footage captured Putin telling Xi that he did not think anyone had expected things to go so well.
The declaration, which Chinese state media called a peace declaration, is short and general. On the United Nations, the three governments commit to advancing reforms to more effectively address global challenges, without saying which reforms or by when. On energy, they say they plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all countries and reaffirm the importance of a stable flow of energy. On nuclear weapons, they agreed to hold dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation and committed themselves to upholding strategic stability and international security. Chinese and Russian accounts said the leaders also reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. Chinese state media said the three exchanged views on the Ukraine crisis, the prevention of nuclear proliferation, the situation in the Middle East and the Korean Peninsula, but the published text, as reported, names only nonproliferation among them. There are no warhead limits, no fuel volumes and no mechanism for follow-up talks beyond the word dialogue.
The fourth point is the one most likely to be read closely in capitals far from Shenzhen. It affirms the principle of state consent and respect for the immunity of state officials, and states that the International Criminal Court and similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction. Putin is the subject of an ICC arrest warrant tied to alleged war crimes linked to Ukraine, which Russia rejects. None of the three governments is a party to the court's founding treaty, and all three have accused it of overreach and bias, a charge the court denies. The wording does not name any case, and it does not say what practical steps, if any, the three countries would take to back it. Whether it is intended as a message to the court itself or to other governments weighing whether to enforce its warrants is something the text leaves open.
The energy pledge is the clause with the most direct link to the Iran war. Trump said earlier in the day, after meeting Xi, that the United States and China both have an interest in energy flowing through the Strait of Hormuz and that the two agree Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon. The declaration mentions neither Iran nor the strait, and it speaks of refined products such as fuel rather than crude oil, with no countries, volumes or dates attached. Shipping through the waterway remains contested on the water. Iran widened its attacks to Kuwait after a U.S. strike on Qeshm Island, saying its army targeted U.S.-used drone and missile installations at the Ali Al Salem air base, and its navy and army have announced mine strikes on tankers almost daily, claims that could not be independently verified. Trump said in a television interview this week that he does not need help from Xi or Putin on Iran and that the United States has total control of the strait. A pledge to raise refined-fuel output is not a plan for reopening a shipping lane, and none of the three leaders explained on Thursday how the two would be connected.
Earlier in the day Trump sat down with Putin for about 40 minutes, their first formal talks since the Alaska summit in August 2025. Trump greeted the Russian leader as his friend and told him that good outcomes could come from the meeting, or at least begin there. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said afterward that the war in Ukraine was the main subject, along with bilateral relations and preparations for the trilateral, that neither side made any particularly important statements, and that Putin left in an excellent mood. Moscow has ruled out a ceasefire while negotiations continue, and nothing reported from Shenzhen suggests that position has moved. Putin said after the trilateral that the three countries have numerous shared interests in settling regional conflicts, including the one in Ukraine, and accused Kyiv and European governments of not being ready for compromise. Alexander Dugin, a Russian nationalist commentator, said the summit shows who matters in the world.
Ukraine was not in the room, and its government said so. President Volodymyr Zelensky called Trump's one-on-one meeting with Putin a mistake and said that matters concerning Ukraine must be decided with Ukraine's participation. In an interview, he said Washington and Beijing together hold enough economic power to stop Putin in a single meeting if they chose to use it. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha urged both capitals to press Moscow to end the war and warned against any signal that great powers can divide countries into spheres of influence. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are due to meet Ukrainian and European officials in Berlin on Thursday, where German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is hosting a Coalition of the Willing summit, and Zelensky has said the envoys would brief Kyiv on the Shenzhen talks. As the leaders met, the war continued. Russian strikes hit Odesa's historic center three times on Wednesday, killing four people and wounding at least nine, and Ukrainian authorities reported a barrage of Onyx missiles and 98 drones overnight into Thursday. Ukraine struck the Crimean Bridge on Monday and again on Tuesday, when part of the road span fell into the sea, and attacked its rail section once more overnight into Thursday, the third attack in a week. The Russian-installed governor of Crimea said two people were killed in the region in Tuesday's attack.
The U.S.-China track ran in parallel and was calmer. Thursday was Trump's third meeting with Xi this year and the fourth of his second term, and it followed an unusual welcome on Wednesday, when Xi greeted him in person at the Shenzhen airport with an honor guard and a fighter-jet flyover. It was the first time Xi had personally greeted a visiting foreign leader at an airport since becoming president in 2013, according to reports. Trump opened the bilateral by saying the U.S.-China Board of Trade, which the two sides agreed to form at their Beijing summit in May, had brought greater balance to a lopsided relationship and that the tariffs had been divided fairly. He called Xi his friend and said that as long as the two of them are in charge, the countries will never have a problem. In the Chinese readout, Xi called ties stable and trending positively, urged more cooperation on trade, drug trafficking, immigration and online fraud, and asked for closer coordination on artificial intelligence safety, saying AI should remain under human control.
The Chinese readout also carried the meeting's sharpest line. Xi urged the United States to do the right thing to avoid major setbacks in the relationship, a reference to Taiwan, and according to the Chinese account, Trump told him that the United States does not support Taiwan independence. That wording comes from the Chinese side. The readout did not mention any extension of the trade truce, which is set to expire on Jan. 10, 2027, and the semiconductor curbs and rare-earth exports at the center of that truce remain unresolved. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said some deliverables have not been perfect on the Chinese side.
Around the edges of the meetings, the region's other capitals watched for signals. Taiwan's defense ministry said two Russian Tu-95 bombers flew east of the island on Thursday after approaching from the south, then exited to the northeast. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, on her first visit to China since her remarks on Taiwan angered Beijing a year ago, met Putin on Wednesday, according to Tokyo, but had not held a formal meeting with Xi by Thursday afternoon. She said she wants a constructive and stable relationship with China and that Japan's position on Taiwan has not changed. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese were among the other leaders at the APEC gathering. Chinese state media said the three leaders discussed the Korean Peninsula, but no account of what was said on that subject was released.
Arms control was the item Trump put first, and it is where the distance between ambition and text is widest. The New START treaty, which capped U.S. and Russian strategic arsenals, lapsed in February, and Trump has promoted a three-way arrangement that would bring China in. The declaration offers only dialogue. China has repeatedly objected to joining talks at the U.S.-Russia level, since its arsenal is far smaller than either country's, and analysts say that disparity complicates any three-way deal. According to Chinese state media, Xi called nuclear weapons the sword of Damocles hanging over humanity, and Russian-language reports said he called for them to be banned and destroyed entirely, a position far from anything in the published text. Trump said it is not an easy thing to give up nuclear weapons, but that it is vital for the three countries to work together against their spread to other nations, and he named Iran. The result is a shared sentence about nuclear war with no mechanism attached.
The format drew immediate comparisons to the 1945 Yalta Conference, a framing that was especially common in Russia and Ukraine. Analysts were divided on how much the meeting mattered. Henry Huiyao Wang, a former senior adviser to the Chinese government who heads the Center for China and Globalization in Beijing, said the summit is more than symbolic and that face-to-face dialogue of this kind can help calm many of the world's conflicts. Others noted that the three governments remain deeply divided over Ukraine, Iran, nuclear weapons and trade, which makes a durable outcome hard to imagine, and that smaller countries have been unnerved by the prospect of their interests being set aside by larger ones.
What each capital took from the day is easier to list than what the three agreed. For Beijing, the staging was much of the point. It hosted both leaders, set the format, and published the first account of the declaration, framing the meeting as a peace initiative. China says it is neutral on Ukraine and wants to be a potential peace broker. For Moscow, being seated as an equal beside Trump and Xi, and securing language on the immunity of state officials, carries value apart from any movement on the battlefield or at the negotiating table. For Washington, the gains are a shared sentence on nuclear risk, Trump's account of a common interest with Xi in keeping Hormuz open, and a trade relationship that Trump described as balanced, even as the questions on chips, rare earths and export controls stay open ahead of the truce deadline.
The trilateral was one part of a crowded APEC program. Xi opened the leaders' meeting by calling for lower barriers to trade and investment, pledged lower tariffs and wider market access for foreign manufacturers, and cast China as a defender of free trade. Trump told the gathering that he opposes globalist regulation of any form. A separate APEC leaders' document, called the Shenzhen Outlook, was limited to pledges on trade, technology innovation and economic growth, including a commitment to respect intellectual property rights in digital and emerging technologies and to cooperate on cross-border data flows and data protection. Before arriving in Shenzhen, Trump had attended the ASEAN summit in the Philippines, met President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and held talks with the Quad in Manila, where he announced critical-minerals agreements with India, Australia and Japan. Chinese officials barred a U.S. reporter from covering the trilateral after she shouted a question during the Trump-Xi bilateral. The White House said it had pushed for her inclusion, and Chinese officials said shouting questions is considered rude.
The calendar, rather than the declaration, sets the next tests. The Berlin talks among U.S. envoys, Ukrainian officials and European leaders are the first to follow Shenzhen. The U.S.-China trade truce expires on Jan. 10, 2027, with chip curbs and rare-earth exports still unsettled. And Washington has invited Putin to the Group of 20 summit in Miami in December, an invitation the Kremlin has confirmed receiving.

Trump-Xi summit brings no breakthrough on Iran. Here’s why
Beijing has reasons to help de-escalate the conflict, but its ability to deliver Tehran is limited, and its cooperation with Washington is unlikely to come without conditions.
You're reading an excerpt from Al-Monitor China-Middle East, where we analyze China's deepening engagement with the region. To get this newsletter in your inbox weekly, sign up here.
WASHINGTON — Another trip to China, another round of expectations that Chinese President Xi Jinping can help President Donald Trump find an exit from the Iran war. Their third substantial meeting since the start of the war began with hopes for a breakthrough, but once again, none emerged.
Beijing has reasons to help de-escalate the conflict, but its ability to deliver Tehran is limited, and its cooperation with Washington is unlikely to come without conditions.
Let’s unpack,
Joyce (sign up on LinkedIn or online here)
Leading this week
Ahead of the talks in Shenzhen, Trump told Fox News that Washington did not need Chinese or Russian assistance to end the Iran war.
“We don’t need any help,” Trump said in Shenzhen. “We’ve defeated their navy, we’ve defeated their air force, we’ve defeated their anti-aircraft.”
China could help through economic incentives, diplomatic pressure or guarantees supporting an agreement, but Beijing, for now, is in no rush. Four incentives are driving it to stay largely on the sidelines.
1. High price for the US
The 10-month-old conflict with Iran continues to tie down US forces that could otherwise be deployed elsewhere, in particular to contain Chinese expansion in Asia. The arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt in the Middle East on Sunday, as Jared Szuba reports, briefly brought the number of US aircraft carriers in the region to three before the USS George Washington departed soon thereafter.
The Congressional Budget Office estimated that operations for the Iran war had cost the Pentagon approximately $38 billion through Aug. 1, including replacement munitions, equipment losses and additional operating expenses.
The United States' energy cushion is also under strain. As of Nov. 13, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve had fallen to 276.4 million barrels, down from 415.4 million barrels before the war.
2. Chinese limitations
China’s economic relationship with Iran gives it leverage, but not control, over Tehran’s decision-making. Iran’s new leaders are more hardline than their predecessors and are pursuing changes to the country's nuclear doctrine, with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in the driver’s seat on regional military strategy.
Beijing also cannot deliver relief from US sanctions or guarantee a smaller US military footprint in the Gulf, both key demands by Iran.
3. Regional deals easier
China may have greater success supporting regional security arrangements than brokering a comprehensive US-Iranian settlement. Its role in the 2023 Saudi-Iranian rapprochement offers a model.
Beijing's side deals with the Houthis and its recent diplomatic engagement with Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia could pave the way for narrower understandings protecting Gulf territory, energy infrastructure and shipping. Any such arrangements would serve Chinese interests without requiring Beijing to assume responsibility for enforcing peace.
4. Cooperation with concessions
Beijing could view assistance on Iran as leverage in negotiations with the United States over tariffs, technology and Taiwan.
These issues, however, are part of a broader strategic relationship. Given the Republican Party's midterm election losses, Trump is even less likely to make major concessions and will face greater congressional oversight.
What comes next
With no deal in sight, the current state of “no war, no peace,” as Iran’s parliament speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf put it, is likely to persist. An escalation in the form of renewed US-Israeli strikes remains possible, but it would only further entrench the current stalemate.

sources.news_title: Trump Opens First-Ever Three-Way Talks With Xi and Putin: 'We Are Really Making History'
sources.text:
Trump, Xi and Putin Issue Joint ‘Declaration Toward Peace’ After Historic Three-Way Talks
UPDATE: President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin issued a four-point “U.S.-Russia-China Heads of State Declaration toward Peace” on Thursday after their first formal three-way meeting, according to a White House statement. Russia and China released matching texts.
The leaders met for about 90 minutes at a lakeside villa in Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, the BBC reported.
The declaration says the three countries, as permanent members of the U.N. Security Council, are “committed to reform the UN so that the UN can respond more effectively to global challenges.” It also says they “plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations” and reaffirmed “the importance of stable energy flows.”
On international courts, the three said the principle of state consent and “respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance,” and that the International Criminal Court and “other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction.” The court issued an arrest warrant for Putin in 2023. Neither the United States nor China is a member.
They also reaffirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought” and said they “will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.” The declaration does not set out a framework for cutting nuclear arsenals, the Guardian reported, and it does not mention the wars in Ukraine or Iran.
After the meeting, Putin called it an “important chapter in the history of diplomacy” and said Ukraine and Europe were not yet ready to make the compromises needed to end the war, the BBC reported. China’s official broadcaster CCTV quoted Xi describing the talks as “positive, constructive, and highly productive.”
President Trump sat down with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday for the first formal meeting ever held among the three leaders.
“We are really making history,” Trump said in opening remarks around a large round table at a lakeside villa, Reuters reported. “The three of us have a great deal to discuss.”
Trump said the United States, China and Russia are “uniquely positioned” to discuss reducing their nuclear stockpiles, but he added, “It’s not an easy thing to do, give them up,” CNA reported.
Putin said the three countries have “numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine.”
Xi, who Chinese state media said was presiding, did not mention Ukraine. “History tells us that when major powers live in harmony, the world is at peace. When major powers clash, the world falls into turmoil,” he said.
Xi also said nuclear weapons should be “comprehensively prohibited and completely destroyed” and that a nuclear war “cannot be won and must never be fought,” according to China’s official Xinhua news agency, CNA noted.
Trump told the two leaders that the International Criminal Court is “out of control,” the Guardian reported, citing Reuters. The court issued an arrest warrant for Putin in 2023 over the alleged deportation of Ukrainian children. Neither the United States nor China is a member.
‘I Wouldn’t Do That’
Before the meeting, Trump sought to ease fears in Kyiv and Europe that he would cut a deal over Ukraine’s head. Asked about it in a Fox News interview from Shenzhen, he said, “I wouldn’t do that,” Bloomberg reported.
He did not answer a follow-up question about whether he had spoken with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Hindustan Times reported. Zelenskyy said U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner would brief Ukraine’s allies on Thursday.
Trump also met one-on-one with Putin for roughly 35 to 40 minutes. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told Russia’s state news agency Tass that the talks covered Ukraine and bilateral relations and that Putin left in an “excellent” mood, according to the Guardian.
Trump and Xi held a separate meeting of just over an hour earlier in the day at the same villa. Trump called Xi a friend and said the two share a “special relationship.”
China’s official readout of that meeting quoted Trump as saying Washington “does not support Taiwan independence” and had Xi warning that the United States “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks,” the Guardian reported. The White House had not publicly confirmed that wording.
The last nuclear arms treaty between the United States and Russia, New Start, expired in February. Trump wants a new agreement that includes China, but Beijing has signaled it will not accept limits on its smaller arsenal.
Analysts have set low expectations for concrete breakthroughs, and the gathering has drawn comparisons to the 1945 Yalta Conference, CNA reported. Smaller nations in Europe and Asia have voiced fears that their interests could be ignored.
Xi greeted Trump on the tarmac when he arrived in China on Wednesday. The joint declaration was released later Thursday after the talks concluded.

sources.news_title: "World's Three Largest Nuclear Powers Have A Special Responsibility": Trump At Xi-Putin Summit
China and Russia say they and US agree on UN reforms, boosting fuel supplies and dialogue to reduce nuclear risks
sources.text:
SHENZHEN, China (AP) — For U.S. President Donald Trump, the meeting with the leaders of two other nuclear powers -- China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin -- was supposed to be a diplomatic triumph: It would serve as proof that Trump could negotiate with two of America’s toughest rivals.
Before the trio met Thursday in a villa in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, the U.S. president sought to flatter both Xi and Putin as his friends. They were to discuss the wars in Ukraine and Iran and how to reduce the dangers posed by nuclear arsenals.
But after roughly 70 minutes behind closed doors, they agreed to a far narrower agenda. They would like to reform the United Nations, refine more fossil fuels and curb the reach of the International Criminal Court.
What was billed as a historic trilateral meeting in the end looked like a fleeting photo op. Trump quickly left the villa and boarded Air Force One without saying a word to reporters about his time with Xi and Putin.
The agreements were modest, but the rhetoric that came at the start of the trilateral was not.
“We are really making history,” Trump said. “The United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk of those weapons being used."
Xi earlier said the meeting would focus on “promoting world peace.” Putin, for his part, said the countries “hold joint responsibility for maintaining international peace.”
After the meeting, Xi called it positive, constructive and fruitful, while Putin described the trilateral talks as open and candid, calling the format “useful and substantive.”
“It is a serious collaborative work,” he said in response to a question about whether the image of the meeting itself mattered more than the substance.
The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New START, expired in February, and Trump has said he wants “a new, improved and modernized” deal that includes China. But China has less motivation to accept limits given that its arsenal of more than 600 warheads is far smaller than the more than 5,000 warheads believed to be in each of the U.S. and Russian stockpiles.
Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, said the meeting could at best start a process that would eventually lead to a sustained set of talks for reducing nuclear arsenals.
“We need more than diplomatic theater and photo opportunities between Xi, Putin and Trump,” Kimball said. “And one meeting will not likely produce dramatic breakthroughs.”
The leaders also talked about Iran and trade
The U.S. president earlier had a separate one-on-one with Xi, their third substantial meeting this year.
Trump said they had a shared interest in having oil flow through the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil shipments from the Middle East that was repeatedly shut because of attacks in the Iran war. Trump suggested he would push Xi to buy more agricultural products from America.
Xi said that relations between the U.S. and China have been “generally stable and improved” during Trump's presidency. The official Chinese news agency Xinhua reported that Xi discussed Taiwan with Trump and said the two countries needed to improve communication on economic and trade issues.
Trump also added to his calendar a separate sit-down with Putin, marking the first time the leaders have met for talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal on Russia’s war in Ukraine.
“Wonderful things can come out of this — or at least start,” Trump said, calling Putin “my friend."
Trump has frequently boasted of his rapport with Putin, as relations between the U.S. and Ukraine appear to have cratered recently. Trump rejected new Russia sanctions, while Kyiv was undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war.
After their trilateral meeting, the three leaders took aim at the International Criminal Court for overstepping its jurisdiction, saying government officials should enjoy immunity from its prosecutions. Putin is wanted by the court, and Trump’s administration has imposed sanctions on ICC officials and the institution itself as part of a campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the United States and its allies, including Israel.
Trump boasts about his relationships, but the ties between Xi and Putin are stronger
The U.S. president's ambitions going into the meeting recalled an era of great power politics when wealthier countries felt entitled to decide the fate of seemingly lesser nations. Trump was negotiating with China and Russia without the involvement of Ukraine — or allies like Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Japan and South Korea that also have stakes in the outcome of any talks.
Trump has long believed his ability to create personal connections gives him a diplomatic edge. Xi made a symbolic gesture of friendship Wednesday by taking the unusual step of greeting Air Force One on the tarmac, and the two leaders turned their handshake into a one-armed hug.
But for all the compliments the U.S. president has showered on the two autocrats, he did not always appear to have the same deep relationship based on common interests that Xi and Putin share.
On Wednesday at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, Xi greeted Putin by calling him “my old friend.” The Russian leader responded by declaring Xi to be his “dear friend.” China has helped economically support Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, providing Putin with a financial lifeline after the U.S. and its allies imposed new sanctions.
By contrast, when Xi went to the White House for a state visit in September, he was far more restrained with Trump, saying they had built a "personal rapport and stayed in touch.” Trump and Xi have one more meeting planned this year, at the G20 summit in Florida in December.
There were also signs of friction Thursday in the U.S.-China relationship despite Trump’s praise of Xi.
Chinese officials blocked a Bloomberg reporter from the trilateral meeting after she asked a question at the earlier Trump-Xi session. And Chinese television showed a video of Trump appearing drowsy, while the White House posted a clip of Trump helping Xi up an escalator.
Associated Press writers Darlene Superville, Didi Tang and Will Weissert in Washington, Huizhong Wu in Bangkok and Kanis Leung in Hong Kong contributed to this report.
